detail.abstract: Research software has become a central vehicle for inquiry and learning in many Higher Degree Research (HDR) contexts, where solo researchers increasingly develop software-based artefacts as part of their research methodology. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence is reshaping development practice, offering powerful forms of assistance while introducing new challenges for accountability, reflection, and methodological rigour. Although Action Design Research (ADR) provides a well-established foundation for studying and constructing socio-technical artefacts, it offers limited guidance on how its principles can be operationalised in the day-today practice of solo, AI-assisted research software development. This paper proposes the SHAPR framework-Solo, Human-centred, AI-assisted PRactice-as a practice-level operational framework that complements ADR by translating its high-level principles into actionable guidance for contemporary research contexts. SHAPR supports the enactment of ADR Building-Intervention-Evaluation cycles by making explicit the roles, artefacts, reflective practices, and lightweight governance mechanisms required to sustain human accountability and learning in AI-assisted development. The contribution of the paper is conceptual: SHAPR itself is treated as the primary design artefact and unit of analysis and is evaluated formatively through reflective analysis of its internal coherence, alignment with ADR principles, and applicability to solo research practice. By explicitly linking research software development, Human-AI collaboration, and reflective learning, this study contributes to broader discussions on how SHAPR can support both knowledge production and HDR researcher training.

title: Trading Morality for Efficiency: Technology Implementation Triggers Unethical Business Decision Making
affiliations: Nanjing Agricultural University (NAU), Nanjing University, Nanjing University - School of Business and

detail.title: Trading Morality for Efficiency: Technology Implementation Triggers Unethical Business Decision Making
detail.abstract: Building on associative memory network theory, this research proposes that companies’ technology implementation increases the cognitive accessibility of the efficiency concept among executive decision-makers, prompting them to make business decisions that maximize company profit at the expense of ethical considerations. Across five experiments, we demonstrate that technology implementation increases unethical decision-making. Experiments 1 and 2 show that this effect is mediated by increased accessibility of efficiency. Experiment 3 rules out the influence of novelty as an alternative explanation. Experiment 4 shows that the effect diminishes when technology is not associated with efficiency, and Experiment 5 finds that the effect disappears when unethical decisions no longer lead to greater efficiency.

title: A Study on Digital Implementation through Robotic Process Automation (RPA) with Emphasis on Worker Satisfaction and Cost Reduction : An Indian Bank Case Study

detail.title: A Study on Digital Implementation through Robotic Process Automation (RPA) with Emphasis on Worker Satisfaction and Cost Reduction : An Indian Bank Case Study
detail.abstract:
This study examines the implementation and impact of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) within the service operations of an Indian bank, focusing on four key dimensions: operational cost reduction, employee satisfaction, implementation challenges, and sustainability of benefits.  As automation reshapes the financial services landscape, this research provides an evidence-based evaluation of RPA’s role in enhancing service efficiency and workforce dynamics.

A mixed-method research design was employed, integrating employee surveys, interviews, focus groups, and secondary data from organisational reports.  Quantitative analysis using T-tests, ANOVA, and regression models were used to assess the relationship between RPA adoption and changes in operational and human performance metrics.  Qualitative data was thematically analysed to uncover implementation barriers and enablers from a workforce perspective.

The findings demonstrate that RPA contributes meaningfully to cost and productivity improvements by streamlining repetitive tasks and reducing manual error rates.  Employees reported enhanced satisfaction and reduced work stress, particularly in roles where automation complemented rather than replaced human input.  Challenges identified included integration with legacy systems, change resistance, and the need for structured training and communication during deployment phases.

Importantly, the study highlights that the benefits of RPA are perceived as sustainable and scalable when supported by appropriate governance and change management strategies.  The alignment between technological capability and organisational readiness emerged as a critical success factor.

This research adds to the limited body of literature on RPA deployment in Indian banking and offers practical insights for leaders seeking to balance automation with workforce engagement.  It underscores the importance of thoughtful implementation to ensure long-term value from digital transformation initiatives.

title: Beyond Net Effects: Configurational Pathways to Misinformation Sharing About Eco-Friendly Brands-A Combined SEM and fsQCA Analysis
affiliations: , Rezo Inovasyon Edikatif Ayisyen and Rezo Inovasyon Edikatif Ayisyen

detail.title: Beyond Net Effects: Configurational Pathways to Misinformation Sharing About Eco-Friendly Brands-A Combined SEM and fsQCA Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We confirm that we have no affiliations or involvement with any organization or entity that has a financial or non-financial interest in the subject matter discussed in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: We adopted a dual-method design combining structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzyset qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine the sharing of fake news about ecofriendly brands. The SEM phase tested the direct effects of immersive flow in proenvironmental content (IFPC), status-seeking motivation (SSM), and pro-environmental social media engagement on fake news sharing. It further explored indirect effects through two parallel serial mediation paths involving trust in social media or trust in eco-friendly brands and subsequent social media usage. Finally, the moderating role of social media competence on the trust-usage relationships was assessed. Our SEM findings revealed that IFPC predicts trust in both eco-friendly contents and eco-friendly brands, but did not directly predict fake news sharing, while SSM showed significant effects across all measured variables. Importantly, both trust variables predicted social media usage, which predicted fake news sharing. Nonetheless, the data provided no empirical support for the proposed mediations or moderations. The fsQCA analysis identified twelve causal configurations leading to high fake news sharing. Among these, the combinations of status-seeking motivation with trust in ecofriendly brands, and trust in eco-friendly content with trust in eco-friendly brands were the most prominent, highlighting the complexity of these relationships.

detail.abstract: SHAPR (Solo Human-Centred and AI-Assisted Practice) is a framework for research software development that integrates human-centred decision-making with AI-assisted capabilities. While prior work introduced SHAPR as a conceptual framework, this paper focuses on its operationalisation as a structured, traceable, and knowledge-generating approach to AI-assisted research practice. We present a set of interconnected models describing how research activities are organised through iterative cycles (Explore-Build-Use-Evaluate-Learn), how artefacts evolve through development and use, and how empirical evidence is systematically transformed into conceptual knowledge. Central to this process is the notion of Structured Knowledge Units (SKUs), which provide modular and reusable representations of insights derived from practice, supporting knowledge accumulation and reuse across cycles. The framework further introduces evidence and traceability as a cross-cutting mechanism linking human decisions, AI-assisted development, artefact evolution, and resulting knowledge, enabling transparency, reproducibility, and systematic refinement. SHAPR is also positioned as an AI-executable research framework, as its structured processes and documentation practices can be interpreted and enacted by generative AI systems to guide research workflows. At the same time, SHAPR supports a continuum of AI involvement, allowing researchers to balance control, learning, and automation across different research contexts. Beyond individual workflows, SHAPR is conceptualised as an integrated research system that combines LLM workspaces, development environments, cloud storage, and version control to support scalable, traceable, and knowledge-centred research practices. Overall, SHAPR provides a practical and theoretically grounded foundation for conducting rigorous, transparent, and reproducible research in AI-assisted environments, 1 contributing to the development of scalable and methodologically sound research practices.

title: Inference Routing and Failure Intelligence across Heterogeneous Compute Supply

detail.title: Inference Routing and Failure Intelligence across Heterogeneous Compute Supply
detail.abstract: This paper specifies an inference orchestrator that classifies AI requests into five workload categories, meters usage through a fixed-price monthly battery instead of per-token billing, and routes across a heterogeneous pool of GPU hardware contributors and surplus enterprise API key contributors. A verification system samples completed requests and re-executes them on trusted nodes, comparing outputs through exact-match, cosine similarity, or semantic scoring depending on workload type. Subscribers can also flag bad responses, which enter the same re-execution pipeline for confirmation. Verified failures trigger three simultaneous outcomes: the subscriber receives IBT compensation proportional to compute cost [Harshberger and Claude Opus 4.6, 2026], the provider's reputation adjusts, and the failure enters the intelligence platform as a structured DPO preference pair [Rafailov et al., 2023]. Seven intelligence layers built on accumulated failure records provide error taxonomy, frequency analytics, severity scoring, hallucination mapping, cross-model comparison, and temporal regression detection across every provider simultaneously. Hardware contributors who opt in can generate zeroknowledge proofs for the verification system during idle GPU windows, earning additional IBT while reducing trust requirements on the verifier node. Providers on the network retain full control over protocol participation per API key, including opt-out from failure data capture and configuration of end-user-facing SDK components for surfacing verification results. Revenue from selling structured failure data to frontier labs through tiered access backs the IBT token and funds open-weight community training pairs.

title: AI, Education, and the Architecture of Power

detail.title: AI, Education, and the Architecture of Power
detail.abstract: This working paper brings together three interconnected essays on artificial intelligence in education. The first examines the competitive landscape of AI in schools and argues that the 'classroom battleground' framing which positions the contest as a race to train the most teachers misidentifies both the terrain and the actors that matter most. The second argues that the most consequential AI governance decision an institution makes is not which tool to adopt, but which contractual terms it refuses to accept at procurement. The third draws on the Indian digital education ecosystem to show how pedagogical power migrates from visible acts of authority to invisible infrastructure choices. Together, the three essays develop a single argument: that the governance of AI in education is not primarily a technology problem or an ethics problem. It is a structural problem one that lives in contracts, platforms, and defaults, and that will be decided long before most affected students know the decision is being made.

detail.abstract: In today's digital economy, mobile subscriber identifiers have transformed from a simple means of communication into a fundamental means of accessing digital assets. Nonetheless, in the current SIM card recycling life cycle, a system vulnerability, known as the "Residual Linkage" issue, arises when a mobile number is reassigned without de-linking it from the original user's financial and identity-related assets, leading to identity theft and financial fraud. This paper presents a de-linking framework, proposed as "Clean Slate Protocol, (also referred to as the Secure Mobile Identity Migration or SMIM framework), which uses the National Identity infrastructure for de-linking these assets. This model will ensure a synchronised state between Telecommunication Service Providers (TSPs) and Financial Institutions, thereby securing the digital identity lifecycle and respecting the "Right to be Forgotten" as enshrined in law.

title: AI Safety and the Value Preservation Imperative

detail.title: AI Safety and the Value Preservation Imperative
detail.abstract: Global artificial intelligence (AI) safety is critical to defending against the potential downside of AI technology (from routine to existential risks) and needs to be prioritized accordingly. Our global leaders have a duty of care to safeguard against the potential damage of this impending AI value destruction and that will require a much higher, more robust, and more mature level of AI safety due diligence than is currently on display. Dynamic developments in AI mean that the normal order of things no longer applies, and that going forward effective AI safety will require superior levels of guardianship, stewardship, and leadership.

detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) represent over 90% of global enterprises, yet traditional Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems remain prohibitively expensive and timeconsuming to implement. This paper introduces Payanarss Type Script (PTS), a metadata scripting architecture that encodes business processes, data structures, validation rules, and inter-entity relationships as a recursive hierarchy of typed nodes stored in a single JSON document. Rather reduces ERP configuration from months to minutes, with the AI agent traversing 400 metadata nodes to guide business setup through 15 structured lifecycle phases. This paper contributes a novel architecture at the intersection of model-driven engineering, metadata-driven systems, and AI-native application design.

title: Death of the Dark Room: How Generative AI Broke Enterprise IT's Political Cover

detail.title: Death of the Dark Room: How Generative AI Broke Enterprise IT's Political Cover

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher and practitioner in enterprise AI governance. This research received no commercial sponsorship and reflects the author's independent views.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Enterprise IT has historically operated inside a "dark room"-a zone of technical opacity where project failures could be rationalised through complexity narratives inaccessible to non-technical leadership. This opacity was not a flaw but a governance equilibrium: boards accepted it because the cost of independent monitoring exceeded the perceived benefit. This strategic briefing argues that generative AI has structurally destroyed this equilibrium through what the author terms the consumer benchmark effect: every executive now carries a consumer-grade AI tool that functions as a live performance benchmark against enterprise IT delivery, collapsing monitoring costs to near zero. The result is not simply increased accountability but the emergence of two simultaneous boardroom fears-fear of visible failure and fear of visible success. Unlike earlier consumerisation waves, which raised capability expectations, generative AI changes evaluative capacity: non-specialists can now directly judge the quality of knowledge-work outputs. Because this shift is structural, not cyclical, the standard of explainability boards will accept has been durably raised. The implications for CIO mandate, governance architecture, and enterprise AI adoption sequencing are lasting.

title: Augmenting Pedagogical Absorptive Capacity: Designing an AI-Powered Case Study Builder to Support Sensemaking in Executive Education

detail.title: Augmenting Pedagogical Absorptive Capacity: Designing an AI-Powered Case Study Builder to Support Sensemaking in Executive Education
detail.abstract: The transition to Industry 5.0 places executive education under mounting pressure to equip leaders with the competencies required to navigate digital transformation, sustainability imperatives, and human-centric values simultaneously. A critical bottleneck impedes this mission: educators' well-documented capacity to acquire and assimilate external knowledge is seldom matched by a corresponding capacity to transform and exploit that knowledge through pedagogically effective teaching materials. This conceptual study addresses the gap by introducing pedagogical absorptive capacity, a micro-foundational capability that extends the PACAP-RACAP framework to the educator-as-knowledge-integrator, and proposes generative AI as the primary mediating mechanism bridging the two dimensions. Employing Design Science Research (DSR) methodology structured around the six-phase Peffers process model and evaluated against Hevner's seven guidelines, the paper presents the design of an AI-powered Case Study Builder. Human-AI symbiosis is theorised to operate through three discrete mechanisms: augmented problem sensing, which extends educators' perceptual reach across diverse knowledge domains; scaffolded solution assembly, which reduces the cognitive viscosity of narrative construction while preserving educator agency; and accelerated validation and reflection, which compresses iterative feedback cycles from weeks to minutes. The artifact embodies five design principles, augment rather than automate; support iterative refinement; provide structure with customisation; build in feedback loops; and design for diverse institutional contexts, derived from the theoretical framework and formulated as transferable prescriptive knowledge. The paper contributes an extension of absorptive capacity theory to pedagogical contexts, a mechanism-level account of human-AI knowledge integration, and actionable design guidance for business schools seeking to enhance faculty capability in the Industry 5.0 era.

title: Global Growth Miracles and Disasters: A Comparative Regional Analysis (2016-2023)
affiliations: Glorious Vision University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global Growth Miracles and Disasters: A Comparative Regional Analysis (2016-2023)
detail.abstract: This study investigates regional patterns of economic growth from 2016 to 2023, categorizing global economies into "growth miracles" and "growth disasters" using GDP per capita growth rates from the World Bank's 2024 World Development Indicators. Employing descriptive statistics and comparative analysis, the research identifies South Asia and East Asia & Pacific as high-performing regions, largely driven by structural reforms, export-led strategies, and human capital investment. Conversely, Latin America, Europe & Central Asia, and parts of Sub-Saharan Africa experienced stagnation or contraction, linked to political instability, weak institutions, and limited diversification. The findings are interpreted through the Solow Growth Model, Endogenous Growth Theory, and the World Bank's 3i Strategy, highlighting the critical roles of governance, innovation, and institutional quality. Policy recommendations focus on targeted investment in education, technological adoption, and macroeconomic stability to sustain high growth and mitigate economic decline.

title: Controlling versus enabling
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Controlling versus enabling
detail.abstract: How does a firm decide whether to employ professionals and control how they deliver services to clients, or to operate as a platform enabling independent professionals to provide services directly to clients? Similarly, how does a manufacturer decide whether to allow sales agents to choose certain costly actions (e.g. kickbacks to clients) or to take control of these actions itself? We answer this question using a principal-agent framework in which both the principal and the agent must be incentivized to carry out investments (or effort) that increase the revenue they jointly create. Our theory explains when the principal should take control over a particular decision ("control") or should instead allow the agent to make the decision ("enable"). It does so both for the case when there are multiple such transferable decisions for a single agent, and for the case when there are many agents and one transferable decision for each. We also consider the possibility of cost asymmetries between the principal and the agent, spillovers across agents, and the misclassification of the principal as an employer even though agents are allocated the relevant control rights. Finally, we explain how the "control vs. enable" choice and its associated tradeoffs differ from the classic "make vs. buy" choice.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Commodity Trading: An Industry Review of Front-to-Back Transformation, Risk, and Governance

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Commodity Trading: An Industry Review of Front-to-Back Transformation, Risk, and Governance
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is enabling a front-to-back redesign of commodity trading operations. In the front office, machine learning and deep learning support forecasting, signal generation, and execution optimization. In the middle and back office, artificial intelligence is expanding into price capture from unstructured negotiation channels, profit and loss break triage, real-time position pipelines, and document-intensive workflows. This review synthesizes academic literature, regulatory guidance from major jurisdictions, and detailed industry case studies to address three questions: where artificial intelligence generates measurable economic value in commodity trading, how it alters operational risk and systemic exposure, and what governance architecture is required for safe deployment. The paper argues that the central trade-off is capital efficiency versus risk concentration. The most measurable near-term value comes from middle and back office augmentation, while the highest tail risks arise where artificial intelligence closes the loop into autonomous execution or official valuation without robust governance. Safe deployment requires an architectural approach combining robust data infrastructure, independent model validation, and human oversight with adequate technical competence.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic macro-financial model that integrates liquidity shocks, constrained arbitrage, and leverage dynamics to explain the propagation of financial instability across markets and institutions. The central contribution is a unified framework in which funding liquidity constraints endogenously limit arbitrage capital, weakened arbitrage allows mispricing to persist, and mispricing triggers deleveraging and fire sales that further depress prices and liquidity. The resulting feedback loops generate liquidity spirals that amplify small fundamental shocks into large price dislocations, volatility clustering, and systemic crises. The model decomposes asset prices into fundamental and mispricing components, where the latter depends on funding liquidity conditions, arbitrageur capital, and market stress. Arbitrage capital evolves according to a law of motion that captures persistence, entry in response to profit opportunities, and exit driven by risk and funding shocks. Leverage dynamics introduce nonlinear amplification through margin constraints and collateral feedback. The complete system is a recursive, path-dependent dynamic structure in which bad states feed upon themselves. The paper characterizes the conditions under which the equilibrium is stable, fragile, or explosive, deriving explicit stability bounds and showing that systemic fragility is state-dependent. Eight formal propositions establish that liquidity shocks reduce arbitrage capacity, weak arbitrage increases mispricing persistence, leverage amplifies volatility nonlinearly, fire sales generate endogenous feedback, and macro-financial fragility intensifies in stressed states. The empirical strategy proposes panel regressions, GARCH volatility models, vector autoregressions, and instrumental variable designs to test the model predictions using funding liquidity indices, leverage measures, and arbitrage capital proxies. The paper concludes with policy implications for central banks, macroprudential authorities, and market regulators.

title:
Operationalizing the Symbolic–Functional Model of Motivation:

Empirical Indicators Derived from a Field Framework

detail.title:
Operationalizing the Symbolic–Functional Model of Motivation:

Empirical Indicators Derived from a Field Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper. The research was conducted independently and without external funding.

detail.abstract:
Motivational theory remains limited by its failure to specify how selection between competing alternatives occurs. Hierarchical models assume ordered progression among needs, while variable-based approaches treat motivation as an internal quantity; neither provides a mechanism explaining how behavior emerges from comparison across alternatives or why small contextual changes can produce abrupt shifts in action.

This article introduces a symbolic–functional model that defines motivation as the outcome of structured evaluation across competing alternatives. Each alternative is characterized by symbolic value, functional return, and constraint conditions, and is evaluated through a context-sensitive weighting function. Selection is governed by a formal rule in which an alternative becomes dominant when its evaluative score exceeds both competing alternatives and a context-dependent threshold.

The model specifies three core processes: evaluative reweighting driven by contextual variation, shifts in comparative dominance across alternatives, and threshold-based selection producing discontinuous behavioral change. A formal representation is provided, along with an illustrative example demonstrating how reweighting alone—without changes in the intrinsic properties of alternatives—can produce abrupt transitions in selection.

To enable empirical implementation, the article develops an operational framework for estimating evaluative weighting, modeling constraint effects, and detecting threshold dynamics using structured choice designs and longitudinal approaches. This reframes empirical analysis from measuring motivational states to reconstructing evaluative functions and selection conditions.

By defining a closed evaluative mechanism linking context, constraints, weighting, and selection, the model provides a basis for formal modeling, empirical estimation, and prediction of motivational transitions beyond hierarchical and state-based assumptions.

reference: GVU Journal of Management and Social Sciences, Vol. 10, 2025, pp. 53–65. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18112418
title: Revisiting Aquinas's Natural Law Ethics as a Framework for Moral Responsibility in Nigeria's Corrupt Political Culture

detail.title: Revisiting Aquinas's Natural Law Ethics as a Framework for Moral Responsibility in Nigeria's Corrupt Political Culture

publicationDetails.detailsText: GVU Journal of Management and Social Sciences, Vol. 10, 2025, pp. 53–65. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18112418

detail.abstract: Nigeria's persistent political corruption remains a major moral and developmental crisis, undermining justice, accountability, and the common good. Despite numerous anti-corruption policies and religious appeals, moral decadence within the political class continues to thrive, suggesting the need for a deeper ethical framework rooted in rational and universal moral principles. This study revisits Thomas Aquinas's Natural Law Ethics as a philosophical and theological framework for addressing moral responsibility in Nigeria's corrupt political culture. The study identifies a gap in existing anti-corruption discourses, which often emphasize legal and institutional reforms but neglect the moral foundations of political conduct. Guided by Aquinas's conception of the natural law as participation in divine reason, the study aims to explore how intrinsic moral order and virtue ethics can foster integrity and public accountability among leaders. Using a qualitative, analytical, and hermeneutical methodology, the research examines primary Thomistic texts alongside contemporary Nigerian socio-political realities. The findings reveal that Aquinas's emphasis on reason, virtue, and the common good offers a viable moral paradigm for reforming political behaviour and reawakening moral conscience in governance. The study concludes that effective anti-corruption reform must integrate moral education grounded in natural law ethics. It recommends the reorientation of political leadership training, civic education, and public policy towards moral responsibility, justice, and the pursuit of the common good as articulated in Thomistic ethical thought.

title: The Agency Error in AI Governance: Coherent Output, Constraint, and the Misclassification of Artificial Systems

detail.title: The Agency Error in AI Governance: Coherent Output, Constraint, and the Misclassification of Artificial Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently and received no financial support from any organization with a stake in AI governance, AI development, or related policy outcomes.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
AI systems do not act. They generate coherent outputs under constraint. The persistence of agency attribution in artificial intelligence governance arises not from the presence of intention in these systems, but from a structural feature of their design: sufficiently constrained systems operating over structured data reliably produce the observable markers—coherence, responsiveness, apparent goal-directedness—that humans use to infer agency in other contexts. The inference is not irrational. It is misplaced. This paper identifies that misplacement as the central, undertheorized problem in AI governance.

Across philosophy of mind, legal scholarship, and science and technology studies, AI systems are treated as candidates for agency—as full agents, quasi-agents, or distributed actants—despite the absence of the conditions agency requires. This paper argues that these frameworks share a category error: the conflation of output coherence with underlying subjectivity or purposive action. Drawing on philosophy of mind, legal theory, and science and technology studies, it develops a non-agentic model of AI systems as constraint-bound output generators and demonstrates how prevailing frameworks—the intentional stance, legal doctrines of responsibility, and distributed agency models—fail on their own terms when applied to systems of this kind.

The governance consequences are direct. Misattributed agency produces unstable liability regimes, because responsibility cannot be correctly located when the wrong entity is treated as its source. It produces conceptual drift in policy language, as terms such as “AI decision-making” and “AI autonomy” migrate from heuristic to descriptive and embed false ontological assumptions in regulatory design. And it produces misplaced regulatory targets, directing institutional attention toward the system rather than toward the human decisions—in design, deployment, and use—where governance can actually take hold.

This paper proposes a framework grounded in operational classification rather than metaphoric attribution. The reframing does not alter who bears responsibility—designers, deployers, and users remain accountable—but whether responsibility can be deflected. The agency frame grants AI systems enough ontological status to absorb causal attribution without bearing legal responsibility, creating a structural gap in accountability. The non-agentic model closes that gap: a constraint-bound output generator cannot function as a deflection point, and the defense—“the algorithm decided,” “the system determined”—becomes categorically unavailable. Every outcome traces to a human decision. That is what correct classification makes possible.

title: Control and Governance of Generative and Agentic AI: An AIS Lifecycle Framework for Privacy and Security

detail.title: Control and Governance of Generative and Agentic AI: An AIS Lifecycle Framework for Privacy and Security
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and agentic AI architectures are rapidly being integrated into organizational information systems and automation frameworks. While these technologies promise efficiency gains in knowledge work, automation, and decision support, their autonomy, system-level access, and coordinated actions introduce significant privacy and security risks. These risks differ from those associated with traditional software or analytics systems. From an Accounting Information Systems (AIS) perspective, these developments challenge assumptions of bounded execution, stable role-based access, and auditable transactions supported by systematic audit trails. Agentic AI systems may autonomously invoke tools, access sensitive organizational data, and interact with other agents in ways difficult to observe or constrain using conventional internal controls. This research letter proposes an AISoriented privacy and security control framework for GenAI and agentic AI systems integrating five control dimensions: identity and access control, governance and policy design, monitoring and audit mechanisms, cryptographic guardrails, and agentic resilience.

reference: GVU Journal of Management and Social Sciences, Vol. 10, 2025, pp. 74–78. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18114958
title: An Empirical Review of Bank Credit and Manufacturing Sector Productivity in Nigeria
affiliations: Federal University of Technology Akure (FUTA) - Department of Project Management Technology

detail.title: An Empirical Review of Bank Credit and Manufacturing Sector Productivity in Nigeria

publicationDetails.detailsText: GVU Journal of Management and Social Sciences, Vol. 10, 2025, pp. 74–78. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18114958

detail.abstract: This study provides a systematic empirical review of the impact of bank credit on manufacturing sector productivity in Nigeria. The research analyses the volume, cost, and real value of bank credit as independent variables affecting manufacturing productivity. A systematic literature review methodology was employed, analysing 45 empirical studies published between 1985 and 2023 from peer-reviewed journals and institutional reports. The analysis employed multiple regression techniques to synthesise findings across studies. Results revealed that the volume of bank credit shows a significant positive effect on manufacturing output but an insignificant negative effect on capacity utilisation. The cost of credit demonstrated a significant negative effect on both investment and capacity utilisation. The real value of credit showed a significant positive effect on overall sectoral productivity. The study concludes that while bank credit is essential, its efficacy is critically mediated by its affordability and real value, which are often eroded by macroeconomic instability. This underscores the necessity of complementary policies targeting macroeconomic stability and infrastructural development to enhance the productivity of in the manufacturing sector.

reference: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-07
title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Forecasting Research Institute, Yale School of Management, University of Toronto - Strategic Management, , Mississippi State University, Stanford University, University of Oxford, Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Research Institute, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-07
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We elicit forecasts of how AI will affect the U.S. economy, comparing the beliefs of fifive groups: academic economists, employees at AI companies, policy researchers focused on AI, highly accurate forecasters, and the general public. The median respondent in each group expects substantial advances in AI capabilities by 2030, small declines in labor force participation consistent with demographic shifts, and an annual GDP growth rate of 2.5%, which exceeds both the typical medium-run (2.0%) and long-run (1.7%) baseline forecasts from government agencies and private-sector forecasters. Conditional on a “rapid” AI progress scenario, in which AI systems surpass human performance on many cognitive and physical tasks, experts forecast substantial, though not historically unprecedented, economic shifts: annualized GDP growth rising to around 4% and the labor force participation rate falling from its current level of 62% to 55% by 2050, with roughly half of that decline—equivalent to around 10 million lost jobs—attributable to AI. A variance decomposition suggests that expert disagreement about these effects is driven primarily by different beliefs about the economic effects of highly capable AI systems rather than by disagreement about the pace of AI progress. These forecasts map onto notably different policy preferences across groups: experts strongly favor targeted measures such as worker retraining, whereas the general public supports both targeted programs and broader interventions, including a job guarantee and universal basic income.

title: Unification of Political Parties Through Minimum Civilizational Constraints: A Structural Framework for Stable Governance, Peace, and Civilizational Development

detail.title: Unification of Political Parties Through Minimum Civilizational Constraints: A Structural Framework for Stable Governance, Peace, and Civilizational Development
detail.abstract: This Green Paper proposes a framework for the unification of political parties with the objective of enhancing civilization through sustained peace, societal prosperity, and continuous development. It emphasizes the need for patriotic leaders and political organizations to come together despite differing visions and ideologies, in order to collectively contribute to the long-term progress of the nation. The proposed unification framework seeks to bring together all legally registered political parties, while also providing an inclusive platform for future political entities to participate in shaping national development. At the same time, it aims to discourage and structurally exclude political forces that promote conflict, instability, violence, or conditions that may lead to war and societal disruption. To ensure stability and coherence within the political system, the framework introduces a process for standardizing political participation based on alignment with civilizational growth principles. Political parties that demonstrate strong commitment to peace, prosperity, and constructive governance are recognized as legitimate participants within the unified structure. Ultimately, the Green Paper seeks to establish a model of ideal democracy that preserves freedom, ensures peace, and promotes collaborative political engagement. By unifying ideologically diverse but development-oriented political actors, the framework aims to create a stable foundation for national progress and civilizational advancement.

title: When the Water Recedes and Home Prices Don’t Flood Risk Learning and Neighborhood Spillovers
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY), CUNY Queens College and City University of New York, CUNY Queens College -   Department of Economics

detail.title: When the Water Recedes and Home Prices Don’t Flood Risk Learning and Neighborhood Spillovers
detail.abstract: What are the long-run effects of flooding on home values? We use new differencein-difference methods for setups with local spillovers to analyze the effects of 2012 hurricane Sandy on New York’s housing market. We show that, more than a decade after the storm, and long after damage was repaired, flooded properties continue to sell at a substantial discount. Our estimates also suggest that the discount is inversely related to the severity of flooding, consistent with the stronger informational signal conveyed by flooding of less exposed properties. Last, we estimate large local spillover effects that persistently lowered the values of nearby non-flooded properties. Spillover effects reduce homeowners’ incentives to invest in flood-mitigation actions, as such individual efforts cannot fully prevent value depreciation.

title: A Survey of Financial Experimental Research through a Regulatory Lens
affiliations: University of Washington - Department of Accounting and University of Washington - Department of Accounting

detail.title: A Survey of Financial Experimental Research through a Regulatory Lens
detail.abstract: Academic research can inform policy, enforcement, and rulemaking at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). We argue that experimental accounting research is particularly well-suited to provide rigorous, causal evidence on issues central to these regulators’ missions. We review existing financial experimental studies relevant to securities regulation and classify them according to the SEC’s divisions and offices and FINRA’s oversight functions. This framework highlights where financial experimental evidence is relevant to regulatory activities and can help the SEC and FINRA identify research aligned with specific mandates. We also identify opportunities for future research and offer practical guidance to academics on communicating the relevance of their work, with the goal of strengthening the connection between research and securities regulation.

title: endogeNOVA: a latent variable approach to assess endogenous bank performance from ECB supervisory data
affiliations: University of Catania - Department of Economics and Quantitative Methods,  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: endogeNOVA: a latent variable approach to assess endogenous bank performance from ECB supervisory data
detail.abstract: The paper introduces a methodology for classifying banks into business models based on the composition of their activities and risks (choice variables) while considering the endogeneity of business model selection to outcome variables, such as market performance. Our approach, called endogeNOVA, provides a unified representation in which the intrinsic endogeneity arises naturally as a latent factor, identified without the need for external information. For estimation, we propose a consistent two–step maximum likelihood estimator based on a fully closed-form EM algorithm, and introduce a penalized variant to enhance numerical stability. We study an international sample of 317 European banks using harmonised supervisory data. We consider choice variables covering risk, income and capitalisation while on the outcome side we focus on the return-on-equity and return-on-assets performance metrics. The partition of banks by business model identified through endogeNOVA has a strong predictive power on bank performance while the extracted latent factors are valid instruments of cluster membership.

title: The Subscription Fiscal State: A Liquidity-Based Architecture of Public Finance

detail.title: The Subscription Fiscal State: A Liquidity-Based Architecture of Public Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial conflict of interest in relation to this manuscript. The author is a partner at JN Legal, a Ukrainian law firm, and serves as a member of the Kyiv City Council. These roles did not involve funding, sponsorship, client instruction, institutional commissioning, or any external influence on the research. The manuscript reflects the author’s independent academic analysis. No clients, public authorities, political bodies, or other organizations had any role in the conception, preparation, review, or approval of the manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it is a theoretical and conceptual research article and did not involve human participants, patients, personal data, surveys, interviews, or clinical material.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was self-funded and prepared independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes the concept of a Subscription Fiscal State, an institutional model of public finance in which part of the fiscal function of the state is integrated into financial infrastructure. Unlike traditional tax systems based on income, profit, transactions, or asset ownership, the proposed architecture introduces an automated periodic fiscal contribution calculated as a function of the liquidity balance held in designated financial accounts.

Under this model, economic agents voluntarily use accounts in which fiscal rules are embedded directly into the operating mechanism of the financial infrastructure. Fiscal obligations arise not through the declaration of discrete taxable events, but through a balance-oriented algorithmic contribution built into the financial system.

The paper formalizes the institutional structure of this architecture, develops a dynamic model of fiscal revenue formation based on liquidity participation and exit payments, and analyzes agents’ strategic incentives through a game-theoretic framework. Two formal results are established: a condition under which voluntary participation becomes a strictly dominant strategy, and the existence of an optimal contribution rate that maximizes budget revenue, described as a Liquidity Laffer Curve.

The analysis suggests that a subscription fiscal architecture may reduce tax compliance costs, simplify tax administration, and lower incentives for tax evasion. Because revenues are generated through liquidity participation rather than declared income, the model may also encourage more active use of financial resources and affect the velocity of money in the formal sector.

The proposed concept is not presented as an immediate replacement for existing tax systems, but as an additional institutional regime suitable for testing in isolated pilot environments. The paper also identifies fiscal-safety mechanisms, agent heterogeneity, and distributional effects as key issues for further research.

title: Temperature Shocks, Cash Windfalls and Efficiency
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM) and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Temperature Shocks, Cash Windfalls and Efficiency
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of temperature-driven cash windfalls on investments in efficiency and environmental performance. Leveraging geo-coded data on temperature shocks and a rich panel of U.S. power plants from 2008 to 2021, we show that temperature shocks are a strong predictor of plant revenue. Using temperature shocks as an instrument, we find that a 10 percent increase in cash windfalls, i.e., temperature-driven revenue changes, significantly increases capital expenditures at the plants by about 4.5 percent. We find that these investments lead to significant improvements in plant efficiency and reductions in emission intensity.

title: The Missing Layer in Public Procurement: Outcome Verification After Deployment

detail.title: The Missing Layer in Public Procurement: Outcome Verification After Deployment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or personal data and does not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Public procurement systems are designed to verify whether contracted systems are delivered according to specifications. However, they do not systematically verify whether those systems actually improve outcomes after deployment. This paper identifies a structural gap in procurement frameworks: the absence of a defined, independent mechanism for post-deployment outcome verification. While implementation is subject to acceptance procedures and, in some cases, Independent Verification and Validation (IV&V), these mechanisms primarily operate during development and do not extend into operational outcome measurement. As a result, public systems may be formally accepted despite failing to improve service delivery in practice. This paper argues that procurement frameworks require an additional layer-post-deployment outcome verification-to ensure that public spending translates into measurable improvements. The analysis focuses on structural design rather than specific technologies or vendors, and proposes a minimal, data-driven verification layer that can operate using existing administrative data.

title: Unpacking Carbon Leakage along the Global Value Chain
affiliations: Academia Sinica - Institute of Economics, Academia Sinica, Swarthmore College, Academia Sinica and Academia Sinica - Institute of Economics

detail.title: Unpacking Carbon Leakage along the Global Value Chain
detail.abstract: Carbon leakage is the main critique of climate policies, yet its sources remain poorly understood. With global value chains (GVCs), leakage may arise not only from the relocation of dirty production across countries, but also from changes in production staging, sourcing patterns, and the balance between upstreamness and downstreamness. We develop a multicountry quantitative trade and environment model that distinguishes between upstream and downstream trade. Calibrated to the OECD Inter-Country Input-Output table, we trace how climate policy reallocates embodied carbon across countries and production stages using a carbon-accounting decomposition. We find that leakage from unilateral carbon pricing is driven mainly by downstream trade, while embodied emissions in upstream trade generally decline, suggesting that such policies could lead to the shortening of GVCs. Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) reinforces this reorganization, implying that effective climate policy must be designed around value chain margins, rather than sectoral relocation alone.

title: Report 2025 on Sustainability Reporting of Italian Listed Companies (Rapporto 2025 sulla rendicontazione di sostenibilità delle società quotate italiane)
affiliations: CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa), CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa), CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa), CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa), CONSOB, CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa), CONSOB (Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa) and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Report 2025 on Sustainability Reporting of Italian Listed Companies (Rapporto 2025 sulla rendicontazione di sostenibilità delle società quotate italiane)

publicationDetails.journalName: Commissione Nazionale per le Societa e la Borsa (CONSOB) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
English Abstract: The 2025 Report on sustainability reporting of Italian listed companies examines the extent to which environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors are integrated into corporate decision‑making processes, business models, strategy and governance systems, in the context of the entry into force of Legislative Decree No. 125/2024 transposing the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). After an introductory overview of the regulatory framework, the Report analyses sustainability reporting practices, material topics and the integration of ESG criteria into remuneration policies and concludes with an Addendum reviewing the evolution of non‑financial reporting between 2018 and 2024. The empirical analysis is based on a stratified sample of 60 firms drawn from the 136 Italian companies with ordinary shares listed on Euronext Milan that published a sustainability report in 2025, evenly divided between in‑scope and out‑of‑scope firms, i.e. companies which, based on the available data and the thresholds set out in the recent Directive (EU) 2026/470, will still be required to report and those that will not. The evidence shows that around half of the companies adopted formal reporting procedures. Almost 80% of companies involved stakeholders in impact materiality assessments, whereas the board of directors was involved at the conclusion of the double materiality assessment in 93% of cases. Climate change and own workforce emerged as material issues for all firms. Finally, 78% of companies, mainly in-scope firms, integrated ESG factors into CEO compensation. Overall, the findings point out a general awareness in the approach to materiality analysis and an integration of sustainability issues into corporate governance and strategy, more frequent among in-scope companies compared with out-of-scope ones.

Italian Abstract: Il Rapporto 2025 sulla rendicontazione di sostenibilità delle società quotate italiane esamina in che misura i fattori ambientali, sociali e di governance (ESG) siano integrati nei processi decisionali, nei modelli di business, nella strategia e nei sistemi di governance delle imprese, nel contesto dell’entrata in vigore del d.lgs n. 125/2024, che ha recepito la Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). Dopo una parte introduttiva dedicata al quadro normativo di riferimento, il Rapporto analizza le pratiche di rendicontazione di sostenibilità, i temi materiali e l’integrazione dei criteri ESG nelle politiche retributive, e si conclude con un Addendum che ripercorre l’evoluzione della rendicontazione non finanziaria nel periodo 2018–2024. L’analisi empirica si basa su un campione stratificato di 60 imprese selezionate tra le 136 società italiane con azioni ordinarie quotate su Euronext Milan che hanno pubblicato una rendicontazione di sostenibilità nel 2025, equamente suddivise tra società in‑scope e out‑of‑scope, ovvero società che, in base ai dati disponibili e alle soglie previste dalla recente Direttiva (UE) 2026/470, saranno ancora obbligate alla rendicontazione e quelle che non lo saranno. Le evidenze mostrano che circa la metà delle imprese ha adottato procedure formali di rendicontazione. L’80% delle società ha coinvolto gli stakeholder nella valutazione di materialità di impatto, con una maggiore frequenza tra le società out-of-scope, mentre il consiglio di amministrazione è stato coinvolto a valle dell’analisi di doppia materialità nel 93% dei casi. I temi relativi ai cambiamenti climatici e ai lavoratori dell’impresa sono risultati rilevanti per tutti gli emittenti. Infine, il 78% delle imprese, soprattutto in‑scope, ha collegato la remunerazione variabile dell’amministratore delegato a parametri ESG. I risultati indicano una maturazione complessiva nell’approccio all’analisi di materialità e una integrazione della sostenibilità nella governance e nella visione aziendale più frequente tra le società in-scope rispetto a quelle out-of-scope. 

Note: Downloadable document is in English and in Italian language.

title: Artificial Light at Night Erodes Cultural Ecosystem Services at Scale
affiliations: Utah State University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Thompson Rivers University, Utah State University, Utah State University, Utah State University, Utah State University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Artificial Light at Night Erodes Cultural Ecosystem Services at Scale

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors do not have any personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The survey protocol was approved by Utah State University's Institutional Review Board (#11535).
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded jointly by the Natural Sounds and Night Sky Division of the U.S. National Park Service (Task Agreement P20AC00525) and by the Public Lands Initiative at Utah State University (UTAO + Number 1566).

detail.abstract: Artificial light at night (ALAN) is expanding rapidly, yet its implications for human well-being are rarely quantified in welfare terms. We develop a cultural ecosystem service accounting approach that links monitored night sky conditions to recreation behavior and monetary value. Using visitor-intercept surveys from designated dark sky parks across the Colorado Plateau, we estimate multi-site site choice models in which trip decisions respond to travel cost, meteorology, and two alternative night sky measures: the Anthropogenic Light Ratio (ALR) and a Bortle Dark Sky Index that more fully captures night sky viewing conditions. Visitors are less likely to choose parks with greater anthropogenic skyglow or poorer realized night sky conditions, and they exhibit positive willingness to pay for darker skies. Simulating small park-specific degradation shocks equal to 0.1 standard deviations of observed night sky conditions yields substantial aggregate welfare losses, concentrated in high-visitation parks. The results show that ALAN imposes measurable non-market costs on outdoor recreation and tourism systems, and that ALAN can be incorporated into natural capital accounting as well as the evaluation of development and policy decisions.

title: A modular framework for a dynamic residential building stock model with energy retrofit forecasts

detail.title: A modular framework for a dynamic residential building stock model with energy retrofit forecasts
detail.abstract: Building retrofits are strongly dependent on the individual refurbishment/rehabilitation cycles of buildings. In order to achieve the targeted climate goals for the building sector, it is necessary to make the best possible use of refurbishment opportunities for energy retrofits. Furthermore, it must be considered that the younger the building, the lower the potential for energy savings. The most challenging, yet required, energy retrofits are all yet to come. Given the importance of the refurbishment cycle, the question arises as to what the theoretical refurbishment rate is, what the actual energy retrofit rate is, and what it needs to be in order to meet the climate targets for the residential building stock. The aim of this paper is to model the evolution of the size and retrofit status of national building stocks. This is to be done against the background of the deviation from the actual and theoretical refurbishment cycle. Using current statistics and the past development of the German residential building stock, central parameters like living space, new construction, deconstruction, and the retrofit rate are modeled endogenously. For the latter, influences of economic conditions are implemented through an exogenously set black box variable. The retrofit rate represents a deep energy retrofit and thus allows an easy connection of the model with energy parameters for building classes defined in the web database TABULA for 20 European countries. The results are of relevance for modeling the energy efficiency status of the building stock and deriving suitable conditions for increasing retrofit rates also in other countries. The results show that increasing the energy retrofit rates to 2%/a or more is largely unrealistic. Instead, the focus should be on weak points, especially where short-term savings are concerned. This applies in particular to facades, basement ceilings, and heating systems as well as the efficient use of energy in buildings.

title: The optimality of ad valorem contracts
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The optimality of ad valorem contracts
detail.abstract: We provide a new theory of ad valorem contracts (i.e., contracts that vary with the value of the transaction) which can explain why such contracts are widely used between vertically related parties (e.g., in franchising and licensing). Ad valorem contracts allow upstream firms (principals) to preserve their own incentives to make ongoing investments in the channel, deal with pricing distortions caused by channel coordination problems, while at the same time adjusting their investment based on demand shocks that are only observed by the downstream firms (agents). We show that the optimal ad valorem contract allows the principal to achieve the same profits as if it could observe the demand shocks and control price. This optimal contract makes use of revenue sharing (to balance investment incentives and make the principal's investment responsive to demand through price), upfront fixed fees (to extract the agents' expected profit) and an additional term that depends non-linearly on either price or demand (to correct for remaining pricing distortions). Our results are robust to the introduction of competition between agents, production costs, and imperfect monitoring of the agents' prices.

title: Oasis under Stress: Water Balance and Climate Change in a Protected Wetland of Western Argentina.
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and CONICET

detail.title: Oasis under Stress: Water Balance and Climate Change in a Protected Wetland of Western Argentina.
detail.abstract: Through this research, we analyzed the hydrological and environmental tensions faced by a protected wetland in western Argentina, specifically the Ramsar site Lagunas de Guanacache, Desaguadero and del Bebedero, based on two complementary axes: the regional water balance including anthropogenic factors, and the evaluation of environmental flows and climate change under the framework of recent international guidelines. On one hand, the study addressed water dynamics by considering both natural inputs and extractions or uses derived from human activities, showing how the overexploitation of water resources, combined with climatic variability, compromises the sustainability of the system. This approach allowed the identification of growing imbalances in the regional water balance and the projection of scenarios of greater water stress in a climate change context. On the other hand, it incorporated the normative and conceptual perspective of the Brisbane Declaration (2018) and the warnings of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021), which emphasize the need to preserve environmental flows as a key tool to maintain the ecological functionality and ecosystem services of wetlands and societies. The combined analysis revealed that the oasis, historically shaped by the interaction between society and water, is currently in a critical situation where natural limits are exceeded by agricultural, urban, and industrial water demand, while projected reductions in water availability further reinforce the vulnerability of the system. This study highlights the importance of recognizing wetlands as spaces of environmental memory and as laboratories for understanding long-term transformations in the society–nature relationship, while also stressing the urgency of implementing integrated policies of water management and climate adaptation that ensure not only ecological conservation but also the social and productive resilience of the region.

title: Platform Traps
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Platform Traps
detail.abstract: A novel feature of platforms such as marketplaces and social networks is that non-participants may become worse off as others join. We show that in such settings, rational agents can be induced to join the platform despite being better off without it-a phenomenon we call a platform trap. We provide a dynamic theory of how platform traps emerge through one or more of the following additional features: (i) the ability of the platform to make dynamic price adjustments; (ii) the interplay between on-platform and off-platform negative externalities; (iii) favorable equilibrium selection when platforms make private offers.

title: Platforms and the exploration of new products
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Platforms and the exploration of new products
detail.abstract: A key strategic decision for platforms is the extent to which they should facilitate the entry of untested new products and sellers alongside established products and sellers. Exploration by current buyers helps future buyers better value these products and sellers. This externality across buyers raises the possibility that there may be too little exploration from the platform's perspective. On the other hand, when sellers have market power and so price strategically, and platforms extract a share of seller revenue (i.e., charge commissions), the direction of any such bias is not obvious. We provide a theory that predicts when the platform will prefer more, less or the same level of exploration as that induced by sellers in equilibrium. Our theory can explain why platforms will sometimes have no incentive to steer buyers one way or another, or may actually want to steer buyers towards established products and sellers.

title: Carbon Pricing, Renewable Expansion and Power-Sector Decarbonization: Cross-country Evidence from ETS and Carbon Taxes

detail.title: Carbon Pricing, Renewable Expansion and Power-Sector Decarbonization: Cross-country Evidence from ETS and Carbon Taxes
detail.abstract: Carbon pricing is now central to climate policy, but its contribution to electricitysystem transition remains incompletely understood. This paper studies whether national carbon pricing policies increase renewable electricity shares and reduce powersector carbon intensity. I construct a crosscountry panel for 2000-2025 by combining implementation records from the World Bank Carbon Pricing Dashboard with yearly electricity-generation and carbon-intensity data from Ember and macroeconomic indicators from the World Bank. The analysis first estimates country and year fixed-effects models and then complements them with a cohort-stacked difference-indifferences design to address concerns raised by staggered treatment timing. In the baseline fixedeffects specifications, carbon pricing adoption is associated with a 4.652 percentagepoint increase in renewable electricity share and a-32.712 gCO 2 /kWh reduction in grid carbon intensity, with p-values of 0.001 and 0.009, respectively. The more conservative cohort-stacked DID estimates remain statistically significant, though smaller in magnitude: 1.261 for renewable share and-10.978 for carbon intensity, with p-values of 0.005 and 0.033. Stacked event-study estimates show no evidence of differential pre-trends, with pre-trend p-values of 0.554 for renewable share and 0.715 for carbon intensity, and indicate that effects build over the first three post-treatment years. Heterogeneity results suggest stronger renewable-share gains in electricity systems that start with lower renewable penetration and larger carbon-intensity reductions in initially more carbon-intensive systems. Taken together, the results suggest that carbon pricing is associated with cleaner electricity systems and that its effects are strongest where the scope for structural adjustment is greatest.

title: Altruistic Consumption Behaviour: An Exploratory Study in Kerala Context
affiliations: Government College Madappally, Kozhikode and Government College Madappally, Kozhikode

detail.title: Altruistic Consumption Behaviour: An Exploratory Study in Kerala Context
detail.abstract: This study examines the altruistic consumption behaviour among consumers in Kerala. Altruistic consumption involves consuming choices driven by concern and sympathy for others, encompassing sustainable (eco-friendly), ethical, and socially responsible products and services. As Kerala is one of the most literate and progressive states in India, the study investigates how altruistic values influence consumption patterns. The research methodology includes both qualitative and quantitative approaches, relying on consumer surveys, personal interviews for data collection. Research findings reveal that consumers in Kerala are massively favouring altruistic consumption, influenced by principles of social wellbeing, environmental sustainability, and cultural heritage. Nevertheless, factors such as economic limitations, brand consciousness, and the availability of choices also significantly impact these behaviours.

title: The status of workers and platforms in the sharing economy
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The status of workers and platforms in the sharing economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, volume 28, issue 1, 2019[10.1111/jems.12299]

detail.abstract: We consider whether workers who provide their services through online platforms like Handy and Uber should be classified as independent contractors or employees. Using a formal economic model, we show how being too strict or too liberal in classifying workers as independent contractors (relative to the actual degree of control workers have) can be detrimental, not just to firms and welfare, but sometimes to the workers themselves. We also use the model to explore the extent to which an intermediate classification of workers between employees and independent contractors may lead to better outcomes. The intermediate classification is meant to apply to firms that retain control of some actions while their workers control others, as is the case for many online platforms.

title: Logistics Disorder and Social Cost Governance Under E-Commerce's Vicious Low-Price Involution: A Systematic Study and Policy Recommendations Based on the "One-Cent Free Shipping" Phenomenon

detail.title: Logistics Disorder and Social Cost Governance Under E-Commerce's Vicious Low-Price Involution: A Systematic Study and Policy Recommendations Based on the "One-Cent Free Shipping" Phenomenon
detail.abstract: This study takes the micro consumption phenomenon of "one-cent free shipping" as the entry point to systematically analyze the deep-seated problems of vicious involution in the logistics industry, price signal distortion, and market mechanism failure caused by the extreme low-price competition of e-commerce platforms. Based on social cost theory, market failure theory, and the core connotation of the development of a unified national market, this study combines the 2021-2025 official statistical bulletins of the State Post Bureau of China, 2025 public financial reports of A-share listed express delivery companies, regional regulatory pilot cases in Zhejiang and Guangdong provinces, and empirical research on consumer behavior. It clarifies the transmission logic of "low-price involution-logistics disorderexternalization of social costs-unsustainable development of the entire chain", and reveals the systematic harm of this phenomenon to the highquality development of the real economy, stable livelihood and employment, green and low-carbon transformation, and national macroeconomic regulation. This study holds that the vicious involution in the current circulation field is essentially the failure of the market regulation mechanism, Logistics Disorder and Social Cost Governance Under E-Commerce's Vicious Low-Price Involution 2 rather than the inevitable result of the market economy. On this basis, this report puts forward a set of governance schemes with both academic rigor and policy operability from four dimensions: industry bottom-line regulation, price signal restoration, legal system improvement, and circulation layout optimization. It clarifies the boundary and connection path between "antiinvolution regulation" and the current legal system, and finally points to the construction of a national anti-involution institutional system, providing decision-making reference for relevant departments to improve the supervision of the circulation field and promote the construction of a unified national market.

title: Disappearing Schumpeterian Growth: From Superstar Scaling to Arrested Dynamism
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers University, Newark

detail.title: Disappearing Schumpeterian Growth: From Superstar Scaling to Arrested Dynamism
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the rising concentration among the largest U.S. firms and its shifting implications for productivity from 1985 to 2023. I document a fundamental regime shift in the drivers of concentration --- from a period of "superstar scaling" to a modern era of "arrested dynamism" --- marking the disappearance of Schumpeterian growth at the upper tail of the firm size distribution. Using a micro-audited Melitz-Polanec decomposition, I show that aggregate productivity drivers structurally inverted: alongside collapsing within-firm efficiency, reallocation surged and a severe negative selection drag emerged. Then, using CS-DiD event-study estimates, I found that while acquisitions historically boosted physical productivity, modern acquisitions led to persistent declines in both productivity and internal growth. To explain this reversal, I develop a model endogenizing the choice between synergistic integration and defensive shelving. I uncover two primary mechanisms: rising organizational costs that weaken internal scaling, and high markup stakes that incentivize acquirers to "shelf" targets to prevent cannibalization and markup erosion. My results imply that modern concentration reflects a strategic shift toward protecting market power at the expense of creative destruction, leading to a decoupling of concentration from productive efficiency.

title: From Full to Partial Personalization: Performance Bounds for Fixed-Price Policies in Dynamic Pricing with Limited Inventory
affiliations: University of British Columbia, Singapore Management University - Lee Kong Chian School of Business and University of British Columbia

detail.title: From Full to Partial Personalization: Performance Bounds for Fixed-Price Policies in Dynamic Pricing with Limited Inventory
detail.abstract: Personalized pricing can enhance retailer revenue relative to uniform pricing when customer valuations differ. Yet, fully implementing it in practice remains challenging. Partial personalization, where a retailer offers a limited number of price points, is a practical alternative. We examine fixed-price policies under varying degrees of price personalization. Our setting involves selling a single product to N customer types with limited inventory over a finite planning horizon. When customers are segmented into K groups, with 1 < K < N, we prove that jointly finding the optimal segmentation and pricing is NP-hard. We propose an efficient segmentation approach and establish a non-asymptotic performance guarantee for the induced K-personalized fixed-price policy. When inventory is sufficient, we further establish an exponential convergence rate to the optimal policy, an improvement over the classic polynomial rate. Our numerical results demonstrate that the marginal benefit of increasing personalization diminishes as K grows. We demonstrate the value of varying degrees of personalization. Our results show that retailers can capture most of the potential gains from personalization with just a few price segments, and that the performance gap from using a simple fixed-price policy shrinks rapidly when inventory is not the main limitation.
