detail.abstract: This paper aims to examine the impacts of the interest rates imposed by the central bank of India-the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)-on real estate companies and, more specifically, how much debt the companies have accumulated. We use financial data from three large developers, DLF, Godrej Properties, and Oberoi Realty, to monitor the increase and decrease in the cost of borrowing and profits of these companies as interest rates rose and fell between 2021 and 2026. The main conclusion is that although an increase in rates does raise the cost of borrowing, it does not affect all companies equally. Those that reduced their debt prior to an increase in rates were mostly not affected. In contrast, those with substantial debt experienced much more prominently negative effects. However, it is the common domestic buyers who have had to bear the largest financial burden of all.

title: Investigating the relationship between generative AI usage and wellbeing: a multi-dimensional analysis of work and private life
affiliations: , International University of Japan, International University of Japan and International University of Japan

detail.title: Investigating the relationship between generative AI usage and wellbeing: a multi-dimensional analysis of work and private life

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All study participants provided informed consent, and the study design was approved by the appropriate ethics review board. The name of the research ethics review committee is GLOCOM Research Ethics Review Committee, and the approval number is GE25001.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by Google Japan, JST Moonshot R&D Grant Number JPMJMS2215. We would like to express my deepest gratitude to them.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether generative AI (GenAI) is accepted from the perspective of well-being, and aims to derive policy and practical implications for its diffusion. Using large-scale survey data from Japan, it investigates how GenAI use and usage frequency are associated with multiple dimensions of well-being and whether these associations differ between work-related and private use. The results show that the relationship between GenAI use and well-being is not uniform, but varies according to the context of use and the dimension of well-being. Although GenAI use was associated with well-being in both work-related and private contexts, the patterns differed. Private use was more strongly linked to positive affect and the factors of connections and gratitude, whereas work-related use was more strongly linked to lifetime satisfaction and the factors of self-realization and growth. Furthermore, some dimensions show an inverted U-shaped relationship with usage frequency, suggesting that excessive use may reduce well-being. These findings highlight the limitations of understanding the relationship between the GenAI and well-being through a single indicator or a simple distinction between use and non-use. The novelty of this study lies in three points: distinguishing between work-related and private use within the same sample, measuring well-being as a multidimensional construct rather than as a single indicator, and examining not only whether GenAI is used but also how frequently it is used. These findings suggest that the relationship between GenAI and well-being should be understood as multidimensional and conditional on the context and intensity of use.

title: Dam Trouble: Transdisciplinarity and the Case of a Riverine Livelihood Study in Northeastern Cambodia
affiliations: Institute of Asian Studies and University of Brunei Darussalam

detail.title: Dam Trouble: Transdisciplinarity and the Case of a Riverine Livelihood Study in Northeastern Cambodia

keywords: transdisciplinarity ; knowledge co-production; non-academic stakeholders; riverine livelihoods; hydropower dams; social conflict theory; politics of scale

detail.abstract: This chapter considers the impact of the state-capital-development nexus on transdisciplinary projects in the Global South. By recounting fieldwork experiences from a riverine livelihood study of dam-induced issues in northeast Cambodia, it details how eliciting and integrating credible knowledge co-production from relevant stakeholders is especially vulnerable to such influence. Adopting a social conflict-cum-politics of scale lens, the chapter analyses the weight various actors brought to bear. At the same time, it critiques a tendency to overemphasise methodological challenges in transdisciplinary projects. Instead, we redirect attention to the impact of inimical and asymmetrical relationships among non-academic stakeholders on project aims and rationales.

title: Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures and Swaps: A Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: EIM European Institute of Management, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Perpetual Futures and Swaps: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: This systematic literature review synthesizes research on cryptocurrency perpetual futures and perpetual swaps. It examines 22 substantive studies, comprising 15 peer-reviewed publications and 7 academic working papers, with emphasis on work published from 2021 to April 2026, while retaining directly relevant foundational contributions. Reported in line with PRISMA 2020, the review asks how the literature defines perpetual contracts, explains pricing and funding mechanisms, characterizes basis behavior and convergence, evaluates market quality and price discovery, analyzes leverage and liquidation, compares centralized and decentralized exchange designs, and addresses legal classification and regulation. The evidence indicates that pricing and no-arbitrage theory are the most mature strands of research. Peer-reviewed studies generally find that funding-based design reduces rollover frictions and improves spot tracking relative to dated futures. Yet perpetuals do not eliminate risk. They relocate risk into funding windows, leverage choice, liquidation cascades, informed trading, venue architecture, and regulatory fragmentation. The empirical literature is strongest on market microstructure and risk management, but remains thinner on trader behavior and systematic CEX-DEX comparison. Legal scholarship shows persistent instability in classification and cross-border arbitrage. The review concludes that the next research frontier lies in funding-rule design, spot-market spillovers, stress transmission, and exchange-architecture comparison.

title: The Bluem Constant (B₀): A Baseline Parameter for Modeling Minority Effects, Behavioral Conversion, and System Sensitivity

detail.title: The Bluem Constant (B₀): A Baseline Parameter for Modeling Minority Effects, Behavioral Conversion, and System Sensitivity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently and without external influence from institutions, organizations, or commercial entities.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental interventions. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted as part of the author’s independent research activities.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Bluem Constant (B₀), a model-based baseline parameter for representing persistent minority deviation from dominant norms in socio-economic systems.
A recurring challenge in modeling such effects lies in the heterogeneity of empirical estimates, which limits cross-context comparability and integration into generalized system models.

B₀ addresses this gap by providing a synthetic, model-relative reference value that captures the structural persistence of norm-deviating subpopulations without relying on empirical calibration.
Rather than representing a tipping point or threshold, B₀ functions as a stable baseline parameter that enables sensitivity analysis and behavioral conversion modeling across heterogeneous scenarios.

The paper formalizes the role of B₀ within a minimal analytical framework linking baseline deviation, conversion dynamics, and system-level impact.
By separating structural recurrence from empirical variability, the Bluem Constant supports consistent modeling of minority-driven effects in systems characterized by non-linear responses under constraint conditions.

title: Tracing the First Science Textbook Written in Korean by Korean to be used by Korean: Focusing on the Science Textbooks in Primorsky Krai 1930s
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Tokyo

detail.title: Tracing the First Science Textbook Written in Korean by Korean to be used by Korean: Focusing on the Science Textbooks in Primorsky Krai 1930s
detail.abstract: Having textbooks written in the native language plays a crucial role in providing contextualized and culturally grounded education. However, in South Korea, it has generally been understood that Koreanwritten science textbooks first appeared in the 1950s. This study challenges that assumption by examining science textbooks written and translated in Korean by Korean, and used by Korean diaspora (고려인) in the 1930s in the Primorsky Krai (연해주) region, particularly in Khabarovsk schools. By analyzing both the historical context and the content of these materials, this research aims to broaden the understanding of the history of science education in Korea. The primary sources for this study consist of 1930s Korean-written science textbooks collected from the Russian State Library in Moscow. The first author, specializing in science education, conducted the primary analysis of the textbook content, while the second author, an expert in East Asian history, examined the historical context surrounding their production and use. Chapter II describes the Korean communities residing in the Primorsky region in the early 20th century. Chapter III briefly reviews the characteristics of Korean science textbooks during the Enlightenment period and the Japanese colonial era (1900s-1930s), situating the 1930s diaspora science textbooks within this broader trajectory. Chapter IV provides content analysis of the textbooks. Finally, Chapter V discusses the implications of these findings for the history of science textbooks and science education, and suggests directions for future research.

title: Private Equity and the Organization of Firms
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam - Erasmus School of Economics, University of St. Gallen - School of Finance and Tsinghua University, SEM

detail.title: Private Equity and the Organization of Firms
detail.abstract: We study how private equity (PE) buyouts reshape the internal organization of firms. Using data on over 10,000 U.S. PE buyouts combined with resume information of more than five million employees, we track changes in hierarchies, managerial control spans, and functional structure. Contrary to a widely cited view that PE streamlines and flattens organizations, we find that hierarchies become deeper after buyouts and managerial control spans shrink. PE-owned firms reallocate employment from product-related functions toward administrative and operative roles, while management expands into more specialized functions. These organizational changes hold across deal types and outcomes and persist after PE exits. Overall, our evidence suggests that PE buyouts create value by strengthening firms' organizational capabilities-enhancing how tasks and decision-making are structured and coordinated within the firm-rather than concentrating decision-making in flatter hierarchies.

detail.abstract: Il paper analizza il divario tra la crescente digitalizzazione dei contratti pubblici e il ricorso prevalente agli affidamenti diretti sotto la soglia dei 140.000 euro. Strumenti come la Banca Dati Nazionale dei Contratti Pubblici e il Fascicolo Virtuale dell’Operatore Economico aumentano la trasparenza nelle gare competitive, ma non incidono sulla zona opaca degli affidamenti diretti. Il lavoro evidenzia la tensione tra trasparenza algoritmica e scelte discrezionali non digitalizzate, proponendo un rafforzamento dei presidi nelle aree più esposte all’opacità. This paper examines the gap between Italy’s advanced digitalization of public procurement and the dominant use of direct awards below the €140,000 threshold. While tools such as the National Public Contracts Database and the Virtual File of the Economic Operator enhance transparency in competitive procedures, they remain ineffective in the opaque area of direct contracting. The paper highlights the tension between algorithmic transparency and non‑digital discretionary choices, arguing for stronger oversight where opacity is structurally concentrated.

title: Sexual Corruption in Ireland and Northern Ireland
affiliations: Dublin City University Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Dublin City University - School of Law and Government and Transparency International

detail.title: Sexual Corruption in Ireland and Northern Ireland
detail.abstract:
This report presents new evidence on sexual corruption - the abuse of public power for sexual gain - in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. Here, sexual corruption refers to situations in which a public official implies, either openly or suggestively, that a public service or benefit will be granted in exchange for sexual favours. The report draws on original survey research designed by the DCU Anti-Corruption Research Centre (ARC) in collaboration with Transparency International (TI) Ireland and the Transparency Legal Advice Centre and funded by Research Ireland under the New Foundations scheme.

The findings indicate that sexual corruption is present across a range of public service settings in both jurisdictions. Among respondents who answered the sexual corruption questions in the survey, 10.9% in the Republic of Ireland and 7.1% in Northern Ireland reported that they or someone they knew had encountered sexual corruption in at least one public service domain. Even under a conservative assumption that all respondents who opted out of the sensitive module had encountered no such corruption, estimated prevalence remains higher in the Republic of Ireland (8.5%) than in Northern Ireland (6.6%).

These findings are consistent with earlier evidence pointing to the risk of sexual corruption in Ireland, though the estimates are not directly comparable. TI’s 2021 Global Corruption Barometer (GCB), which found that 4% of the Irish respondents reported direct experience or knowledge of sexual corruption with 68% believing that it was likely to be a problem. Our survey asked about specific areas of interaction with public services, which may help to explain the higher reported incidence observed here by prompting respondents to think about specific public service settings and concrete experiences, rather than asking only for a general assessment of the issue.

Reported experience spans multiple domains of public administration. In the Republic of Ireland, the highest reported prevalence is in policing, schools and universities, and immigration or passport services. In Northern Ireland, the highest reported prevalence is in schools and universities, policing, and local government. Education and policing therefore emerge as particularly important areas of concern in both jurisdictions.

Taken together, the evidence suggests that sexual corruption is not an isolated or purely anecdotal phenomenon. Rather, it affects a meaningful minority of adults across both jurisdictions and warrants sustained institutional attention, effective reporting pathways, and stronger safeguards across vulnerable public service domains.

title: Inflation Expectations, Firm Investment, and Production-Network Propagation
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey

detail.title: Inflation Expectations, Firm Investment, and Production-Network Propagation
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether inflation expectations shape firms' real decisions in a high-inflation environment. We use the CBRT's Business Tendency Survey, which directly elicits firm-level inflation expectations and investment plans, and match it with unique administrative datasets covering Turkish manufacturing firms over 2010--2024. The results show a strong expectations channel. Firms with higher inflation expectations report weaker investment, sales, employment, and macroeconomic expectations. These effects extend to realized outcomes: higher inflation expectations reduce investment, sales, employment, value added, TFP, R\&D spending, and automation adoption. The effects are substantially larger for SMEs, highly leveraged firms, and during the high-inflation period, indicating that financial frictions and nominal instability amplify the real consequences of inflation beliefs. We also show that inflation expectations propagate through production networks: firms exposed to suppliers and customers with higher inflation expectations experience weaker plans and lower realized performance, with supplier-side exposure playing the dominant role. Overall, the findings show that inflation expectations affect not only firms' sentiment, but also capital accumulation, productivity, and technology upgrading, highlighting the importance of expectation anchoring for investment and long-run growth.

detail.abstract:
Korean Abstract: 일본 스마트폰법은 EU 디지털시장법(DMA)과 마찬가지로, 디지털 시장에서 새롭게 제기되는 경쟁 우려와 사후적·사건별 경쟁법 집행 방식의 한계에 대응하기 위한 일종의 경쟁 규제로 이해되어 왔다. 나아가 동법은 DMA에 비해 규율 범위가 더 표적화되어 있고, 정당화 사유 등을 통해 더 유연한 접근을 취한다는 점에서 보다 실용적인 규제 모델로 평가되기도 한다. 그러나 이 글은 이러한 일반적 설명에 의문을 제기한다.  일본의 맥락에서 스마트폰법의 도입은 경쟁법인 독점금지법의 실체법적 불충분성 때문이라기보다, 독점금지법의 문언과 실제 집행 현실이 괴리된 구조적 과소집행 문제에 의해 더 잘 설명될 수 있다. 다시 말해, 일본 독점금지법은 디지털 시장의 경쟁 우려에 대응할 수 있는 수단을 이미 충분히 보유하고 있었지만, 실제 집행에서는 이들 수단이 제대로 활용되지 못하였고, 스마트폰법은 이러한 과소집행의 현실을 배경으로 도입된 것으로 보아야 한다는 것이다. 이러한 관점에서 볼 때, 스마트폰법은 다른 관할권에서 일반적으로 참고할 수 있는 입법례라기보다 일본 고유의 지속적인 집행 제약에 대응하기 위한 일종의 대증요법으로 이해할 수 있게 된다. 그리고 이러한 이해는 일본식 디지털 경쟁 규제 모델의 도입을 검토하는 관할권이 일본 스마트폰법의 내용과 장단점을 따지기에 앞서, 먼저 자국의 경쟁법 집행 체계가 일본과 같은 과소집행 문제를 겪고 있는지 신중히 검토할 필요가 있다는 결론으로 이어진다. 이러한 맥락적 차이를 간과한 채 비교·검토되거나 도입되는 제도는 자국의 경쟁 문제에 대한 해결책이 아니라 추가적인 규제 비효율과 사회적 비용을 초래할 위험이 있으므로 지양해야 한다.

English Abstract: Japan’s Mobile Software Competition Act (MSCA), like the Digital Markets Act (DMA), has generally been understood as a regulatory response to emerging competition concerns in digital markets and the inherent limits of ex post, case-by-case competition law enforcement. Moreover, the MSCA has been viewed as a more targeted and flexible alternative to the DMA and, in some accounts, as a potentially superior regulatory model. This paper challenges that conventional account. It argues that, in the Japanese context, the introduction of the MSCA is better explained not by the substantive insufficiency of the Antimonopoly Act (AMA), Japan’s competition law, but by the structural under-enforcement of the AMA itself. This perspective suggests that jurisdictions considering a Japanese-style model of digital competition regulation, such as Korea, should proceed with greater caution, asking first whether their own competition law systems suffer from comparable under-enforcement. Rather than serving as a generalizable model, the MSCA is better understood as a symptomatic remedy for Japan’s own persistent enforcement constraints; regardless of the MSCA’s ultimate success, Japan still faces the deeper institutional task of revitalizing AMA enforcement against unilateral conduct. Ignoring these contextual differences risks importing not a solution to domestic competition concerns, but an additional layer of regulatory inefficiency.

Author's note: This paper is a preprint of an article forthcoming in Competition Journal (경쟁저널), Issue 233 (2026).

detail.abstract: This paper is part of the "Internal Resistance Series" within the broader research program "Economic Guarantees of Security (EGS)". This paper develops the concept of Economic Guarantees of Security by introducing and analyzing the mechanism of internal economic resistance as a key element in the prevention of aggression. In contrast to traditional approaches to deterrence, which are primarily based on external military and political instruments, the proposed approach focuses on the transmission of the economic consequences of aggression into the internal structure of the aggressor state.

title: ISOLATING THE NON-LINEAR RESIDUAL IN HARMONISED XGBOOST-SHAP AND WALKER TVP ATTRIBUTIONS RESEARCH NOTE

detail.title: ISOLATING THE NON-LINEAR RESIDUAL IN HARMONISED XGBOOST-SHAP AND WALKER TVP ATTRIBUTIONS RESEARCH NOTE

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This research note extends a baseline-centred harmonisation of feature attributions across XGBoost models, interpreted via SHAP values, and Walker time-varying parameter (TVP) models (Myrland 2026). Once both frameworks are expressed on a common baseline-relative scale, estimated on the same restricted feature set, and fit under a common sampling and information design, the residual difference between their block-level attributions becomes substantially more interpretable. We formalise this quantity as an architecture-sensitive attribution gap and describe how it should and should not be read. The residual is not a purified measure of non-linearity: it may reflect threshold effects, asymmetries, interactions, regularisation differences, and alternative routing of predictive information under correlated predictors. We propose regime-conditional summaries based on withinregime variance and mean absolute magnitude, and provide an R implementation that builds directly on the harmonisation template of the companion note.

title: HARMONISING FEATURE ATTRIBUTION ACROSS XGBOOST-SHAP AND WALKER TVP MODELS RESEARCH NOTE

detail.title: HARMONISING FEATURE ATTRIBUTION ACROSS XGBOOST-SHAP AND WALKER TVP MODELS RESEARCH NOTE

declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: This research note proposes a methodological framework for harmonising feature attribution narratives between XGBoost models, interpreted via SHAP values, and Walker time-varying parameter (TVP) models. While both frameworks offer additive decompositions of predicted values, they differ fundamentally in their reference points: SHAP measures contributions relative to a global baseline, whereas raw TVP contributions are expressed in levels. We introduce a baseline-relative reformulation of the Walker model that centres regressor contributions around sample means, yielding a time-varying baseline that permits more disciplined comparison with SHAP. To account for multicollinearity and model architecture differences, we advocate for aggregating feature-level attributions into economically motivated blocks and evaluating both signed and absolute contribution shares.

title: Giving as a Strategic Response: How Demand Uncertainty Drives Corporate Donations
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Giving as a Strategic Response: How Demand Uncertainty Drives Corporate Donations
detail.abstract: This study examines whether firms strategically adjust charitable donations in response to demand uncertainty. We develop a newsvendor model where a firm jointly chooses inventory and per-unit donations that boost demand through consumer warm-glow but reduce margins. Using stochastic dominance analysis, we show that higher demand uncertainty increases optimal donation amounts under mild conditions, while higher cost discourages giving. We then test these directional predictions using a large panel of North American firms from 2002 to 2024. The empirical results reveal a positive association between demand uncertainty and relative donation intensity. This positive effect is amplified for firms with greater operational slacks but attenuated for those facing higher earnings volatility, consistent with slack resource theory rather than pure signaling mechanisms. We further instrument demand uncertainty with peer firms' average in a two-stage least squares (2SLS) setting to address potential endogeneity concerns. Our findings suggest that firms deploy charitable giving as a strategic operational response to turbulence, with implications for integrating philanthropic considerations into risk management. Finally, we present several key managerial implications for enterprises, policymakers, and stakeholders.

title: Beyond Scale Effects: Agricultural Emission Drivers, Decoupling Dynamics, and Environmental Kuznets Curve Evidence in Nigeria
affiliations: , Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P) and Africa Business School, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University

detail.title: Beyond Scale Effects: Agricultural Emission Drivers, Decoupling Dynamics, and Environmental Kuznets Curve Evidence in Nigeria
detail.abstract: This study examines the drivers and long-run dynamics of agricultural greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Nigeria using annual time-series data from 1990 to 2021. The analysis integrates three complementary approaches: Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition, Tapio decoupling elasticity analysis, and an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL)-based Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) regression. The LMDI results show that population growth and agricultural emission intensity emerged as the co-dominant positive drivers of emissions, while agricultural energy intensity provided the only substantial mitigating effect. Tapio decoupling analysis identifies weak decoupling as the dominant state; however, the frequency of expansive negative decoupling episodes increased markedly after 2005, signalling a deteriorating emissiongrowth relationship. The ARDL bounds test supports a stable long-run cointegrating relationship, and the long-run coefficients are consistent with a U-shaped income-emission intensity relationship. Taken together, the results indicate that scale effects currently outpace efficiency gains, suggesting that continued income growth may not translate into lower emission intensity without structural intervention. The decomposition evidence highlights biological intensification as a priority policy target. These findings carry direct implications for Nigeria's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) commitments and for the broader challenge of achieving development while decarbonising agricultural systems in Sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Monte Carlo Simulation for Indian Early-Stage Venture Capital Fund Analysis

detail.title: Monte Carlo Simulation for Indian Early-Stage Venture Capital Fund Analysis

keywords: and the FX Trap Venture Capital

detail.abstract: This study uses a comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation approach to analyse Indian early-stage Venture Capital (VC) fund performance, referenced against real-world performance benchmarks from Accel India, Peak XV Partners (previously known as Sequoia India), Blume Ventures, and Elevation Capital. Ten thousand independent iterations across a 22-company portfolio over a ten-year fund lifecycle were executed to model complete fund lifecycles under conditions specific to India including: power law return distributions; the existence of secondary dominant exit routes; currency devaluation effects from the INR/USD exchange rate; and, LP cashflow waterfall mechanics inclusive of full carried interest and management fee structures. The primary results show that the median Indian VC fund produces a net internal rate of return (IRR) of 1.1% and a net multiple of invested capital (MOIC) of 1.7x, which are dramatically lower than the first quartile benchmarks (Peak XV's benchmark IRR = 31.0%; Accel India's benchmark IRR = 28.5%) and confirm that returns are highly concentrated among a small number of top-performing fund managers. Holding period was identified in the sensitivity analysis as the largest driver of IRR, therefore far exceeding the combined impact of failure rate, portfolio size, and follow on ratio. Finally, a new analysis called FX Trap demonstrates that 20% IRR in Indian Rupee (INR) terms can lead to sub-12% IRR in United States Dollar (USD) terms for international LPs, due to a historical average annual depreciation of 3.5% for INR relative to USD-representing a structural risk that has been grossly under-disclosed in marketing materials produced by Indian VC funds. There were material J-curve implications associated with liquidity management versus long-term return optimisation inherent in how portfolios were constructed using four different strategies. The paper contributes an India-specific quantitative framework to VC analysis literature, addressing the gap between US-centric academic models and the distinctive structural features of Indian private capital markets.

title: Who controls the global petrochemical industry, and how might that change?

detail.title: Who controls the global petrochemical industry, and how might that change?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-4
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Petrochemicals—used in everything from fertilizers, solar panels, clothing, and cosmetics to electric vehicles, electronics, and medicines—are integral to food security, manufacturing, and clean energy. They are also becoming the fastest-growing source of demand for oil. The 2026 conflict in the Middle East has exposed vulnerabilities in petrochemical supply chains, especially since Middle Eastern producers account for much of the global supply of key petrochemical products, including fertilizers, and one-third of global seaborne fertilizer trade transits the Strait of Hormuz. Understanding the petrochemical industry, including its size, geographical distribution, and ownership and control structure, is essential to reduce risks from geopolitical shocks, hostile takeovers, and fragile supply chains.

title: Solving the Housing Crisis Through Incentive Redesign: A Game-Theoretic Policy Framework with Application to Spain

detail.title: Solving the Housing Crisis Through Incentive Redesign: A Game-Theoretic Policy Framework with Application to Spain
detail.abstract:
Housing serves two functions: shelter provision and wealth storage. When the investment function dominates, individually rational accumulation produces a collectively destructive equilibrium. Prices decouple from incomes, younger cohorts are excluded from ownership, and urban form degrades as workers are displaced from employment centers.

Spain exemplifies this dynamic. Price-to-income ratios exceed 10× in Madrid and Barcelona. Only 15% of individuals aged 18–34 live independently. Simultaneously, 3.83 million dwellings remain vacant while urban housing supply is constrained.

Cross-country evidence from fifteen markets shows that isolated supply-side or demand-side interventions fail. A coordinated framework is required. The proposed system consists of nine instruments grounded in mechanism design theory, Pigouvian taxation, and new economic geography:

  • Limited vacation-rental licensing

  • Residency-based purchase restrictions

  • Income-indexed pricing

  • Progressive property accumulation taxation

  • Supply-linked youth access incentives

  • Institutional investor deterrence

  • Intergenerational transfer protections

  • Strengthened property-rights enforcement

  • Territorial rebalancing mechanisms addressing geographic concentration as a coordination failure

These instruments shift the system from an accumulation-dominant Nash equilibrium to an access-dominant equilibrium.

The optimal tax structure is defined as:

 𝜏(𝑛)= 𝜏0·exp(𝛼(𝑛−1))

This function renders accumulation unprofitable beyond four to five properties. Estimated fiscal impact: €7 billion annually after behavioral adjustment (€14.3 billion pre-adjustment).

Legal feasibility aligns with the Spanish Constitution (Articles 47, 33, 128) and Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. The closest precedent is the secondary-residence restriction regime in Austria.

The framework operates on observable data and incentive-compatible compliance, minimizing reliance on discretionary enforcement. It generalizes to other European markets exhibiting similar structural imbalances.

title: Digital Transformation and Systemic Risk in Nigeria's Banking System

detail.title: Digital Transformation and Systemic Risk in Nigeria's Banking System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced the design, conduct or reporting of this study. This research was conducted independently and is free from any conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based entirely on secondary data drawn from publicly available institutional sources, including the Central Bank of Nigeria Financial Stability Reports, NIBSS annual statistics, World Bank Databases, IMF Financial Soundness Indicators, and published bank audited financial statements. No human participants, patient data, or private personal information were involved. Formal ethics committee approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was self-funded and conducted independently by the author in connection with doctoral research preparation.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study is an empirical econometric analysis of bank sector data and does not in volve any clinical trial or intervention research

detail.abstract: This study provides the first comprehensive empirical analysis of the relationship between digital transformation maturity and systemic risk in Nigeria's banking system, situating Nigeria within the broader Sub-Saharan African (SSA) context. Nigeria represents the most significant case study within the region: it is simultaneously Africa's largest economy by GDP, one of its most densely populated fintech ecosystems, with over 200 fintech firms and electronic payment transactions exceeding ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2024, and a banking sector historically characterized by recurrent fragility, oil sector concentration risk, and supervisory gaps. The study constructs a novel Digital Transformation Maturity Index (DTMI) integrating five dimensions including mobile money adoption, digital payment activity, internet banking penetration, mobile banking usage, and digital infrastructure, calibrated specifically for Nigeria and SSA banking systems. Employing a two step System Generalized Method of Moments (sys-GMM) estimator to address system-intrinsic variation, the study analyses panel data covering 26 licensed commercial banks in Nigeria and a comparative cohort of 61 banks across 11 other SSA countries over the period 2012 to 2025. Results reveal a statistically significant non-linear, inverted U-shape relationship Digital Transformation and Systemic Risk in Nigeria's Banking System Mustapha Ayobami Jamiu | 2 between digital transformation and bank stability measured by the bank level Z-score and the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio. The estimated stability maximizing DTMI threshold is approximately 43 to 47 index points, and beyond this threshold, systemic risk escalates, which is consistent with a synthesis of Schumpeterian creative destruction theory and network fragility theory. Nigeria's current average DTMI of approximately 54 places it above this threshold, rendering the country's banking system particularly exposed to the second phase systemic risk associated with advanced digitalization. The 2025-2026 CBN recapitalization programmes, which raised ₦4.65 trillion in new capital, partially mitigates these risks but leaves structural vulnerabilities, including a rising NPL ratio of approximately 7 per cent at end of 2025, legacy infrastructure fragility, and nascent cyber-risk governance, unaddressed. Regulatory quality emerges as a critical positive moderator of the digital stability nexus, with Nigeria's removal from the FATF grey list in 2025 signaling institutional improvement. Policy implications are elaborated for the Central Bank of Nigeria, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and international development partners.

title: Frontier AI and the Financial Services Threat Model: Implications of Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview for UK Banks and Building Societies

detail.title: Frontier AI and the Financial Services Threat Model: Implications of Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview for UK Banks and Building Societies

keywords: AI Security Institute. JEL Classification: G21 (Banks

detail.abstract: Anthropic announced Claude Mythos Preview on 7 April 2026. The company chose not to release the model publicly, citing its demonstrated ability to find and exploit software vulnerabilities autonomously across every major operating system and every major web browser. Access is instead being channelled through Project Glasswing, a restricted partner programme covering roughly 40 to 50 critical-infrastructure operators. Within days of the announcement, the UK AI Security Institute published an independent evaluation confirming that the model represents a material advance in autonomous offensive cyber capability, and the Governor of the Bank of England warned publicly that Mythos could, in his words, crack the whole cyber risk world open. This paper examines what Mythos actually changes for the threat model facing UK banks and building societies, and what a proportionate response looks like. It argues that Mythos does not introduce new categories of vulnerability, but that it compresses time-to-exploit, lowers the cost of chained multi-stage attacks, and accelerates supply-chain risk propagation. Drawing on the AISI evaluation, NCSC defensive guidance, the Bank of England's public statements, and the peer-reviewed literature on large language models in cybersecurity, the paper sets out five sector-level recommendations covering third-party assurance, vulnerability management tempo, chained-attack exercising, identity hardening, and board-level governance. The paper concludes that existing frameworks, including the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework, Cyber Essentials, ISO/IEC 27001 and the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, remain fit for purpose. What changes is the cost of the residual risks those frameworks were already designed to manage.

detail.title: Operational Efficiency and Service Lead Time Reduction During Peak Demand Cycles

detail.abstract: This technical report presents a Lean Six Sigma (LSS) case study focused on optimizing operational efficiency and reducing service lead time at a Halal restaurant in Miki, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan. During peak demand cycles, specifically Friday congregational prayer windows, the facility experienced service delays of up to 35 minutes, exceeding customer expectations and leading to a high rate of order cancellations. By implementing the DMAIC (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) framework and utilizing tools such as Value Stream Mapping (VSM) and Root-Cause Analysis, the project identified critical bottlenecks in the service flow. The proposed interventions, including workload balancing (Heijunka) and 5S workplace organization, target a 48% reduction in lead time and a 25% increase in throughput capacity.

title: Behavioral Finance, Consumer Protection, and Financial Decision-Making: Strengthening Economic Stability Through Cooperative Financial Institutions in the United States

detail.title: Behavioral Finance, Consumer Protection, and Financial Decision-Making: Strengthening Economic Stability Through Cooperative Financial Institutions in the United States
detail.abstract: Behavioral biases significantly influence financial decision-making, often leading individuals to make suboptimal choices that contribute to financial instability, debt accumulation, and longterm economic vulnerability. While traditional financial models assume rational behavior, extensive research in behavioral finance demonstrates that cognitive limitations, emotional influences, and structural barriers shape how individuals interact with financial systems. This article examines the role of behavioral finance in consumer financial protection, with a specific focus on cooperative financial institutions such as credit unions in the United States. It develops a leadership-driven framework that integrates behavioral insights into financial product design, risk governance, and consumer protection strategies. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature in behavioral economics, financial regulation, and organizational leadership, the study argues that credit unions are uniquely positioned to mitigate behavioral risks and enhance financial wellbeing. The findings highlight that incorporating behavioral finance into cooperative financial leadership represents a matter of substantial merit and national importance, contributing to financial inclusion, consumer protection, and long-term economic stability.

title: Negotiating a win-win end to the lose-lose US-China trade war over technology and critical minerals

detail.title: Negotiating a win-win end to the lose-lose US-China trade war over technology and critical minerals

declarations.funderStatement: PIIE gratefully acknowledges the financial support from One True North LLC for the research presented in this Working Paper. The research was conducted independently; funders are never given the right to review a publication before its release.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-5
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The United States and China put parts of the global economy at risk in 2025 through their trade war over critical minerals and technology. A series of escalatory tariffs and export restrictions led to shortages of essential inputs, nearly forcing automakers worldwide to shut down production. The costly policies reflected uncoordinated and uncommunicated efforts by both countries to reduce their mutual economic dependence. This paper explores a novel path for the United States and China to "cooperate" over how they reduce their dependence on each other in technology and critical minerals, with the aim of limiting future escalation risks and avoiding unnecessary costs. The proposal draws on a version of the reciprocal approach to negotiations developed under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, modified to accommodate a mutual reduction in each country's market dominance in key sectors.

title: Wealth Thermalization Phase Transition Equation and CRJ Intensity Model: A Diagnostic and Policy Tool for Wealth Condensation from an Econophysics Perspective

detail.abstract: Wealth polarization represents the most severe structural challenge of the postindustrial era. Traditional inequality measures, such as the Gini coefficient, are insensitive to extreme tail dynamics and lack connections with statistical physics phase transition theory. Drawing on dissipative structure theory and the Rayleigh-Jeans condensation analogy, this paper derives and quantifies two coupled diagnostic tools from microscopic stochastic dynamics: the wealth thermalization phase transition equation and the Capital Re-concentration Junction (CRJ) intensity model.

title: Cross-Border Financial Systems and Economic Integration: The Strategic Role of U.S.-Canada Cooperative Banking in Strengthening North American Financial Stability

detail.title: Cross-Border Financial Systems and Economic Integration: The Strategic Role of U.S.-Canada Cooperative Banking in Strengthening North American Financial Stability
detail.abstract: The increasing interconnectedness of global financial systems has elevated the importance of cross-border financial integration as a driver of economic stability, trade efficiency, and institutional resilience. Within North America, the financial relationship between the United States and Canada represents one of the most stable and strategically significant bilateral systems in the world. While much of the existing literature focuses on large commercial banks and capital markets, the role of cooperative financial institutions, particularly credit unionsm, remains underexplored. This article examines the contribution of cross-border cooperative banking to financial stability, small business development, and regional economic integration. It develops a leadership-driven framework for enhancing cross-border collaboration, regulatory alignment, and risk governance within credit unions operating in or interacting with U.S.-Canada markets. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature in international finance, banking regulation, and organizational leadership, the study argues that strengthening cross-border capabilities within cooperative financial institutions represents a matter of substantial merit and national importance. The findings highlight how credit unions can serve as strategic intermediaries in facilitating economic integration, enhancing financial inclusion, and supporting long-term economic resilience across North America.

reference: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-6
title: Lessons from three global collective action problems

detail.title: Lessons from three global collective action problems

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Working Paper No. 26-6
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper compares three global collective action problems, those involving climate change, international trade, and international taxation. First, each problem is assessed in terms of fundamental elements that stymie global collective action: concentrated interests that deter action in the face of larger yet diffuse benefits, cross-jurisdictional policy spillovers, and free-rider incentives at the jurisdictional level. Second, each problem is assessed in terms of four key elements that help address global collective action problems: (i) broad understanding of the policy problem, (ii) formation of a coalition willing to take policy action, (iii) enforcement mechanisms that incentivize policy adoption and protect adopters from nonadopters, and (iv) leadership. The paper concludes by discussing lessons from the three global collective action problems, set in the context of contemporary geopolitical developments. Although all solution elements are important, adequate incentive mechanisms are a pivotal factor in resolving global collective action problems; such mechanisms can also strengthen global collective efforts in the face of would-be spoilers.

title: Belonging, Moral Economy, and Effective Demand: Reinterpreting Adam Smith for Inclusive Development

detail.title: Belonging, Moral Economy, and Effective Demand: Reinterpreting Adam Smith for Inclusive Development
detail.abstract:
This paper reinterprets Adam Smith as a theorist of moral and institutional coordination and extends this framework through the Economics of Belonging. It argues that economic participation depends on structures of belonging that integrate individuals into stable institutional systems.

The paper introduces a central proposition: effective demand is the economic expression of belonging, and the middle class is its structural carrier. A formal analytical framework shows that below a threshold level of belonging, increases in income do not translate into sustained demand or growth.

This perspective provides a reinterpretation of economic development in which sustained growth emerges from the expansion of a socially integrated middle class rather than from capital accumulation alone. The paper contributes to institutional economics, post-Keynesian demand theory, and moral economy.

title: Wealth Management Costs in Brazil: ETF vs. Active Funds under Different Advisory Models

detail.title: Wealth Management Costs in Brazil: ETF vs. Active Funds under Different Advisory Models
detail.abstract: This dissertation quantifies how the cost of different advisory remuneration models, and product, shape long-run investor outcomes in Brazil. Using monthly data from January 2010 to December 2024, we implement a deterministic cash-flow engine that nets fees and taxes in their exact order and timing, and a Monte Carlo module with common shocks across three architectures: (H1) ETFs under fee-based advice, (H2) actively managed mutual funds under fee-based advice with cashback and come-cotas, and (H3) actively managed mutual funds under commission-funded distribution. Gross return paths are held identical across architectures to isolate cost and tax mechanics. Deterministic and stochastic results show H1 dominates on terminal wealth and exhibits tighter downside; H2 underperforms due to higher ongoing costs and tax pre-collection; H3 is intermediate. In simulations (10,000 paths, 20-year horizon), mean terminal wealth equals R$4.82m for H1, R$3.44m for H2, and R$3.93m for H3; with median findings consistent. A portfolio-level break-even alpha of ≈1.9 pp per year is required for active configurations to simply match H1, a hurdle that is improbable to be achieved according to empirical literature. Sensitivity tests on advisory and administration fees, and rebalancing cadence/frictions, leave rankings unchanged. The findings support cost-minimizing implementation with fee-based advice and suggest policy value in transparency over embedded inducements.

detail.abstract: Despite rapid growth in formal financial account ownership across emerging and developing economies, a persistent gap between account access and active digital payment use remains a barrier to financial inclusion. Drawing on Technology Acceptance Theory (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003) and Institutional Theory (North, 1990; Scott, 1995), we employ multilevel logistic regression on 143,887 individuals nested within 139 economies from the World Bank Global Findex 2021. An intraclass correlation of 0.564 establishes that 56.4% of the variance in digital payment adoption is attributable to country-level factors, reframing adoption as an institutional rather than an individual-behavioral phenomenon. Formal account ownership is an exceptionally strong predictor of digital payment adoption (Firth-corrected OR ≈ 20.3, p < .001), net of mobile phone ownership, confirming that financial access, not digital connectivity, is the binding individual-level constraint. Institutional quality significantly moderates this relationship (β = 0.594, p < .001): predicted adoption among account holders rises from 27.5% in lowgovernance environments to 78.5% in high-governance environments, a 51 percentage-point spread that is 1.8 times larger in low-and middle-income countries than in high-income economies. Government Effectiveness and Regulatory Quality are the dominant moderating channels. Results replicate across seven robustness specifications. While the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, these findings reframe digital financial inclusion as an institutional governance challenge and provide central banks and financial regulators in emerging economies with specific, actionable investment priorities for closing the access-to-usage gap.

title: China's Online Mutual Aid Platforms and Inclusive Insurance: Access Expansion, Operating Logic, and the Limits of Platform-Based Risk Sharing
affiliations: Indiana State University - Scott College of Business

detail.title: China's Online Mutual Aid Platforms and Inclusive Insurance: Access Expansion, Operating Logic, and the Limits of Platform-Based Risk Sharing
detail.abstract: China's online mutual aid platforms were a major experiment in inclusive insurance. Their rapid expansion showed that digital ecosystems can extend insurance-like protection to populations underserved by conventional insurance. Their retrenchment, however, showed that scale and lowfriction enrollment do not by themselves create durable risk-bearing institutions. This article provides a critical review of the Chinese mutual-aid experience, focusing on how the platforms operated, why they expanded access, what current research implies about their welfare and equilibrium properties, and whether the model is viable over the long run. It argues that mutual aid is best understood not as a stable substitute for insurance, but as transitional inclusion infrastructure. Its strength lay in reducing entry barriers through digital distribution, low upfront price salience, embedded trust, and simple contract design. Its weakness lay in ex post cost sharing, limited coverage, selection pressures, and legal ambiguity. The article concludes that the most promising future lies in hybrid platform-insurer models.

detail.abstract:
This paper identifies a fundamental architectural flaw in the modern global economy: the progressive decoupling of productivity from consumption driven by systemic automation and capital financialization. As automation displaces labor at a rate that outpaces the creation of new roles, the primary mechanism by which households receive a share of economic output — wages — breaks down. Simultaneously, sovereign monetary systems create a structural incentive to debase currency, making reliable economic measurement impossible. Together, these dynamics produce a Velocity Crisis: capital pools in non-productive assets, the consumer base undergoes secular exhaustion, and Knightian Uncertainty accelerates the hoarding feedback loop that caused the initial stagnation. To address this, the author proposes a jurisdiction-agnostic economic protocol centered on three integrated mechanisms: (1) the Universal Anchor, a protocol-defined unit of account maintained by collective adoption rather than sovereign control — analogous to a measuring standard rather than a backed currency — that makes monetary debasement visible in real time; (2) an automated, possession-based demurrage fee on non-productive idle assets, designed to penalise stagnation rather than productivity and financed through self-enforcing ledger compliance; and (3) a Global Universal Basic Income floor, denominated in Anchor units and funded by the demurrage, that maintains systemic circulation and converts Knightian Uncertainty into manageable risk at population scale. Moving beyond traditional UBI models, this specification treats the GUBI as a mechanical maintenance requirement for market stability — coolant, not charity. The protocol utilises network exclusion and asset illegitimacy rather than state coercion to drive adoption, creating a self-reinforcing equilibrium in which the cost of non-participation exceeds the cost of demurrage compliance. This document is presented as Draft Specification v1.0, establishing the foundational physics of the system while identifying five open design challenges for collective engineering.
This specification was developed through the iterative dialogue documented in the companion paper: A Commoner and Two AIs Walk into an Economy (available separately on SSRN).

title: A Cautionary Note on Interpretable Machine Learning for Macro-to-FX Transmission: Evidence from SHAP, Permutation Testing, and Walk-Forward Validation

detail.title: A Cautionary Note on Interpretable Machine Learning for Macro-to-FX Transmission: Evidence from SHAP, Permutation Testing, and Walk-Forward Validation
detail.abstract: We ask a simple question: can interpretable ML reliably detect macroeconomic transmission to exchange rates? To find out, we apply XGBoost with SHAP to four EURbase currency pairs over 2000-2024, then run multiple layers of validation-permutation testing with bootstrap confidence intervals, Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg correction, publication-lag robustness, a logistic regression benchmark, Granger causality pre-screening, and walk-forward Diebold-Mariano evaluation against the random walk. The short answer: one signal out of twelve survives uncorrected permutation testing, none survive multipletesting correction, and none produce forecasts that beat the random walk. The EUR/USD rate differential is the only feature whose SHAP importance is statistically non-random (|SHAP| = 0.7991, p = 0.030), and it survives a publication-lag correction that drops CPI and GDP importance by roughly 20%. Granger tests find the CPI differential has linear predictive content for EUR/USD and EUR/GBP that SHAP distributes between collinear features without isolating. Rolling window analysis shows rate differential importance is time-varying, tracking the Fed-ECB divergence cycle. But none of this survives to useful forecasts. Walk-forward Diebold-Mariano testing shows XGBoost produces probability forecasts that are significantly worse than always predicting 0.5 across all four pairs, with Brier scores 16-19% higher than the random walk baseline-a direct replication of the Meese-Rogoff puzzle using a modern ML framework. The paper's contribution is a reproducible template for honest interpretability in FX research: you can find the features, but finding them does not mean you can predict with them.

detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine the relationship between institutional quality and corporate cash holdings using a panel data regression analysis, consisting of 20,988 firms across 27 countries for the period of 2010 to 2023. Institutional quality is proxied by judicial efficiency and control of corruption. The study reveals that firms operating in corrupt environments are expected to hold more cash because of both precautionary purposes and the need for liquid assets to facilitate bribery. The findings of the study show a strong positive relationship between corruption and cash holdings. However, a major contribution of this study is that judicial efficiency significantly mitigates this effect. The positive relationship between corruption and cash holdings is weaker in countries with more efficient judicial systems. These results are more noticeable in emerging economies, where legal systems are often weaker, reinforcing the agency cost hypothesis and highlighting the importance of institutional quality in corporate financial decisions.

title: From Runway to Code -Fashion's Evolution from 1.0 to 6.0 Through the Lens of Bourdieu's Capital
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Silesia in Katowice - Poland Faculty of Law and Administration and Mackenzie Presbyterian University

detail.title: From Runway to Code -Fashion's Evolution from 1.0 to 6.0 Through the Lens of Bourdieu's Capital
detail.abstract: This study explores the convergence of fashion and modern technology-a phenomenon now popularly termed "fashtech"-through the lens of Pierre Bourdieu's theory of capital. As the industry integrates innovations ranging from smart textiles and wearables to digital marketplaces and artificial intelligence, the traditional notions of economic, cultural, social, and symbolic capital require redefinition. By revisiting Bourdieu's framework, this paper investigates how technological progress reshapes the accumulation and distribution of these capitals. It is argued that digital advancements not only enhance creative expression and community connectivity but also redefine brand prestige and consumer identity in an increasingly digital economy. Additionally, the role of intellectual property (IP) is discussed as a critical yet complex variable that both complements and challenges Bourdieu's original framework. New insights are offered on how these dynamics impact power relations and status within the contemporary fashion landscape. The paper concludes by discussing future directions and proposing that a holistic integration of technological, legal, and sociocultural perspectives is vital for understanding the evolving interplay of capitals in fashion.

detail.abstract: This document is the companion record to The Closed-Loop Economy: Draft Specification v1.0. It reconstructs the full iterative dialogue between a human author — a formally trained economist reasoning outside institutional frameworks — and two AI systems (Gemini and Claude) across multiple rounds of exchange. The dialogue covers the initial argument-building, subsequent stress-testing against economic objections and external critique, the corrections that arose from that testing, and the final architectural decisions that shaped the published specification. It includes the moments where the AI systems defaulted to conventional economic thinking and were corrected by the human author, making visible the process by which the protocol's core arguments were built and hardened. The dialogue is presented not as supplementary material but as an independent contribution to the question of how human-AI collaborative reasoning can produce original intellectual work. It is offered as both a proof of process and a model of a way of thinking.

title: From Payouts to Payrolls: Corporate Payouts and the Real Economy *
affiliations: School of Business, University of Kansas

detail.title: From Payouts to Payrolls: Corporate Payouts and the Real Economy *
detail.abstract: Corporate payouts have grown substantially in recent decades, sparking debate over their broader economic consequences. Using IRS county-level dividend data, I find that higher dividend income is associated with greater local job creation, particularly at small and young establishments. To identify the causal effect, I exploit plausibly exogenous variation from a shift-share instrument and a difference-indifferences design around special-dividend surges in 2010 and 2012. The effect operates through two channels: higher local consumer spending and greater small business lending driven by increased bank deposits. The employment effect is weaker when households are more likely to reinvest dividends, consistent with the interpretation that payouts affect the local economy primarily when capital is directed into the local community through households. Overall, the findings suggest that corporate payouts facilitate capital reallocation from mature public firms to the local economy, implying that policies limiting payouts may have unintended consequences.

title: The gender gap in fisheries and climate policy: insights from Southeast Asia
affiliations: University of Leeds, Universitas Pelita Bangsa, University of Rhode Island, , University of the Philippines Visayas and University of Leeds

detail.title: The gender gap in fisheries and climate policy: insights from Southeast Asia

declarations.funderStatement: This work was part of the ClimateREEFS project (Grant no: 110141), co-funded by the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the International Development Research Centre (IDRC) Ottawa, Canada as part of the Climate Adaptation and Resilience (CLARE) initiative. The views expressed herein do not necessarily represent those of the UK government, IDRC or its Board of Governors.

detail.abstract: Climate change poses significant challenges to coastal communities in Southeast Asia, where fisheries are not only vital for food security and livelihoods but are also deeply gendered. Women play essential roles across the fisheries value chain, yet their contributions and vulnerabilities remain largely invisible in policy frameworks. Here, we analysed the extent of gender integration in fisheries and climate policies (n = 115) in Indonesia and the Philippines-two countries with high female participation in fisheries and significant climate vulnerability. Our findings reveal a greater level of gender integration in the Philippines, particularly at higher governance levels, with Indonesia's efforts to mainstream gender at a nascent stage. However, both countries lack actionable strategies and resource allocation to operationalize gender commitments at local levels. Policies also represent gender equality as a women's issue and primarily portray women as homogeneously vulnerable, overlooking intersecting identities and local contexts. This approach has led to gender strategies that focus on institutional structures or women as beneficiaries, with limited attention paid to gender dimensions at a community level. Our results emphasise the need to strengthen implementation mechanisms at local levels, embed intersectional perspectives, and improve coordination between governance levels and sectors to support gender-responsive and inclusive climate adaptation in the fisheries sector.

title: A scalar metric of the real quantity of capital for the case of heterogeneous capital a working paper

detail.title: A scalar metric of the real quantity of capital for the case of heterogeneous capital a working paper
detail.abstract: Any economy can be defined as a composition of two sectors, an "integrated" consumption good sector that produces net output of a consumption good or a composition of consumption goods while reproducing its own capital inputs and an integrated capital goods sector that produces real growth capital for the entire economy while reproducing its own capital inputs. If the composition of the capital of the two sectors is identical, capital is said to be "homogeneous," although the real capital-labor ratios in the two sectors need not be identical. In prior work, this construct was used to define a scalar metric of real capital quantity, the integrated labor time of its production-the labor time required to produce the capital as a net output while reproducing capital inputs without growth. The value of capital in consumption good can then be decomposed into a real quantity and a necessary price, independent of the quantity, equal to the ratio of the per capita rnet products of the two sectors. Per capita r-net product is defined as the per capita net output of a sector in integrated production, net of profits, at a common profit rate r. The per capita r-net product of a sector is de facto its real wage rate. This paper applies those concepts to the case of "heterogeneous capital" in which the real capitals of the two sectors do not have the same composition. This lays the foundation for analysis of the neoclassical theory of production and distribution on the basis of a mathematically consistent metric of real capital quantity for capitals of arbitrary compositions.

title: Private Equity Industry Spotlight: Turning Profit-Maximizing Financiers Into Stewards of the Public Interest

detail.title: Private Equity Industry Spotlight: Turning Profit-Maximizing Financiers Into Stewards of the Public Interest
detail.abstract: This industry spotlight on private equity aims to demystify the underlying business and market structures of the private equity industry to inform conversations about how to ensure that this industry's products and actions contribute to the public interest. We propose a vision for how private equity firms could serve the public interest of a democratic society, both in their role as financial service providers and as temporary owners of companies in the "real" economy. Next, we explore the private equity business model, along with common tactics that private equity funds use to extract value from their portfolio companies. This analysis shows how far private equity is from upholding our proposed civic vision for the industry. We conclude by discussing policy strategies for aligning the private equity industry with the public interest, including regulations for private equity, guardrails for other industries in which private equity is investing, and strategies for building countervailing power among other economic stakeholders.

title: The Value Inertia Paradox Theory: A Model of Capital Sovereignty in the Era of Programmable Monetary Systems (CBDC) (Teoria Paradoksu Inercji Wartości: Model suwerenności kapitału w warunkach programowalnych systemów monetarnych)

detail.title: The Value Inertia Paradox Theory: A Model of Capital Sovereignty in the Era of Programmable Monetary Systems (CBDC) (Teoria Paradoksu Inercji Wartości: Model suwerenności kapitału w warunkach programowalnych systemów monetarnych)
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework, the Value Inertia Paradox, to analyze capital theory within increasingly digitized monetary ecosystems, specifically focusing on Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC). Drawing on Copernicus's monetary principles and Shoshana Zuboff's surveillance capitalism theory, the author posits that digital transformation shifts the function of money from a neutral medium of exchange to an instrument of potential economic programming. The core of the study is the formalization of the Sovereignty Value Model 𝑉𝑠 = 𝐼 * 𝑅 𝐾 𝛼 which quantifies the relationship between behavioral inertia (I), systemic rigor (R), and kinetic pressure (K). The research identifies a "Point of Utility Singularity," where excessive systemic control leads to an asymptotic collapse of money's perceived utility, triggering capital flight into non-monitored assets.

title: Local Financial Capability and Firm Investment Efficiency
affiliations: University of Arkansas, Fayetteville - Department of Accounting and

detail.title: Local Financial Capability and Firm Investment Efficiency
detail.abstract: Local financial capability (LFC) reflects the financial expertise and investment activity of firms' local labor pool and stakeholder base. Based on the resources-based theory, we expect firms headquartered in areas with high LFC, measured using publicly available tax data, to be associated with better investment outcomes. We find a positive association between high LFC and investment efficiency that is consistent with both a direct labor pool and an indirect stakeholder effect. We find that accounting and finance occupational intensity, as opposed to educational intensity, explains the overall association, differentiating our measure from those used in prior studies. We also show that high LFC is positively associated with future firm-level returns on capital investment. Our LFC measure provides practitioners with a unique way to identify pools of financially capable capital investment funders or internal investment decisionmakers.

title: X Influencers, Personality, and Incremental Returns

detail.title: X Influencers, Personality, and Incremental Returns
detail.abstract: Social media platforms such as X have reshaped retail investor activity and market behavior. This study documents that Big Five personality traits extracted from X posts about U.S. equities exhibit a systematic link to excess returns. Conscientiousness (CON) alone is tied to positive near-term performance that diminishes at longer horizons, consistent with the market correctly pricing a credibility signal whose directional content, absent accompanying positive substance, becomes less favorable as subsequent information arrives. When combined with positive sentiment, CON corresponds to returns that rise steadily across horizons without correction, consistent with conscientious optimism serving as a leading indicator of earnings outcomes that are confirmed gradually over the quarter and correctly priced as each piece of fundamental information is revealed.

title: Painting the Resumes: Employee LinkedIn Revisions and Future Firm Performance
affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland and

detail.title: Painting the Resumes: Employee LinkedIn Revisions and Future Firm Performance
detail.abstract: We examine whether employees' labor-market-facing disclosure activity—specifically, their LinkedIn revisions—inadvertently reveals their private assessments of firm prospects, thereby predicting future firm performance. Using a comprehensive sample of current and historical LinkedIn employment profiles, we track revisions in employees' experience descriptions for the same position over time. We first show that employees who make LinkedIn revisions are approximately twice as likely to leave the firm in the subsequent quarter, especially when revisions include not only current but also former positions, consistent with such revisions representing employees' strategic, labor-market-oriented disclosure decisions. Aggregating to the firm level, we find that LinkedIn revision activity incrementally predicts weaker future firm performance, beyond realized turnover and Glassdoor reviews. This predictive effect is stronger for revisions initiated by employees in senior, financial, and managerial roles—employees who are more likely to possess value-relevant private information. Finally, we show that LinkedIn revision activity predicts earnings surprises and stock returns, suggesting that investors do not fully incorporate this information. Taken together, our findings suggest that employees' labor-market-facing disclosure activity reflects their private assessments of firm prospects, highlighting a novel channel through which internal information diffuses to capital markets.

title: Blue Carbon and Mangrove Economics: Knowledge Hubs for the Pacific

detail.abstract: Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) collectively steward an estimated 630,860 hectares of mangrove ecosystems, representing one of the most carbon-dense and ecologically significant blue carbon repositories in the Indo-Pacific region. Despite the extraordinary potential of these ecosystems to generate internationally tradeable carbon credits under the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon market frameworks, the vast majority of Pacific nations remain structurally excluded from meaningful participation in international carbon markets. This exclusion is not primarily attributable to ecological deficit, but rather to a critical and persistent data infrastructure gap: the absence of systematic, standardised, and internationally verified carbon sequestration datasets required by market gatekeepers such as Verra, the Gold Standard, and Article 6 supervisory bodies. This article advances a comprehensive theoretical and operational framework for Pacific Blue Carbon Knowledge Hubs, defined as regionally networked, digitally integrated centres for the collection, validation, standardisation, and dissemination of mangrove carbon sequestration data across Pacific Island nations. Drawing upon secondary analysis of existing scientific literature, policy documents, market data, and institutional assessments, this study argues that Knowledge Hubs represent the decisive institutional innovation required to bridge the gap between Pacific ecological assets and international climate finance. The proposed three-layer architecture encompasses field monitoring and remote sensing infrastructure, an MRV (Measurement, Reporting and Verification) standardisation platform, and a market access gateway linked to voluntary and compliance carbon markets. Our analysis demonstrates that full deployment of the proposed Knowledge Hub network could unlock between USD 24.8 million and USD 89.5 million in annual carbon market revenues for Pacific nations, depending on market price trajectories and coverage expansion. Beyond direct financial returns, Knowledge Hubs would generate significant co-benefits including enhanced food security, coastal protection, biodiversity conservation, and indigenous community economic development.
