detail.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Pandemic-Era Federal Debt Normalization:
A Constitutional Framework for the Fiscal Treatment of Federal Reserve Held Treasury Securities

Kazimieras Venslauskas

Independent Researcher
Founder, Pandemic-Era Federal Debt Normalization Project

April 19, 2026

Abstract

The COVID-19 pandemic required unprecedented fiscal and monetary interventions to stabilize the U.S. economy. In response, the federal government issued several trillion dollars in Treasury securities, a substantial portion of which were subsequently acquired by the Federal Reserve through emergency market operations.

Although these securities are legally indistinguishable from market-held public debt, they exhibit distinct economic characteristics when viewed from a consolidated public-sector perspective, including largely circular cash flows and reduced refinancing exposure. Current statutory and accounting treatment does not reflect these distinctions, potentially overstating their long-term fiscal burden.

This paper presents a constitutionally grounded, one-time framework for normalizing the fiscal treatment of pandemic-era Treasury securities held by the Federal Reserve. The proposal preserves the full faith and credit of the United States, protects private and foreign creditors, maintains Federal Reserve independence, and avoids debt cancellation or monetary expansion.

By situating pandemic-era debt within established constitutional authority and post-emergency fiscal practice, the framework offers a structured approach to improving federal balance-sheet clarity and long-term fiscal sustainability.

Disclaimer:

This paper presents an independently developed policy framework intended to contribute to scholarly and policy discussion. It does not constitute an official position of any public authority or institution.

title: THE LEX AI: MANDATORY AI GOVERNANCE AND THE DIGITAL TRIBUNAL IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION

detail.title: THE LEX AI: MANDATORY AI GOVERNANCE AND THE DIGITAL TRIBUNAL IN INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION
detail.abstract:
Five years. Five cases. Three jurisdictions. One unmistakable pattern. In 2023, a New York federal court sanctioned counsel for submitting AI-generated, fabricated citations and then doubling down when challenged. In 2024, the Second Circuit entered a disciplinary referral against an attorney who submitted a nonexistent ChatGPT-generated authority. In November 2025, the Qatar Financial Centre Civil and Commercial Court in Doha issued a landmark judgment addressing the same conduct in an employment proceeding. In early 2026, the New York Appellate Division sanctioned counsel who continued filing AI-fabricated citations after being warned. And in April 2025, a petitioner argued before a United States federal court that an arbitrator had outsourced the reasoning behind a twenty-nine-page award to artificial intelligence, thereby presenting the first judicial test of whether AI-assisted award drafting constitutes grounds for vacatur under the Federal Arbitration Act. AI governance in international arbitration is no longer a future concern. It is the governing question of present practice.

This article argues that AI regulation now constitutes a distinct mandatory overlay on international arbitral proceedings, analogous to the lex data but constituting a separate and coequal class of obligations. This overlay, designated the lex AI, is anchored in two direct regulatory instruments (the European Union AI Act and ABA Formal Opinion 512) and is further informed by institutional guidance and an emerging indirect regulatory architecture. The article examines Nippon Life Insurance Company of America v. OpenAI, the first tort action naming an AI developer as a defendant in litigation-conduct claims. It critically assesses the ICCA-NYC Bar-CPR Cybersecurity Protocol, identifies a systematic AI governance gap, and proposes five targeted enhancements. The article analyzes the AAA-ICDR AI Arbitrator, the first institutional deployment of AI in the adjudicative function, and its companion Resolution Simulator, identifying their implications for high-risk compliance under the EU AI Act, New York Convention enforcement, and equality of arms. It concludes by presenting a tripartite framework for arbitral governance in the algorithmic age: lex arbitri governs procedural validity; lex data governs informational sovereignty; lex AI governs the digital tribunal. This article is the second of three companion articles constituting what the author proposes to call the Digital Procedural Constitution of international arbitration.

title: Priced out at age 18: Premium Increases and Community Based Health Insurance Disenrolment in Ethiopia -Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design

detail.title: Priced out at age 18: Premium Increases and Community Based Health Insurance Disenrolment in Ethiopia -Evidence from a Regression Discontinuity Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this study

detail.abstract: Does a discrete increase in health insurance premiums cause households to disenroll, and if so, who exits and at what cost to child health? I answer these questions using a regression discontinuity design that exploits a sharp, administratively determined increase in Ethiopia's community-based health insurance (CBHI) contributions triggered when the oldest dependent child reaches age 18; a rule that raises the household premium by as much as 25% of the fixed annual fee at the point of renewal. Applying this design to the 2019 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (N = 6,556 households), I estimate the causal effect of exposure to the surcharge on enrolment, test whether responses reflect adverse selection or liquidity constraints and estimate downstream effects on child vaccination using linked birth records. Crossing the age-18 threshold reduces CBHI enrolment by 9.2 percentage point, a 27.5% decline relative to the predicted enrolment rate at the cutoff, concentrated among rural and poorer households. Households with low baseline health status disenroll at higher rates than healthier households, consistent with liquidity constraints rather than adverse selection. The premium increase also reduces child vaccination completion by 27.2 percentage points, while antenatal care and facility delivery are unaffected. These findings suggest that age-triggered, flat-rate contribution structures undermine both equity and coverage objectives, and that income-graduated premium designs could improve retention among the households CBHI most needs to protect.

title: Path Signatures for Regime Detection in Cryptocurrency Markets: A Rough-Path Framework Using Spot, Perpetual Basis, and Funding Rates

detail.title: Path Signatures for Regime Detection in Cryptocurrency Markets: A Rough-Path Framework Using Spot, Perpetual Basis, and Funding Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that influenced this study. This paper is independent research conducted outside any institutional affiliation, sponsored research program, or employment relationship. The author holds no positions in Bitcoin, Ether, or any cryptocurrency derivative, and has no financial relationship with Binance or any other exchange or market participant referenced in this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses only publicly available aggregated market data from the Binance historical-archive service (data.binance.vision) and involves no human participants, personal data, or identifiable information. No ethics review was required under the Common Rule (45 CFR 46) or equivalent international guidelines.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding from any agency, institution, or private entity. All compute, data access, and software used in this study are either freely available or were accessed through the author's personal resources.

detail.abstract: We study market regime detection in cryptocurrency markets through the lens of rough path theory. Classical approaches -- hidden Markov models (HMMs) on returns, Gaussian mixture models, and rolling-window volatility thresholds -- impose Markovian or memoryless dynamics and summarize path information through low-dimensional moment statistics. In cryptocurrency markets, however, regime transitions are typically driven by reflexive leverage cycles, coordinated liquidations, and perpetual-swap funding imbalances: path-dependent, non-Markovian, multivariate phenomena that these approaches systematically underfit. We propose an alternative based on truncated path signatures, iterated-integral features of transformed price paths originating in the rough-path theory of Lyons [1998]. Our contributions are fourfold. First, we construct a crypto-native multivariate path combining BTC and ETH log-prices, a realized-volatility proxy, the perpetual-spot basis, and hourly funding rates, augmented with lead-lag and time transformations; basis and funding are directly observable measures of leverage positioning and, to our knowledge, have not previously appeared as signature coordinates. Second, we prove a universal-approximation bound (Theorem 3.4) for continuous regime-labeling functionals by linear functionals of truncated signatures, with an explicit depth bound in terms of the modulus of continuity of the target. Third, we benchmark signature-based regime features against Gaussian HMMs and rolling-volatility detectors on strictly out-of-sample downstream tasks using hourly Binance data, January 2020 through April 2026, approximately 5.5 × 10^4 observations. Fourth, we perform an event study across six canonical regime shifts (COVID-19, May 2021, Terra-LUNA, FTX, SVB/USDC, BTC ETF approval). Signature features deliver a 5-7 percentage-point accuracy advantage over returns-based HMM baselines on forward-volatility regime classification; the advantage localizes in third-order iterated integrals, validating the theoretical prediction; and signatures correctly anticipate the out-of-sample SVB/USDC event and correctly abstain on the bullish BTC ETF approval. Signatures do not solve directional return or drawdown prediction at sub-daily horizons, consistent with market-efficiency expectations. Code, data pipelines, and trained-model artifacts are released as a reproducible reference implementation.

title: The Emergence of Intelligent Payment Systems An AI-Driven Framework for Multi-Rail Payment Orchestration

detail.title: The Emergence of Intelligent Payment Systems An AI-Driven Framework for Multi-Rail Payment Orchestration
detail.abstract: The global payments ecosystem has evolved into a fragmented network of heterogeneous financial rails, including traditional banking systems, card networks, real-time payment infrastructures, and blockchain-based settlement layers. While these innovations have expanded capabilities, they have also introduced complexity, inefficiencies, and suboptimal routing decisions. This paper proposes a conceptual framework for artificial intelligence-driven payment orchestration, enabling dynamic routing of transactions across multiple payment rails based on contextual intent. The framework incorporates an intelligence layer that evaluates transaction attributes such as cost, speed, compliance, liquidity, and corridor-specific dynamics. By reframing payments as a decision-making system rather than a purely execution-driven process, this study contributes to the emerging discourse on intelligent financial infrastructure. The paper outlines the architectural components of such a system, discusses potential use cases, and highlights key limitations and areas for further research.

title: The Constitutional Question: Money, Sovereignty, and the Order That Was Never Built

detail.title: The Constitutional Question: Money, Sovereignty, and the Order That Was Never Built
detail.abstract:
Europe has repeatedly posed but never answered the foundational question of its monetary order: who authorises the arrangements that govern the currency, and who decides when those arrangements fail?

This paper traces that question from the Deutsche Mark crisis of 1969 to the Hormuz ceasefire of April 2026. It identifies a recurring mechanism — the "sovereign interval" between operative fact-creation and democratic authorisation — as the defining feature of European monetary governance. At six critical junctures (1972, 1978, 1990, 1993, 2012, 2015), the informal Franco-German axis overrode institutional constraints to preserve the monetary order, each time deepening operative arrangements without addressing the constitutional gap.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it introduces a typology of three post-Bretton Woods discipline regimes: constitutionalised (Germany/Bundesbank), externalised (Britain/City of London), and politicised-then-Europeanised (France). Second, it analyses the LIBOR-to-SOFR transition as a recentralisation of dollar pricing infrastructure — "plumbing sovereignty" — that repositioned Europe from functional core to collateral terrain within the global dollar system. Third, it identifies regulated stablecoins under the GENIUS Act (2025) as a structural analogue to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism: voluntary dollarisation without political backstop.

The analysis is genealogical and diagnostic, drawing on archival sources, central bank communications, and institutional research. It constitutes the monetary strand of a two-part analysis; the companion paper, "The Structural Constraint," traces the security architecture.

title: Menstrual Health Innovations in High-Severity Settings: The Role of Social Norms and Men for Adoption and Well-being
affiliations: , University of Groningen, University of Munich (LMU) and University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Menstrual Health Innovations in High-Severity Settings: The Role of Social Norms and Men for Adoption and Well-being
detail.abstract: Humanitarian organizations are skeptical about integrating reusable menstrual health innovations in high-severity settings. The established practice is to  distribute disposable pads because they do not require washing nor drying, and are known to be socially appropriate.   However,  they require repeated distribution. This paper provides novel evidence on the introduction of an innovative reusable menstrual product in three  high-severity humanitarian settings in Africa. Using primary quantitative data from  749 women, we document a wide adoption of the innovative technology,  substitution away from improvised and disposable products, and improvements in the well-being of women. Surprisingly, adoption of the product occurs even though there are very strict social norms that require all washing and drying of menstrual material to be completely concealed. Information sessions about the product, and extra awareness sessions with men in the household, do not change these social rules. Instead, women adapt how they manage their periods to comply with these norms. Our findings show that reusable menstrual products can improve well-being, as long as the product allows women to navigate social and material constraints in high-severity settings.

title: A documentation dataset for the Australian COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan

detail.title: A documentation dataset for the Australian COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available documents, Freedom of Information (FOI) materials, and official government records. It does not involve human participants, clinical data, or personal information. Accordingly, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This article describes a dataset compiled between 2022 and 2026 to support independent documentary analysis of the Therapeutic Goods Administration’s COVID-19 Vaccine Safety Monitoring Plan (February 2021). The dataset was assembled through Freedom of Information requests, Office of the Australian Information Commissioner review proceedings, Senate testimony analysis, and systematic review of Therapeutic Goods Administration publications. It comprises FOI decision letters, released government documents, OAIC submissions and determinations, Senate Hansard extracts, policy and surveillance documents, and an output-level evidence matrix assessing 19 Plan outputs using a structured four-tier classification framework.


The dataset relates to a vaccination program in which 68.4 million COVID-19 vaccine doses were administered under provisional approval. All materials were obtained through lawful public accountability mechanisms and archived across multiple independent platforms, including Zenodo, GitHub, and the National Library of Australia. The dataset provides a structured evidence base for examining documentation associated with the Plan’s pharmacovigilance strategies and supports reuse in pharmacovigilance research, health policy analysis, public administration, and regulatory accountability settings. This dataset enables systematic evaluation of regulatory transparency, the extent to which published commitments were implemented, and documentation practices in large-scale public health interventions.

title: REGULATORY OVERVIEW FOR GENERIC DRUG PRODUCT REGISTRATION IN CHINA & AUSTRALIA
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies (NMIMS), Students

detail.title: REGULATORY OVERVIEW FOR GENERIC DRUG PRODUCT REGISTRATION IN CHINA & AUSTRALIA
detail.abstract: Any modification to the already approved requirements is considered a change or variation. Post-Approval Changes or Variations are considered vital sections of the maintenance phase of the product life cycle. Changes such as Chemistry, manufacturing and Controls (CMC) are certain due to various reasons which include the change in the needs of an industry, new discoveries or findings and continuous growth. Hence, certain regulations need to be setup so that entire changes would be evaluated and trial as ubstitute regulatory path for implementation, in any case, whether it is a commercial or an investigational product. Failure to abide by the regulatory requirements for post-approval CMC changes caneventually lead to the product being labelled “misbranded” or “adulterated”. The potential safety impact of the marketed product for the vast population, as well as legal, regulatory and business impact for the sponsor depend upon the robustness of the evaluations of the changes and has to be taken very seriously. Considering the QbD model,exploiting the knowledge of product and process and employing a risk-based approach should enable a sponsor to achieve a superior path for implementing the post-approval changes. This study mainly focuses on such change categories.Pharmaceutical product life cycle management (PLCM) refers to the systematic approach to managing a pharmaceutical product's journey from development through to market withdrawal. The gathering of safety and efficacy data for medical treatments frequentlycontinuesevenafter a product has been approved. Regulatory agencies worldwide have specific requirements for conducting further studies following approval-related changes.Post-approval studies may take the form of either interventional CTs or non-interventional observational studies. Post approval studies are required and are mandatory to continuously collect data on the product's safety and effectiveness. The scope of pre-approval clinical trials limits the information that may be presented in regulatory filings for medical invention approval, specifically, drugs and devices. Depending on patient population characteristics, time for treatment, patient population size, and the ability to detect unexpected results, safety and efficacy could be limited.

title: THE EFFECT OF SIBLING SEX COMPOSITION ON FEMALE EDUCATION AND EARLY FERTILITY: EVIDENCE FROM CAPE TOWN, SOUTH AFRICA

detail.title: THE EFFECT OF SIBLING SEX COMPOSITION ON FEMALE EDUCATION AND EARLY FERTILITY: EVIDENCE FROM CAPE TOWN, SOUTH AFRICA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare as there is no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Nothing to declare as ethics clearance was not required for this work.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received.

detail.abstract:
Why does having sisters reduce a girl's chances of finishing school?

In Cape Town, South Africa, the sex of your siblings may quietly determine the course of your life. Using rich longitudinal data from the Cape Area Panel Study, tracking hundreds of adolescents through the critical transition from youth to adulthood, this paper uncovers a striking asymmetry: the sex composition of one's siblings shapes educational trajectories for young women, but leaves young men entirely unaffected.

Young women raised alongside sisters receive significantly less education on average - a finding that holds even after controlling for household size. Men? Unaffected. This gender asymmetry points to deeply embedded household dynamics that economics has yet to fully reckon with.

The implications reach further still. Leveraging sibling sex composition as an instrumental variable, following Case and Butcher (1994), this study reveals that standard estimates have been systematically overstating the returns to schooling for women when measured through reduced teenage pregnancy rates. The story we thought we knew about education and female fertility may need to be rewritten.

For researchers working at the intersection of development economics, gender, and family economics, this paper offers both a methodological contribution and an unsettling empirical result: the siblings beside you at the dinner table may matter more than we ever accounted for.

title: Identifying Agglomeration Spillovers: Evidence from Grocery Store Openings
affiliations: , UNC Kenan-Flagler Business School - Finance Area, Columbia University, Department of Economics and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Identifying Agglomeration Spillovers: Evidence from Grocery Store Openings
detail.abstract: We provide the first large-scale causal estimates of demand-side agglomeration spillovers in the non-tradable service sector, leveraging data on 851 grocery store openings across the United States between 2019 and 2022. We combine a convolutional neural network with propensity score matching to identify credible counterfactual opening sites and compare business outcomes between actual and counterfactual locations. Grocery store openings increase foot traffic to nearby businesses within 0.1 miles by 23.4 percent within 6-12 months, with spillovers decaying sharply beyond this radius. The effects are strongest for wholesale and retail establishments and hospitality services, and are substantially attenuated after COVID-19-from 42.7 to 14.6 percent-consistent with a trip-chaining mechanism. Grocery anchors also reshape the local business landscape: within 0.1 miles, establishment growth rates rise by 7.0 percentage points and employment growth rates by 8.8 percentage points, averaged over the first three post-entry years. Decomposing establishment growth rates, the effect is accounted for by higher entry and fewer exits.

title: Los Angeles Metropolitan Stabilization A Street-to-Home Pipeline Analysis

detail.title: Los Angeles Metropolitan Stabilization A Street-to-Home Pipeline Analysis
detail.abstract: Los Angeles's chronic unsheltered population persists because the pipeline connecting the street to housing has never been engineered. The city contains fifty million square feet of vacant commercial inventory. California has spent twenty-four billion dollars on homelessness programs since fiscal year 2019 with no measurable reduction in the encamped population. The Material Dignity Infrastructure represents an end-to-end industrial pipeline executing five simultaneous operations. A Clinical Field Architecture deploys Assertive Community Treatment teams to every chronic encampment corridor over a twelve-to-twenty-four-month pre-admission period. A Legal Lever System operates CARE Court, Assisted Outpatient Treatment, and LPS Conservatorship as parallel compelled pathways. A Housing Surplus Event opens two thousand pre-matched units at One California Plaza. An Environmental Compliance Enforcement Track addresses hidden riparian encampments operating FLIR-assisted mapping and Clean Water Act abatement proceedings. The Ontological Permanence Architecture sustains residents through STC 65 acoustic sanctuaries, sovereign Asset Limited Modular Units, Dunbar Pod social partitioning, and the Pod Steward. The fiscal model generates an eighty-two-million-dollar annual Efficiency Surplus per tower through municipal service cost elimination alongside capital recovery within twenty-nine months. Cohort-specific placement velocity, retention rates, reencampment metrics, net cost per person, CARE Court throughput, and actual efficiency surplus establish the verification thresholds for scaling this unbuilt street-to-home pipeline. These metrics must be met at the One California Plaza prototype before any expansion to the twenty-tower network.

title: Homelessness in Salt Lake County and the Proposed Utah Campus

detail.title: Homelessness in Salt Lake County and the Proposed Utah Campus

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Neither author has personal or financial relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this study beyond the contractal relationship with the funder of this report which was to produce an independent report.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve patients or research participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The report was funded by the Corporation for Supportive Housing

detail.abstract:
Salt Lake County is experiencing a sharp rise in chronic and unsheltered homelessness, prompting Utah policymakers to propose a large, centralized "transformative campus" of roughly 1,300 beds in the Northpoint neighborhood of Salt Lake City. The proposed facility would combine emergency shelter, a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC), at least 300 civil commitment beds, an "Accountability Center" offering involuntary substance use disorder (SUD) treatment as an alternative to jail, and wrap-around supportive services targeted at "high utilizers" of criminal justice and crisis systems. This report provides an independent, evidence-based assessment of whether the proposed campus is likely to reduce chronic homelessness and improve outcomes for people experiencing homelessness, and it identifies key risks, costs, and unresolved policy questions.

This report draws on Utah Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) and Point-in-Time (PIT) data, stakeholder interviews, peer-city case studies (San Antonio's Haven for Hope, Reno, Dallas, Phoenix, Atlanta, and Miami-Dade County's jail-diversion model), cost benchmarking against peer campuses and Utah's Homeless Resource Centers, and the national research literature. The report finds that: (1) rising homelessness in Salt Lake County is driven primarily by tightening housing markets, stagnant low-income wages, lagging growth in permanent supportive housing, and behavioral health system capacity constraints rather than by declining accountability standards; (2) the population legally eligible for inpatient civil commitment under the Americans with Disabilities Act integration mandate (Olmstead) is likely far smaller than the capacity planned for the facility; (3) evidence on centralized homelessness campuses is mixed, with the best chronic-homelessness outcomes achieved by cities pairing campuses with permanent housing investment; (4) several proposed treatment components, including involuntary SUD treatment, treatment-first sequencing, risk-mixing of low- and high-acuity residents, and CCBHC integration within a large homeless campus, lack strong supporting evidence and may underperform voluntary housing plus services approaches while geographic isolation and distance from transit pose additional structural risks; and (5) construction and operating cost estimates are likely substantially understated, as peer-benchmarked construction cost estimates are $142–165 million versus the cited $75 million, annual operating cost estimates approach $46–53 million versus the cited $34 million, civil commitment beds could cost $485+ per bed per day, and indirect transportation and public safety costs add roughly $13 million annually. Key risks include legal and civil rights exposure from involuntary placements, lack of behavioral health expertise on the Utah State Homeless Board, misalignment between planned capacity and eligible population, and operational complexity across state, county, and local systems. If Utah proceeds, the report recommends clear legal standards for involuntary placements, transparent long-term funding plans, independent outcome evaluation, and sustained parallel investment in permanent supportive housing and affordable housing.

title: Tax Penalty Limitation, Tax Litigation, and Tax Aggressiveness: Empirical Evidence from Companies Listed on B3
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research, FUCAPE Business School, FUCAPE Business School and FUCAPE Business School

detail.title: Tax Penalty Limitation, Tax Litigation, and Tax Aggressiveness: Empirical Evidence from Companies Listed on B3
detail.abstract: This study investigates the effects of the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court's (STF) decision to limit tax penalties on the tax behavior of publicly listed firms, while accounting for the moderating role of tax litigation history. Using an unbalanced panel dataset of companies listed on B3 for the 2010-2024 period, we adopt the Effective Tax Rate (ETR) and Book-Tax Difference (BTD) as proxies for tax aggressiveness. The empirical strategy exploits the institutional change consolidated in 2016 through regression models with interaction terms between the post-decision period and three alternative measures of tax litigation. Results indicate that the effects of penalty limitation are heterogeneous, varying according to firms' historical exposure to tax disputes. Specifically, firms with higher pre-2016 litigation intensity exhibit a relatively larger reduction in ETR after the ruling, consistent with both an economic deterrence channel and a tax risk re-pricing interpretation, while no significant effect is found for BTD, suggesting the mechanism operates through effective tax burden adjustments rather than through book-tax earnings management. The study integrates economic deterrence and institutional legitimacy theories, offering novel evidence on how changes in sanctioning regimes generate firm-level responses conditioned by prior enforcement interactions.

title: The AI Policy Paradox in Emerging Markets: Institutional Readiness vs. Technological Leapfrogging in ASEAN Public Sectors

detail.title: The AI Policy Paradox in Emerging Markets: Institutional Readiness vs. Technological Leapfrogging in ASEAN Public Sectors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The author’s affiliations with the International Legal Advisor at The Hague International Legal Center and THE LAM LAW LLC are provided for institutional identification and do not constitute a conflict of interest regarding the theoretical frameworks presented.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual working paper based on the analysis of existing institutional frameworks and technology transfer theory. It did not involve any human participants, animal subjects, or the collection of non-public personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Emerging markets frequently conceptualize artificial intelligence as a deterministic bypass for legacy administrative inefficiencies. This study dismantles the "technological silver bullet" fallacy prevalent in ASEAN public sector modernization initiatives. By examining the intersection of institutional economics and technology transfer theory, we identify a structural phenomenon, defined here as the Leapfrog Trap. The Leapfrog Trap materializes when state apparatuses procure hyper-advanced generative models without parallel upgrades to the cognitive and regulatory capacity of mid-level bureaucracy. This friction generates severe institutional dissonance. Technologies engineered for high-velocity data processing collide with low-velocity hierarchical analog governance structures. Consequently, the imported technology operates at a frequency that the host institution cannot fundamentally regulate. Drawing on the structural realities highlighted by the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics, this conceptual working paper argues that adopting frontier digital tools within transitioning economies frequently exacerbates existing institutional voids. We propose that substantive human governance and capacity building must aggressively precede algorithmic integration. Otherwise, state modernization efforts will yield a sophisticated structural paralysis.

title: Government support for firms with female-majority workforces: lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) and

detail.title: Government support for firms with female-majority workforces: lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 crisis amplified pre-existing vulnerabilities and posed a significant challenge to sustainable development. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data spanning more than 31,000 firm-year observations across 40 countries, we estimate the differential impact of the pandemic on firm outcomes by gender composition. Female-dominated firms-those with over 50% female employment-exhibit a higher probability of permanent closure and larger contractions in employment, operating hours, and sales relative to industry peers, with no evidence of systematic pre-pandemic performance differences between female-dominated and other firms. While these firms are more likely to receive government support and rely on grants, access is associated with both firm performance and the broader policy environment. Leveraging crosscountry variation in institutional settings and an instrumental-variable strategy to address endogeneity, we show that female-friendly policies attenuate these adverse effects. The results highlight the efficiency and equity gains from gender-responsive policy design in crisis contexts.

title: ENDOGENOUS PRICE STICKINESS AND THE LIMITS OF MONETARY POLICY

detail.title: ENDOGENOUS PRICE STICKINESS AND THE LIMITS OF MONETARY POLICY
detail.abstract: Firms adjust prices more frequently when inflation is high. This paper incorporates this empirical regularity into the New Keynesian Phillips curve by allowing the Calvo stickiness parameter to depend on aggregate inflation. The modification implies that monetary policy is effective at low inflation but loses traction as inflation rises-eventually becoming impotent. Estimating the Phillips curve slope by inflation regime in a global panel, I find a nearly 500-fold increase from low to very high inflation. Nonlinear least squares estimation from micro price-adjustment data spanning seven countries yields a half-life parameter of 28% annual inflation: stickiness erodes rapidly, and monetary policy effectiveness degrades substantially even at moderate inflation rates. Persistent fiscal deficits compound the problem by simultaneously eroding monetary policy space (through higher trend inflation) and fiscal policy space (through debt accumulation and rising sovereign spreads), creating a double trap in which countries lose both stabilization tools at once. The COVID-19 pandemic provides a natural experiment: countries with low pre-crisis inflation deployed effective stabilization policies and recovered quickly, while highinflation countries could deploy neither monetary nor fiscal tools and absorbed the shock through output contraction.

title: Evaluation of plant based indoor air purification in urban environments in Pakistan
affiliations: Beaconhouse National University, Beaconhouse National University, Beaconhouse National University, Beaconhouse National University, Beaconhouse National University, Beaconhouse National University, University of California, University of San Diego, University of Oxford - Rheumatology and Musculoskeletal Sciences and University of Oxford - Nuffield Department of Orthopaedics, Rheumatology and Musculoskeletal Sciences (NDORMS)

detail.title: Evaluation of plant based indoor air purification in urban environments in Pakistan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors declare that no funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: Indoor air quality (IAQ) has emerged as a critical public health concern in rapidly urbanizing cities like Lahore, Pakistan, where ambient pollution levels regularly exceed WHO safety thresholds during annual smog seasons. This study aims to quantify the independent and combined effects of indoor plants and natural ventilation on IAQ through a quasi-experimental design, with implications for affordable IAQ management in smog-affected urban contexts. Eight office spaces across Beaconhouse National University were monitored over three months (July-September) using Awair Element consumer-grade sensors measuring CO 2 , PM 2.5 , PM 10 , and TVOCs at five-minute intervals. Six air-purifying plant species-Dracaena trifasciata, Aloe vera, Epipremnum aureum, Chlorophytum comosum, Rhapis excelsa, and Chamaedorea seifrizii-were deployed to assess remediation capacity under varying ventilation scenarios. Results showed that natural ventilation was highly effective, with windowed spaces exhibiting 96.2% lower PM 2.5 (2 µg/m 3 vs. 53 µg/m 3) and 70.5% lower TVOCs (535 ppb vs. 1,814 ppb) compared to sealed rooms. Conversely, plants in non-ventilated spaces achieved substantial PM 2.5 reductions (96.7%) but paradoxically increased TVOCs by 63.3%, likely due to human activity overwhelming plant metabolic capacity. Temporal analysis revealed that CAM plants effectively reduced nighttime pollutants when occupancy ceased, though daytime human activity in sealed offices generated pollutants faster than plants could metabolize them. These findings demonstrate that phytoremediation effectiveness critically depends on adequate ventilation and appropriate space-to-plant ratios. The study concludes that meaningful improvements in IAQ in Pakistani urban contexts require integrated strategies combining ventilation, strategic plant deployment, and effective policies on human presence in enclosed spaces, particularly during Lahore's severe smog season.

title: Beyond the Symbolic Charter: Independent Ombudsman, Dispute Resolution, and Algorithmic Transparency in the New TaxPayer Defense Code
affiliations: University of Coimbra Institute for Legal Research

detail.title: Beyond the Symbolic Charter: Independent Ombudsman, Dispute Resolution, and Algorithmic Transparency in the New TaxPayer Defense Code
detail.abstract: The enactment of the Taxpayer Defense Code in Brazil (LC No. 225/2026), derived from Complementary Bill No. 125/2022, represents a significant legislative advance toward a model of cooperative compliance in the legal-tax relationship. However, the mere codification of rights does not ensure their effectiveness-a risk that legal doctrine refers to as a "symbolic charter." This article analyzes three structural deficits that threaten the effectiveness of the new law: the absence of a Tax Ombudsman's Office endowed with effective institutional independence; the procedural opacity generated by the Electronic Tax Address (ETA), which imposes on the taxpayer the burden of continuous digital monitoring under penalty of missing deadlines; and the algorithmic opacity in the Artificial Intelligence systems used by the Federal Revenue Service to select taxpayers, examined in light of the recent RFB Ordinance No. 647/2026. Based on empirical data from the IBFD Yearbook on Taxpayers' Rights 2024 and the comparative doctrine of Bentley, De Zeeuw, and Pedrosa López, this paper advocates for the adoption of three pillars: the creation of an independent Ombudsman, the incorporation of alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods, and the establishment of digital guarantees of explainability and mandatory human oversight, which taxpayers can invoke as subjective rights.

title: Large Language Models in Qualitative Research: Governance, Validity, and the Limits of Computational Assistance

detail.title: Large Language Models in Qualitative Research: Governance, Validity, and the Limits of Computational Assistance
detail.abstract: Qualitative and mixed-methods research faces intensifying pressure from expanding data volumes, prompting interest in large language models (LLMs) as analytic aids. However, LLM fluency risks conflating linguistic coherence with interpretation, obscuring judgment and scholarly responsibility. This article examines a protocol for LLM-assisted qualitative coding and literature synthesis. Drawing on qualitative traditions centered on meaning and theory-building, we develop a framework organized around research design, human judgment, and three dimensions of validity: interpretive, integrative, and bibliographic. Two empirical demonstrations ground the framework: a Dual-Coding Experiment on fifteen open-access interview transcripts reveals both “Context Collapse” and “Analytical Reach,” while a Bibliographic Stress Test documents a 63.2 percent distortion rate in LLM-generated literature syntheses. Responsible integration of LLMs requires strengthening—not relaxing—the methodological commitments that define qualitative inquiry.

title: Urban Density and the Variety of Cultural Amenities: Evidence from Movie Theaters
affiliations: , Singapore Management University, Singapore Management University - School of Economics, INSE at Peking University and Institute of Urban Development, Nanjing Audit University

detail.title: Urban Density and the Variety of Cultural Amenities: Evidence from Movie Theaters
detail.abstract: We study how urban density shapes movie variety. Movies are nontradable amenities whose standardized nature enables precise measurement of local variety. Using granular box office data from Chinese cities, we document a density premium: denser neighborhoods offer more distinct films, genres, and foreign productions at similar prices. Exploiting COVID-19induced population redistribution as a shock to localized density in an instrumented difference-indifferences framework, we find that a 10% increase in density raises the number of distinct movies by 0.6%, genres by 0.1%, and non-domestic films by 0.3%. Cultural variety responds endogenously to local demand, implying that policies affecting residential distribution shape cultural opportunities.

detail.abstract: The behavior of the school heads demonstrates how they supervise the teachers, which encompasses the quality of life and its stress. This study explored the quality of life and stress of teachers experiences during pandemic. This research utilized a phenomenological research design to assess the lived experiences of teachers in terms of their quality of life and stress from the pandemic period. The results of the study generate three (3) major themes and two (2) subthemes for teachers and school heads such as: (1) pandemic experiences and communication, a) challenges of pandemic to teachers and b) school head valuing teachers’ importance; (2) teachers and school heads’ adjustments during pandemic, a) different faces of pandemic adjustment and b) empowering the teaching community; and (3) work and leadership behavior, a) stress of extra workload of teachers and b) empathy, sensitivity, and conducive workplace. These findings underscore the urgent need for leadership development programs that equip school heads with the skills to not only manage tasks but to genuinely support the human beings in their charge, thereby transforming schools into environments that foster resilience and well-being for all.

detail.abstract: Promoting inclusive growth, which is economic progress that reduces poverty and inequality, remains a core objective of development policy across various country contexts. However, growth alone does not guarantee equitable outcomes. Public health spending plays a crucial role in determining whether economic gains are distributed equally among income groups. This study examines the impact of public and private health expenditures on the interrelated dynamics of economic growth, income inequality, and poverty. Specifically, it asks: to what extent do different health financing mechanisms affect inclusive growth, and how do these effects vary across country income groups? To address this question, we construct a system of three simultaneous equations that capture the relationships between growth, inequality, poverty, and health expenditures (both public and private), estimated using the three-stage least squares (3SLS) method. Our analysis is based on a balanced panel of 117 countries spanning the period from 2000 to 2021. Our results indicate that public health expenditure has a positive contribution to inclusive growth, particularly by reducing inequality and poverty. These effects are most pronounced in emerging and lowincome economies. By contrast, heavy reliance on out-of-pocket (OOP) payments is associated with weaker poverty reduction and rising inequality. This research contributes to the literature by integrating health financing into the analysis of inclusive development. The findings underscore the need for policy strategies that strengthen the redistributive capacity of health systems as a foundation for sustainable and equitable growth.

title: Applying LLMs: Granular Innovation Assessment Using Corporate Disclosures

detail.title: Applying LLMs: Granular Innovation Assessment Using Corporate Disclosures
detail.abstract: This paper aims to provide a novel methodology leveraging large language models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAl) to address current limitations of innovation assessment. The central methodological goal of this research is the creation of a replicable innovation assessment method. The suggested approach utilizes LLMs to systematically analyze vast amounts of unstructured textual data from corporate annual reports. By developing a comprehensive codebook to classify and by implementing a rigorous validation protocol that requires recursive textual citations for every identified instance, the methodology ensures data accuracy and mitigates common issues such as hallucination in generated outputs. Innovation types and their documented significance are rated on a 1-3 scale and visualized in a 3×3 matrix for an intuitive comparative analysis.

detail.abstract: This research investigates the rationale for additionally taxing addictive products such as alcohol, cigarettes, or drugs, behavioral economics, and public health policy.Addictive products create a host of problems, some directly and some not, affecting market prices, from increased tax burdens to decreased labor productivity. This research examines Pigouvian tax theory and international evidence to explain how well-planned special taxation measures against consumer goods that burden society can reduce such harmful consumption and steadily increase public revenue. The research highlights the importance of a shift towards customized taxation systems and strategic income allocation to combine tax efficiency with long-term public health benefits. While the study presents case studies and showcases successful practices from developing and OECD countries, it also reveals the undesirable consequences of excessive taxation: such as illicit trade and crossborder purchases. Evidence-based and balanced tax policies appear to be one of the most effective ways governments can build healthier societies and maintain economic sustainability. Abstract 1.Introduction Tobacco, alcohol, and increasingly sugary beverages "addictive commodities" pose considerable social and economic burdens in most societies around the world (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2023; World Health Organization, 2021). However, the cost of these addictive products to society is not reflected in market prices, leading to undesirable negative consequences that affect others (Chaloupka & Warner, 2000; Gruber, 2001). For example, smoking-related illnesses burden healthcare systems, while alcohol consumption reduces work productivity and increases accident rates (Anderson, Chisholm, and Fuhr, 2009; Wagenaar, Salois, and Komro, 2009). Excise taxes on such goods serve as a strategic intervention tool for public health and help governments address the problems caused by these addictive substances without allocating additional budgets (López-Nicolás & Stoklosa, 2021; OECD, 2022).

title: BLACK LABOR MATTERS
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: BLACK LABOR MATTERS
detail.abstract:
Black and organized workers increasingly find themselves threatened by two key outside forces: one seeking to stop anti-racism efforts via diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices and the other curtailing employees’ union organizing. This Article argues that a response must be grounded in uniquely local strategies by two specific worker coalitions. One coalition–the New Black Workers Movement (NBWM)–arose from Black Lives Matter civil rights protests in 2020 that captivated the workplace and heightened awareness about anti-Blackness and concerns of systemic racism. The other coalition–the New Labor Workers Movement (NLWM)–developed in 2020 as a workplace response to a global pandemic that reinvigorated concerted employee efforts to pursue comprehensive protections beyond racial justice for rank-and-file workers.

This Article reexamines the anti-DEI narratives that threaten the rights of many Black workers, with a particular focus on the growing legal consequences created by federal government actions and business reactions. To the extent that the federal government and businesses have started to adopt Project 2025’s anti-union agenda, these workers face additional vulnerabilities. The Article proposes that the NBWM and NLWM use local measures at a grassroots level to protect the interests of these vulnerable workers facing anti-DEI and anti-labor conditions.

Most scholars continue to question the viability of coalitions between civil rights and labor movements due to historical tensions between those groups. This Article disputes those concerns by considering a unique approach focused on specific “locations” where each group may thrive independently or via joint collaborations. These coalitions emerge from a rarely considered application of the interest-convergence principle to address matters of race and develop mass-organizing strategies for Black and organized workers. By capitalizing on each movement, these vulnerable workers can find a path to resistance, protect their livelihoods, and add value to the communities where they work. When the law may not provide the best respite for these vulnerable workers, they must do something to survive. Finding “locations” for successful NBWM-NLWM mergers enhances the opportunities for these workers’ continued advancement.

title: Exponentiality is Not an Assumption: An Ex-Post Valuation Model Based on Observed Asset Trajectories

detail.title: Exponentiality is Not an Assumption: An Ex-Post Valuation Model Based on Observed Asset Trajectories

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract:
The narrative that investing in stocks is equivalent to harnessing compound interest suggests that patient reinvestment would lead to exponential growth of wealth. This paper challenges this premise by proposing a simple yet overlooked metric: the Temporal Exponentiality Factor (E). To compute E, two models are fitted to the same price series – a linear model and an exponential model (via logarithmic regression, with predictions converted back to the original scale) – and their coefficients of determination (R²) are compared. When E > 0, the trajectory is better described by an exponential structure; when E < 0, the linear model is superior; when E ≈ 0, both forms are equivalent.

Applying the method to the Ibovespa (73 stocks with at least 15 years of daily data) and to global indices (15 years), the results show that exponentiality is rare: only 12 Brazilian stocks (out of 73) met the criteria of exponential R² ≥ 0.80 and E > 0. Most assets, including the Ibovespa itself (E = 0.035), exhibit a modest exponentiality factor, indicating predominantly linear (scalar) growth.

The paper further develops a hybrid ex-post valuation model that weights linear and exponential projections based on E. Applied to the 12 highest‑E stocks, the model reveals that current market prices are systematically above the hybrid projections (average difference of 48%), highlighting its diagnostic power – not as a forecast, but as an anchor that shows how far prices have strayed from their own historical trajectory.

We conclude that exponentiality is the exception, not the rule. Recognizing this is a necessary step toward a more realistic investment framework, and the Exponentiality Factor provides a simple instrument to identify, measure, and question the presence of this growth pattern.

title: A Fusion Framework for Prospective, Forensic Anomaly Detection in Complex Administrative Panel Data

detail.abstract: Medicare hospital cost reports constitute one of the largest longitudinal administrative datasets describing the financial and operational behavior of U.S.\ hospitals, yet they remain underutilized for proactive oversight and audit prioritization. This study introduces MOSAIC (Multi-Objective Signal Aggregation for Interpretable Classification), a weakly supervised forensic prioritization framework integrating analytical, behavioral, and model-based anomaly signals through multi-objective optimization. Applied to 83,512 hospital facility-years rom the Medicare Hospital Cost Report Information System (HCRIS) dataset (FY2011--2024), MOSAIC learns signal weights on a pre-pandemic Baseline regime (FY2012--2018) and applies them without modification to all other periods and validation data. MOSAIC achieves a Spearman concordance of $\rho_S = 0.5618$ with a financial distress anchor, compared with a maximum benchmark concordance of $\rho_S = 0.1173$. A signal-exclusion robustness analysis yields $\rho_S = 0.5394$, indicating that performance is not driven by anchor-adjacent variables or any single signal family. External validation using independent datasets of hospital bankruptcies and Medicare enforcement actions confirms that MOSAIC risk stratification anticipates real adverse events under a fully prospective design: risk scores constructed from prior-period ($t-1$) data identify high-risk facilities in subsequent periods ($t$), with approximately 53--54\% of events concentrated in the top two risk quintiles versus a 40\% null expectation. These findings demonstrate that distress-aligned anomaly risk in administrative healthcare data is better captured through domain-constrained multi-signal integration than standalone unsupervised or high-capacity reconstruction models, and that MOSAIC provides a scalable and interpretable framework for data-driven audit prioritization.

title: The Charitable Asset Deployment Agreement: A Structural Alternative to Public-Private Partnership Capital Architecture

detail.title: The Charitable Asset Deployment Agreement: A Structural Alternative to Public-Private Partnership Capital Architecture

detail.abstract:
Two prior papers establish a connected diagnosis. The first shows that public–private partnerships fail structurally — not because of poor contracts or weak governance, but because their capital architecture embeds extraction, temporal misalignment, and fragility into systems whose missions require long-horizon continuity (Ghadamian, 2025a). The second shows that PPPs persist not because they perform well, but because public accounting systems lack the categories to represent capital continuity, mission cycles, or deferred fragility — making PPPs appear fiscally responsible when they are merely accountingly convenient (Ghadamian, 2025b). Both papers call for new capital architectures. Neither specifies one.

This paper provides one.

The Charitable Asset Deployment Agreement (CADA) is a recoverable grant instrument designed for the deployment of capital assets — equipment, infrastructure, and physical resources — into public-benefit institutions without creating debt obligations, contingent liabilities, or balance-sheet recognition for recipient institutions. It achieves genuine off-balance-sheet treatment not through accounting arbitrage but through economic substance: the deploying foundation retains title, bears all risk, and in the worst case treats the deployment as a completed grant. There is no enforceable consideration. There is no extraction.

This paper presents the CADA as an existence proof. Using a worked example of diagnostic imaging equipment deployed into a public hospital, it maps the CADA's structural features against the architectural requirements identified in the prior papers — decoupling from fragility cycles, alignment with mission cycles, absence of embedded extraction, and legitimate off-balance-sheet treatment — and demonstrates that each requirement is satisfied. It then analyses the accounting treatment under AASB 16 / IFRS 16, showing why the CADA falls outside the lease classification framework as a matter of economic substance rather than contractual form. The paper concludes by defining the conditions of applicability, the instrument's limits at scale, and the tripartite extension structure for higher-value asset deployments.

The CADA does not resolve every limitation of public capital architecture. It does demonstrate that the alternative the literature calls for is not theoretical. It is constructable, operable, and legally deployable within existing Australian charitable and accounting frameworks today.

title: Longevity Finance: Banking Innovation, AI Governance, and Intergenerational Wealth Transfer in Aging Economies

detail.title: Longevity Finance: Banking Innovation, AI Governance, and Intergenerational Wealth Transfer in Aging Economies
detail.abstract: Financial systems were designed for a demographic reality that no longer exists. Built around assumptions of relatively short retirements, predictable inheritance patterns, and human-mediated financial intermediation, the architecture of contemporary financial markets encodes a particular vision of the economic subject: mobile, cognitively capable, with a finite and predictable financial life cycle. That vision is rapidly becoming obsolete. This article proposes longevity finance as an integrated regulatory category adequate to the convergence of three structural transformations: the largest intergenerational wealth transfer in modern history, the financialization of cognitive decline as a systemic risk, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services precisely at the moment when the intermediary relationship becomes most consequential for aging populations. Drawing on a comparative analysis of Japan, the European Union, the United States, and Latin America, and developing a normative framework grounded in capacity-sensitivity, fiduciary deepening, and institutional layering, the article argues that the redesign of financial systems for longevity is not a technical exercise in product innovation. It is a political choice about whether financial markets will serve the populations that constitute their largest capital base in the coming decades.

title: Rate Cycles and Banking Palsy
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Rate Cycles and Banking Palsy
detail.abstract: The three largest U.S. bank failures in history occurred in 2023, and their loan books were clean. They failed because assets priced at yesterday's rates could not support liabilities priced at today's. This paper develops a dynamic model of banking competition with maturity mismatch, monopsonistic deposit markets, and endogenous entry and exit. Five propositions characterize how monetary policy cycles reshape market structure. A rate hike compresses margins on banks holding loans originated when rates were low, triggering exit. Exit redistributes deposits to survivors but leaves loan markets unchanged, because depositors have nowhere to go and borrowers do. Deposit concentration therefore drifts upward monotonically across incomplete cycles, producing a progressive banking palsy that weakens monetary transmission. The mechanism has a single off switch: if loans repriced as fast as deposits, the palsy would not exist. The palsy is increasing in loan maturity, the speed of the rate cycle, and the fraction of uninsured deposits. The 2020-2023 Federal Reserve tightening tests the model against $549 billion in failed banks. Mean county deposit concentration rose by 79 points, and the Olley-Pakes allocative efficiency measure improved by +0.056. The market-power cost is $8-18 billion per year. The efficiency gain is near $10 billion. The net welfare sign is ambiguous.

title: THE MODERATING ROLE OF ICT IN CLIMATE-INDUCED FOOD INSECURITY: EVIDENCE FROM PAKISTAN
affiliations: International Islamic University Islamabad, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Fatima Jinnah Women University

detail.title: THE MODERATING ROLE OF ICT IN CLIMATE-INDUCED FOOD INSECURITY: EVIDENCE FROM PAKISTAN
detail.abstract: Aim: Meteorological factors pose a significant threat to food security through disruptions in food availability, access, utilization, and stability. Extreme temperatures, erratic precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events adversely affect agricultural productivity, fisheries, and livestock, exacerbating inequalities in food access. This study examines the impact of meteorological factors on food security in Pakistan using the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) and investigates how household-level adoption of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) mitigates these effects across different climatic zones. Material and methods: Using district-level climatic data from NASA Power and household-level ICT adoption indicators sourced from the Pakistan Social and Living Standards Measurement 2019-2020 survey, the study examines the impact of climate factors on food security and examines the moderating effect of ICT. The estimation is done at the national and climatic zones utilizing linear (OLS) and quantile regression. Moreover, the direct and indirect effects of meteorological factors are calculated, and the moderating role of ICT is computed. Results: The findings reveal that all four meteorological variables negatively and significantly affect household food security. Among these, wind speed and precipitation exert the strongest adverse effects, particularly in tropical zones. The results also confirm regional heterogeneity, with the tropical zone being the most vulnerable. The quantile regression shows that the mitigation through ICT is most effective for households with a low level of food security.

title: Apocalypse Next: The Economics of Global Catastrophic Risks: Chapter 1 Introduction

detail.title: Apocalypse Next: The Economics of Global Catastrophic Risks: Chapter 1 Introduction
detail.abstract: The Covid-19 pandemic was, and remains, a global disaster – claiming countless lives and wreaking economic havoc that still reverberates today. But it could have been worse. Much worse. Author Stephen Davies contends the planet ‘dodged a bullet’ this time around. But he warns this was no black swan event: The conflicts in the Ukraine and the Middle East already threaten global stability. And the next existential threat to mankind could happen much sooner than we think – with the chances of it happening increasing exponentially. Here he analyses the potential catastrophes – from nuclear war and climate change to further pandemics, the misuse of Artificial Intelligence and more – that could jeopardise our planet and its people. In this fascinating and at times frightening work, he examines how we assess these risks – and what we can do about them.

title: Implications of a Program of Australian Research on Return-to-Work After Compensable Injury for Vocational Assessment Practice

detail.title: Implications of a Program of Australian Research on Return-to-Work After Compensable Injury for Vocational Assessment Practice

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable as it is a review of research; exempt form ethics committee requirements

detail.abstract: This paper examines the implications of a comprehensive program of research on return-to-work (RTW) after compensable injury-comprising more than 60 publications spanning 1991 to 2026, an archival cohort of 1,674 medico-legal cases and a series of psychometric investigations-for the conduct of vocational assessments in compensation settings. The program established that approximately one-third of compensable injury claimants are working at the time of vocational assessment (typically three to four years post-injury), that this rate has been stable for more than three decades and that the strongest determinants of RTW are occupational group, psychiatric status, claim type and educational attainment-not medical severity alone. Cognitive functioning, particularly information-processing speed, emerges as an underutilised but significant predictor. Key issues for vocational assessors arising from the program include: the need to situate individual assessments within actuarially grounded base rates; the primacy of labour market and structural factors; the ubiquity of psychiatric comorbidity; the limited predictive validity of functional capacity evaluations and impairment ratings as stand-alone tools; and the concurrent value of the Work Ability Index (WAI). The paper provides specific recommendations for assessment practice, reporting and the use of a Return-to-Work Likelihood Profile developed from the research program.

title: GROW YOUR SCOPE™ • RESEARCH SERIES • PAPER 3 OF 5 The Polarity Paradox: A Formal Model of Strength-Shadow Dynamics in Human Development

detail.title: GROW YOUR SCOPE™ • RESEARCH SERIES • PAPER 3 OF 5 The Polarity Paradox: A Formal Model of Strength-Shadow Dynamics in Human Development

detail.abstract: Every human strength, deployed at sufficient intensity without a balancing counter-force, produces outcomes that are the functional opposite of its intention. Discipline becomes rigidity. Empathy becomes collapse. Courage becomes recklessness. Clarity becomes paralysis. This paper proposes that this phenomenon-which we name the Polarity Paradox-is not an exception or an individual failing but a universal, predictable, and formally modelable law of human capacity dynamics. Despite four millennia of philosophical observation-from Aristotle's doctrine of the mean to Jung's shadow theory to Taoist yin-yang dynamics-and despite a growing body of empirical research in positive psychology documenting the 'Too Much of a Good Thing' (TMGT) effect, no existing framework in personal development science has formalised the Polarity Paradox as a law with a predictive formula, specified conditions of emergence, and a structured intervention protocol. This paper makes four original contributions. First, we propose the Polarity Paradox Law: Shadow emergence is deterministic, not probabilistic, given three co-occurring conditions-Intensity above the optimal zone, Isolation from counter-Elements, and Duration beyond the 21-day critical threshold. Second, we introduce the Polarity Index (PI = Intensity ÷ Counter-Element Presence) as the first calculable ratio for predicting Shadow emergence risk in a specific Element. title: The Model-Efficient Market Hypothesis Price Discovery, Consensus Hallucination, and the Limits of Informational Efficiency in LLM-Mediated Markets

detail.title: The Model-Efficient Market Hypothesis Price Discovery, Consensus Hallucination, and the Limits of Informational Efficiency in LLM-Mediated Markets
detail.abstract: The Efficient Market Hypothesis (Fama, 1970) rests on an axiom so foundational that it is almost never named: cognitive independence. Prices are informative because investors process information through separate, uncorrelated reasoning processes; disagreement is the substrate of discovery. We argue that the diffusion of large language models across the investment industry dissolves this axiom. When a dominant fraction of portfolio managers, analysts, and research platforms delegates the step between information and interpretation to a small oligopoly of foundation models, the population of interpreters collapses toward a narrow band of shared posteriors. Information remains abundant and effectively free. What becomes scarce, costly, and price-determining is interpretation itself.

title: DOCTOR, HEAL THY PORTFOLIO: ASYMMETRIC INFORMATION AND EQUITY MARKET PARTICIPATION AMONG HIGH-INCOME PROFESSIONALS

detail.title: DOCTOR, HEAL THY PORTFOLIO: ASYMMETRIC INFORMATION AND EQUITY MARKET PARTICIPATION AMONG HIGH-INCOME PROFESSIONALS
detail.abstract: High-income professionals such as physicians allocate their portfolios as if they face a lemons problem in financial markets. Using the 2022 Survey of Income and Program Participation, I document that physicians hold 52 percent of financial assets in passive retirement accounts and only 9 percent in equity mutual funds-compared to 14 percent for software developers. Decomposing occupational proximity to finance into three channels-formal financial education, coworker exposure, and quantitativedigital fluency (from O*NET)-only the third predicts equity participation (p < 0.001); years of education have no effect (p > 0.08). I extend Akerlof (1970) to a setting where institutional solutions to asymmetric information exist but are not universally observed: uninformed agents perceive an unsolved lemons market and rationally withdraw into consumption, transparent assets, or costly delegation. A counterfactual exercise decomposes the welfare cost at 29 percent of terminal wealth: advisory fees account for 47 percent of the gap, overconsumption for 38 percent, and suboptimal allocation for 15 percent. The mechanism parallels vaccine hesitancy: a physician who cannot evaluate the SEC behaves like a parent who cannot evaluate the FDA. Financial education should target institutional awareness, not compound interest.

detail.abstract: Grand challenges are ecosystem challenges-they hinge on aligning a multilateral set of public and private sector actors whose interactions determine whether a mission is achieved. This study examines how government can orchestrate ecosystem alignment by leveraging distinctive capabilities to deliver solutions at scale with urgency. It uses Operation Warp Speed (OWS), the U.S. government COVID-19 vaccine initiative to explore mechanisms of ecosystem reconfiguration, the choices involved in designing a purpose-built orchestrating entity, and the constraints that bound orchestration scope. The analysis introduces coordinative fiat as a mode of coordination distinct from hierarchy, coercion, or market signals; considers why orchestrating private actors in the external ecosystem required reconfiguring the internal ecosystem of government itself; and identifies orchestration capacity as a constraint on ecosystem strategy.

title: Aggregators, Platform Competition, and the Consumer-Worker Welfare Conflict
affiliations: and University of International Business and Economics (UIBE)

detail.title: Aggregators, Platform Competition, and the Consumer-Worker Welfare Conflict

declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72450003 and Grant No. 72433004).

detail.abstract: We study the welfare effects of an aggregator platform that intermediates between consumers and competing ride-hailing platforms by enabling price comparison. In a three-stage model with heterogeneous consumers-a fraction of whom are comparison shoppers who use the aggregator, while the remainder are loyal to a single platform-and heterogeneous drivers whose supply responds to equilibrium wages, we show that the aggregator's per-ride fee generates a double extraction: it raises equilibrium consumer prices and simultaneously reduces driver wages. The mechanism operates through the labor market-higher prices depress ride demand, which in turn lowers the marketclearing wage. As a result, the aggregator captures surplus from both sides of the market while social welfare is strictly decreasing in the fee. We characterize the socially optimal fee cap and show that it lies strictly below the aggregator's privately optimal fee. An extension to duopoly platform competition confirms that these qualitative results are robust and, in fact, amplified by inter-platform rivalry.

title: Axiomatic Governance for Agentic AI: A Five-Layer Constitutional Framework Derived from First Principles and Validated in Production

detail.title: Axiomatic Governance for Agentic AI: A Five-Layer Constitutional Framework Derived from First Principles and Validated in Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and sole developer of a production SaaS system that implements the ORISMION framework. The theoretical framework is released under CC BY-SA 4.0; implementation-specific materials remain proprietary. No external entity has influenced the design, analysis, or reporting of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involves the development and analysis of a theoretical governance framework for AI systems. It does not involve human participants, biological materials, or personal data collection. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was self-funded by the author as part of an independent research project.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems-capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, and execution-are transitioning from prototypes to production deployment, yet existing governance frameworks provide prescriptive checklists without formal derivation: they specify what rules to follow but not why those rules are necessary or independent of one another. We present ORISMION, a five-layer axiomatic governance framework that derives all rules from a single objective function (survival maximization) through explicit inference chains grounded in thermodynamics, control theory, and epistemology. The framework identifies three irreducible architectural dimensions - cognitive (Ω), engineering (Σ), and governance (Γ)-established through six formal proofs, and enforces their recursive self-similarity at the code level: every API endpoint must exhibit a verifiable layered structure mapping directly to the axiomatic hierarchy. Validated in a production SaaS environment (309 automated tests, 28 architecture decision records, 18 FATAL-level rules), the framework's extensibility was further tested through principled integration of insights from four frontier frameworks (GaaS, IMDA MGF, TRiSM, HAIG), expanding from 28 to 33 defense rules without requiring new architectural dimensions. The construction process itself - in which a non-technical founder and multiple AI agents collaboratively derived the formal framework constitutes a documented case study in human-AI co-construction of governance institutions. We publicly release the theoretical framework and selected decision records; implementation-specific materials remain proprietary.

title: Default, Fraud Classification, and Lender Heterogeneity in COVID-19 Guaranteed Lending: Evidence from One Million Loans
affiliations: University of Leeds - Credit Management Research Centre (CMRC)

detail.title: Default, Fraud Classification, and Lender Heterogeneity in COVID-19 Guaranteed Lending: Evidence from One Million Loans

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the ESRC Project: ES/W010259/1, ESRC grant ES/X010759/1 to the Innovation and Research Caucus (UKRI) and the Department of Business and Trade

detail.abstract: This paper analyses default outcomes and fraud classification in UK COVID-19 governmentguaranteed lending using loan-level data on 1,107,934 limited-company facilities under the Bounce Back Loan Scheme (BBLS) and Coronavirus Business Interruption Loan Scheme (CBILS). Logit models of loan outcomes, Cox proportional hazard models of time to default, and Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) models under alternative parametric distributions are estimated. Three results stand out. First, scheme design dominated risk. Relative to CBILS, BBLS loans show default odds around 3.5 times higher and fraud-classification odds around 186 times higher; the corresponding Cox fraud hazard ratio exceeds 250. In the preferred generalised gamma AFT model, BBLS borrowers' default 40.7 per cent sooner, while a one-unit increase in the loan-to-sales ratio shortens survival time by 60.5 per cent. Second, conventional credit-risk indicators retained substantial explanatory power despite the pandemic setting: pre-loan PD scores, leverage, repayment extensions, director experience, and board structure all remain informative across specifications. Third, measured fraud depends materially on lender detection and classification. Conditional on default, challenger banks and fintech lenders classify fraud at only 37-46 per cent of the major-bank rate. A major-bank benchmark implies roughly 3,300 unclassified challenger fraud cases, or about £90 million. Matching and reweighting estimates place the challenger classification shortfall at about 7 percentage points, and the gap persists in the director-record subsample. External validation using 1,904 objectively ineligible loans from Companies House records shows that major banks classify 45.6 per cent of such cases as fraud, compared with 24.5 per cent at challenger banks and 21.4 per cent at fintech lenders. The evidence suggests that delegated guarantee schemes understate fraud when lender investigative capacity is heterogeneous.

title: Financial Superintendency of Colombia’s (SFC): Smart Supervision
affiliations: Superintendency of Colombia , Superintendency of Colombia , , , , , ,  and

detail.title: Financial Superintendency of Colombia’s (SFC): Smart Supervision
