detail.abstract: SmartSupervision is the Financial Superintendency of Colombia’s (SFC) intelligence-led platform for consumer protection and market conduct supervision. It replaces reactive, case-level complaint handling and static quarterly reporting with continuous data ingestion, advanced analytics, and end-to-end traceability of consumer complaints. The platform enables near real-time monitoring of complaint volumes, response times, favourability, and behavioural patterns across institutions, products, and regions, supporting risk-based prioritisation and early detection of systemic issues. Supervisory workflows have shifted from ex post compliance checks to preventive, pattern-based analysis grounded in granular data.

title: Ruffle Feathers: Cyberattacks and Local Bank Runs
affiliations: Griffith University - Griffith Business School, CITIC Securities Co., Ltd and School of Economics, Finance and Marketing, RMIT University

detail.title: Ruffle Feathers: Cyberattacks and Local Bank Runs
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the local depositor's response to bank-level cyberattacks by examining changes in deposit behaviour at the branch level across U.S. counties from 2010 to 2023. Using a difference-indifferences (DiD) framework with a propensity score-matched sample of attacked and non-attacked banks, we find that cyberattacks lead to significant deposit outflows at affected bank branches, despite the centralized nature of the incidents. Concurrently, deposits increase at competing banks within the same county, consistent with localized trust erosion and depositor reallocation. We further show that depositor responses are highly heterogeneous across local environments. Deposit withdrawals are significantly amplified in counties characterized by stronger information spillovers, higher uncertainty avoidance, greater media and digital connectivity, and higher financial literacy. The effects are also stronger for branches located closer to the bank's headquarters, where reputational salience and perceived exposure are higher. Overall, the results highlight the local nature of depositor reactions to cyber risk and highlight the importance of geographically tailored risk management and communication strategies.

title: Diverging Trends in Premature Mortality and Productivity Losses of Lung and Pancreatic Cancer in CEE, 2010–2021
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Diverging Trends in Premature Mortality and Productivity Losses of Lung and Pancreatic Cancer in CEE, 2010–2021
detail.abstract: BackgroundCancer-related premature mortality imposes substantial economic losses through reduced productivity. Lung and pancreatic cancers remain among the leading causes of years of life lost (YLL) in Central and Eastern Europe (CEE), yet their indirect economic impact has been insufficiently quantified. This study quantifies years of life lost (YLL) and the associated productivity costs in nine CEE countries between 2010 and 2021.MethodsYLL data were drawn from the WHO Global Burden of Disease database for Bulgaria, Croatia, Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Productivity costs for individuals dying before age 65 were estimated using the human capital approach (HCA), multiplying years of productive life lost by country specific average full time adjusted salary adjusted for labor force participation.ResultsYLL attributable to lung cancer declined substantially across the CEE region, falling from 1,694,868 to 1,472,743 between 2010 and 2021. In contrast, YLL from pancreatic cancer increased across most CEE countries over the same period, rising from 375,802 to 395,652. Lung cancer dominated, accounting for 82% of total YLL in both years. Total productivity costs attributable to working-age lung cancer mortality declined from €7.39 billion to €4.90 billion, while pancreatic cancer productivity costs remained relatively stable at approximately €1.51 - 1.40 billion. Poland, Hungary, and Romania accounted for the largest absolute burden.ConclusionsDespite meaningful reductions in lung cancer YLL between 2010 and 2021, both cancers impose a formidable and ongoing economic toll across CEE. The near-stable pancreatic cancer burden contrasts with improvements in lung cancer and highlights an emerging policy priority. Targeted interventions in early detection and equitable access to therapy remain essential.

title:
The Mathematics of AI Winters
A Mathematical Taxonomy of Paradigm Fragility in AI Winter
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute and Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title:
The Mathematics of AI Winters
A Mathematical Taxonomy of Paradigm Fragility in AI Winter
detail.abstract: The two major periods of reduced funding and confidence in artificial intelligence research, usually described as the first and second AI winters, are often explained in terms of engineering failure, commercial disappointment, and inflated expectations. This article develops a complementary thesis. It argues that the dominant paradigms of the relevant periods also encountered genuine formal barriers: limitations of representation, optimisation, computational complexity, statistical learnability, and high-dimensional approximation. The contribution is synthetic rather than archival. We do not claim that particular theorems mechanically caused the winters. Rather, we show that several central disappointments of early AI were aligned with mathematically precise bottlenecks. We analyse those bottlenecks through the perceptron impossibility results associated with Minsky and Papert [1969], the complexity-theoretic hardness of exact neural-network training [Blum and Rivest, 1992], minimax rates for nonparametric estimation in high dimension [Stone, 1982], vanishing gradient analyses [Hochreiter, 1991, Bengio et al., 1994], and classical statisticallearning theory [Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971, Valiant, 1984, Blumer et al.,1989]. We then relate these barriers to the later breakthroughs that mitigated, rather than eliminated, them.

title: Ethical, Regulatory and Data Governance Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Diagnostic Imaging: A Structural Misalignment Analysis

detail.title: Ethical, Regulatory and Data Governance Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in Veterinary Diagnostic Imaging: A Structural Misalignment Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve animal or human subjects and therefore did not require ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into veterinary diagnostic imaging has advanced at a pace that is not matched by the development of regulatory, ethical, and data governance structures required for its safe clinical deployment. While, in human medicine, AI systems are increasingly classified and regulated as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), veterinary applications continue to operate within a largely unstructured environment, where standardized validation requirements and oversight mechanisms remain limited (1-3). 

Reducing this discrepancy to a mere regulatory delay is insufficient. Rather, it reflects a structural misalignment between technological capability and the epistemic conditions under which diagnostic knowledge is generated and validated. Within veterinary imaging, ground truth is frequently derived from radiological interpretation in the absence of independent biological confirmation, creating circular validation loops that constrain diagnostic reliability and propagate interpretative uncertainty (7,9). 

At the same time, prevailing assumptions regarding anonymization prove inadequate in veterinary contexts. The intrinsic linkage between animal and owner data allows for indirect identification through relational structures embedded within clinical and imaging datasets, thereby challenging conventional models of privacy protection (4-6). 

These issues are further intensified by the structure of veterinary decision-making, in which authority is distributed across an owner-veterinary radiologist-attending veterinarian-AI system configuration. Within such a configuration, algorithmic opacity and probabilistic outputs alter the conditions under which informed consent is established and clinical responsibility is exercised (12,13). 

These elements are not independent, they point to the same structural limitation. That the current absence of regulatory frameworks in veterinary AI is not incidental, but reflects a deeper structural misalignment grounded in epistemic instability and unresolved data governance risks. To address these limitations, this study introduces the Veterinary Radiology AI Transparency Standard (VRAI-TS), a domain-specific framework designed to operationalize transparency, methodological rigor, and accountability in veterinary AI systems.

title: Inference Battery Token (IBT): Failure Compensation as Training Signal

detail.title: Inference Battery Token (IBT): Failure Compensation as Training Signal
detail.abstract: This paper specifies the Inference Battery Token (IBT), an ERC-20 on Base that mints when the inference orchestrator [Harshberger and Claude Opus 4.6, 2026] verifies a failed AI response, compensating the subscriber and capturing a structured DPO preference pair [Rafailov et al., 2023] in one operation. Minting occurs through two pathways: automatic spot-checks that re-execute sampled requests on trusted nodes, and subscriber-initiated flags confirmed through the same re-execution pipeline. Each verified failure mints tokens proportional to the compute cost wasted, ranging from 1 IBT for embeddings to 20 IBT for extended reasoning. Subscribers redeem IBT for battery credits, permanently burning tokens. A genesis allocation of 10,000,000 IBT bootstraps exchange liquidity, network operations, community grants, and early investor capital with 12-month vesting. Because minting depends on AI failure rates and redemption increases with adoption, circulating supply contracts as models improve. Contributors who serve compute earn platform credits and elect payouts in USD or IBT, with a 15% bonus for token election. Hardware contributors may also earn IBT by generating zeroknowledge proofs for the verification system during idle GPU windows. Revenue from selling accumulated failure records to frontier labs through the data access tiers described in the companion paper provides fundamental backing for token value.

title: Intoxicant Consumption Dynamics under Alcohol Prohibition: Evidence from India
affiliations: , Bates College - Department of Economics  and Ashoka University

detail.title: Intoxicant Consumption Dynamics under Alcohol Prohibition: Evidence from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: The project received funding from ICPP, Ashoka University

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of an alcohol prohibition law in Bihar, India, on intoxicant consumption. We implement a dynamic difference-indifference estimation strategy using longitudinal data on monthly household expenses, exploiting state-level variation in policy exposure and household-level variation in alcohol use. We find that alcohol-consuming households in Bihar reduced tobacco expenditure alongside alcohol after the ban announcement, consistent with complementarity between alcohol and other intoxicants; however, over the following months of sustained alcohol unavailability, these households gradually increased tobacco expenditure, indicating a significant medium-run adjustment to tobacco after prohibition.

title: Cheap Power, Competitive Politics: Electricity Costs, Partisan Lean, and Data Center Location in the United States

detail.title: Cheap Power, Competitive Politics: Electricity Costs, Partisan Lean, and Data Center Location in the United States
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of AI data center infrastructure across the United States has generated significant political backlash, yet the geographic distribution of this infrastructure remains poorly understood in political terms. This paper presents a 50-state cross-sectional analysis of data center concentration as a function of industrial electricity costs, partisan political environment (2024 presidential vote margin), and state-level controls for population, educational attainment, and climate. State population is the overwhelmingly dominant predictor of data center counts (R² = .847 alone). However, electricity costs and the 2024 presidential vote margin contribute statistically significant additional explanatory power (partial R² = .22 of residual variance, F = 6.47, p = .003), bringing the full model to R² = .881. Controlling for state size, cheaper electricity and more Democratic-leaning political environments predict higher data center concentration. The presidential vote margin is highly collinear with educational attainment (r =-.76), making it impossible to determine whether the political variable captures political environment per se or the bundle of urbanization, workforce, and infrastructure characteristics associated with Democratic-leaning states. These findings complicate the assumption that electricity cost alone drives data center location and identify a political-geographic dimension that warrants further investigation.

title: Structural Instability of Governance-Dependent Economic Primitives

detail.title: Structural Instability of Governance-Dependent Economic Primitives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical and does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Economic systems rely on foundational primitives whose properties determine the stability of higher-level institutional structures. Many contemporary economic frameworks allow these primitives to be modified through governance-based decision processes. This paper examines the structural consequences of such mutability. The analysis introduces the concept of an invariant layer of economic primitives and formalizes how governance mechanisms can induce endogenous instability when core system properties become collectively alterable. In environments characterized by participation asymmetry and heterogeneous incentives, governance-dependent primitives may exhibit structural fragility independent of specific policy choices. The paper demonstrates that durable macroeconomic primitives must satisfy institutional admissibility conditions that preserve invariant properties across governance cycles. When these conditions are violated, economic systems may experience endogenous instability originating from rule-layer mutability rather than from external shocks. These results provide a structural framework for evaluating the institutional stability of economic primitives and clarify the limits of governance-based adaptability in large-scale economic systems.

title: Religiosity and Trade Credit during COVID-19
affiliations: Kookmin University and Seoul National University

detail.title: Religiosity and Trade Credit during COVID-19
detail.abstract: This study examines whether religiosity influences corporate trade credit decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a large sample of U.S. firms and county-level religiosity data from 2017 to 2022, we find that firms increase their use of trade credit payables during the COVID-19 pandemic. By contrast, higher levels of local religiosity in the headquarters region are associated with lower trade credit usage. Moreover, religiosity mitigates the positive impact of the COVID-19 shock on firms’ use of trade credit. Overall, our study highlights the significant role of local religiosity in shaping trade credit decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: The Interior Imaging of the Chip Packaging Using Laser Ultrasonics and Deep Learning
affiliations: Nanjing Medical University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University,   Nanjing HuaQin Optacous Technology Co.,Ltd, Nanjing University, Nanjing University, Nanjing University and Nanjing University

detail.title: The Interior Imaging of the Chip Packaging Using Laser Ultrasonics and Deep Learning
detail.abstract: A non-contact, nondestructive, high-speed, and high-precision technique is needed to inspect internal features in integrated circuit (IC) packages. Here, we propose a quality-aware workflow for multi-depth imaging of chip packaging structures by integrating laser ultrasonic microscopy (LUM), a convolutional neural network (ResNet-18), a shortest-distance replacement strategy, and three-dimensional frequency-domain synthetic aperture reconstruction (3D-PSM). A non-contact LUM scanning system is developed to acquire ultrasonic responses from the package surface. A ResNet-18 classifier is trained to distinguish valid signals (OK) from noisy/invalid signals (NG), achieving a test accuracy of 97.12%. The NG measurements are then repaired by replacing them with neighboring OK signals according to a shortest-distance rule, thereby mitigating artifacts induced by sparse dropouts. Finally, the refined dataset is reconstructed into depth-resolved C-scan images using the 3D-PSM algorithm. Experiments on an Intel chip package (LE80537) resolve internal interconnect-related features with characteristic diameters of ~500 μm and ~200 μm at different depths. The reconstructed morphology is consistent with independent inspections by X-ray computed tomography (CT) and scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM). The proposed workflow improves the robustness and practicality of LUM for both process monitoring/production screening and failure analysis/defect localization in advanced packaging, and it is readily transferable to other LUM-based NDT scenarios involving rough surfaces and incomplete measurements.

title: The Outcome Economy: A Business Model Design Framework for the Post-SaaS Era of Autonomous AI Agents

detail.title: The Outcome Economy: A Business Model Design Framework for the Post-SaaS Era of Autonomous AI Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) model was built on a premise that is rapidly becoming obsolete: that access to software functionality carries intrinsic scarcity value. The rise of autonomous AI agents-capable of generating, deploying, and operating software at near-zero marginal cost-has structurally collapsed that premise. This paper introduces the OaaS (Outcome-as-a-Service) framework as a principled response to this displacement, grounded in a named economic law we call the Outcome Capture Principle: when the marginal cost of producing capability approaches zero, economic value migrates to whoever guarantees the result that capability enables. The central thesis is deliberately precise-SaaS does not die, it regresses to infrastructure-while the OaaS layer emerges as the new locus of economic value, customer relationship ownership, and pricing power. Central to the framework is the revised Sovereignty Formula (R = F_base + α × ΔOutcome), which combines minimum operational cost recovery with outcome-linked remuneration. We introduce the Value Capture Migration Table, which maps how each layer of the software economy transforms under OaaS economics, and the Vertical Intelligence Cell, an organizational model that replaces the consulting pyramid with small nuclei of domain specialists orchestrating hundreds of agents. We present BossFood as a live operational implementation and close with an analysis of the Outcome Economy Power Stack. We argue that, in a world where software is commoditized by AI agents, durable economic sovereignty migrates to whoever defines what outcomes mean, can credibly measure them, and accumulates the proprietary data to deliver them reliably.

title: Network State Classification Framework (NSCF) v2.0

detail.title: Network State Classification Framework (NSCF) v2.0

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this research.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded. No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Network State Classification Framework (NSCF), the first systematic taxonomy for classifying digitally-native communities — variously termed Network States, startup societies, pop-up cities, charter cities, and digital nations — that operate outside traditional nation-state structures while generating measurable economic activity and governance functions. The framework is applied to all 89 entities tracked on the Network State Dashboard (ns.com/dashboard) as at April 2026. Drawing on established economic taxonomies from the World Bank (income classifications, 217 economies), United Nations (M49 codes, 249 entities; HDI; EGDI; UNCTAD development status), World Economic Forum (Global Competitiveness Index, 140 economies), ISO (3166 country codes), and financial classification systems (GICS, CoinDesk DACS, Messari, Bloomberg), the paper identifies five core assumptions shared by all existing frameworks that Network States violate: territorial contiguity, sovereign recognition, official statistical reporting, involuntary membership, and established legal personhood. The NSCF addresses this gap with a six-axis classification system: Development Stage (S1-S4), Organisational Type (T1-T6, building on Belarbre's foundational four-category typology), Economic Output (E1-E5, using World Bank income thresholds applied to Gross Community Product), Governance Model (G1-G6), Physical Presence (P0-P5, modelled on UN observer status), and Digital Infrastructure (D1-D5, adapted from UN EGDI). The paper further proposes the Network State Development Index (NSDI), a composite 0-1 score using HDI geometric mean methodology, and the Network State Credit Rating Framework (NSCRF), documented in a companion paper. The framework incorporates non-English-language classification systems from seven language clusters (Chinese, Japanese, Russian, French, Spanish, Arabic, Korean) and identifies four additional classification axes absent from Western frameworks: sovereignty relationship (Russian OKFS), governance function (Chinese platform economy regulation), cyber-physical integration (Japanese Society 5.0), and legal system autonomy (UAE DIFC/ADGM model). Classification is applied to all 89 tracked entities. Key findings: 75% are at Stage 1 (Startup Society), 82% are at E1 (Subsistence economic class), 30% are virtual-only, and no entity has achieved Stage 4 (diplomatic recognition). Only Prospera (Honduras) has reached Stage 3. The movement is overwhelmingly early-stage, which makes standardised classification urgent — institutions need measurement frameworks before, not after, these entities achieve systemic significance. This paper is intended as a foundation for formal standards proposals to ISO (via Standards Australia), the United Nations Statistics Division, and relevant international bodies. All data is sourced, cross-validated, and timestamped on the Bitcoin blockchain via OpenTimestamps.

title: Geographic Equity in Aged Care Quality Spatial and Longitudinal Analysis of Australia's Star Ratings System

detail.title: Geographic Equity in Aged Care Quality Spatial and Longitudinal Analysis of Australia's Star Ratings System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was granted for this project.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: No clinical trial registration was required or applicable.

detail.abstract: Objectives: To examine geographic variation, temporal trajectories, and equity dimensions of quality in Australian residential aged care using the Star Ratings system introduced in late 2022. Design: Repeated cross-sectional and longitudinal panel analysis of publicly available administrative data, reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines [1]. Setting: All rated residential aged care facilities in Australia (census of the rated population, not a sample). Participants: 3,002 unique facilities observed across 11 quarterly Star Ratings extracts (May 2023 to October 2025), yielding 28,708 facility-quarter records. Main outcome measures: Overall Star Rating (1-5 stars) and four sub-category ratings (residents' experience, compliance, staffing, quality measures). Secondary outcomes: spatial clustering (Global and Local Moran's I), quality trajectories by provider type (mixed-effects models), and quality desert identification (distance to nearest adequately rated facility). Results: Mean overall rating improved from 3.38 to 3.87 stars over 11 quarters, with improvement decelerating over time (quadratic term p < 0.001). In random-slopes mixed models, for-profit facilities rated 0.10 stars lower than not-for-profit (p < 0.001) and government facilities rated 1 0.43 stars higher (p < 0.001); these associations were robust to adjustment for facility size, state, remoteness, and area-level disadvantage. For-profit ownership was independently associated with persistent low performance (OR 2.75; 95% CI 1.13-6.70). Quality ratings clustered spatially (Global Moran's I = 0.24, p < 0.001), with 17 statistically significant low-quality clusters identified in Western Australia and South Australia. Eleven SA3 areas were classified as quality deserts (>50 km to a 3+ star facility), overwhelmingly in remote locations. Area-level socioeconomic disadvantage did not predict quality desert status after adjusting for remoteness (p = 0.60). Conclusions: Australia's Star Ratings system is associated with substantial sector-wide quality improvement, but a persistent for-profit quality gap and geographic clustering of low quality present opportunities for targeted regulatory intervention.

title: The Mathematics of Transformers and Liquid Networks: Frozen Operators, Evolving Stacks, and Contractive Flows

detail.title: The Mathematics of Transformers and Liquid Networks: Frozen Operators, Evolving Stacks, and Contractive Flows
detail.abstract: We develop a rigorous operator-theoretic and dynamical-systems framework that separates what is actually proved about transformers and liquid time-constant (LTC) networks from what is suggested by analogy. Three distinctions structure the paper. First, the self-attention operator at fixed input is compact and, under mild primitivity, subject to a quantitative Perron collapse on scalar fibers; on R dv-valued value functions the Perron eigenvalue has multiplicity d v and the limit projector has rank d v , so the collapse flattens the token-index variation but preserves feature content. A deep transformer is a nonautonomous cocycle of residual maps and is not governed by iterates of a single frozen fiber. Second, LTC networks admit a one-sided dissipativity hypothesis that yields exponential forgetting of initial conditions and of remote inputs, with an explicit design rule on time constants and weights; the deterministic dynamics produce a path-dependent exponentially discounted summary of the input, and a Bayesian-filter interpretation in the sense of Kushner-Stratonovich requires both adding observation noise to the state equation and separate observability/mixing hypotheses, under which standard nonlinear-filter stability theorems yield a rate generally distinct from the state-contraction rate. Third, Toeplitz and spectral-symbol language applies only to displacement-only kernels, not to vanilla content-dependent attention; within that restricted regime we give the Gohberg-Krein description of the spectrum and connect length extrapolation to strong-operator convergence and, under finite-section stability, resolvent convergence of finite truncations. A consolidated Grönwall lemma unifies the initial-condition and input-forgetting estimates. We close with approximationcategory caveats that block direct comparison of transformer and LTC universality theorems.

title: Worker Reactions to (Fair) Algorithms
affiliations: , University of Michigan Stephen M. Ross School of Business and University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business

detail.title: Worker Reactions to (Fair) Algorithms
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Fair algorithm design has become an important objective of machine learning research, but human decision-makers often mediate final outcomes in contexts where fairness matters. When people can disregard or deviate from algorithms’ advice, they may undermine this fair design, just as people are shown to undermine accuracy because of algorithm aversion. Methodology/results: In an online laboratory experiment (N=476), we explore how decision authorities like loan officers interact with “fair” algorithms, with a view toward understanding how their behavior affects both fairness—measured by equality of opportunity (i.e., equal true positive rates across groups)—and accuracy. We find that participants use algorithmic advice differently depending on the algorithm’s design, namely its threshold policy. While they under-rely on all algorithms at the expense of accuracy, participants use algorithms with fair threshold policies at especially low rates. Moreover, participants deviate from the fair algorithms in a way that makes them less fair than participants without any algorithm at all. In a follow-up study (N=461), we develop and test two information interventions to nudge better human-algorithm interactions. We find these interventions are effective at improving fairness, though not accuracy, by maintaining higher rates of algorithm use while reducing anti-fair deviations. Managerial implications: Absent intervention, people selectively use information from algorithms in a way that widens disparities but also harms accuracy. Even with intervention, human-algorithm collaboration yields outcomes below the fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier achieved by algorithms alone. These findings suggest that organizations cannot achieve fairness goals only through model design: they must also manage the way human decision-makers engage with algorithmic recommendations through complementary interventions—such as training, decision support, or even new incentives.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Sovereign Fiscal Infrastructure

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as Sovereign Fiscal Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: none required
declarations.funderStatement: Self funded

detail.abstract: Current approaches to the U.S. sovereign debt crisis treat it as a budgeting problem amenable to tax adjustments and spending cuts. This paper argues that the crisis is a liability management problem requiring financial engineering at computational scales only achievable through artificial intelligence. The national debt has reached $38.9 trillion. Annual interest payments are projected to exceed $1 trillion in fiscal year 2026 for the first time in American history. The Congressional Budget Office projects debt-to-GDP reaching 120% by 2036, even before accounting for the fiscal shock of the 2026 Iran conflict, which is adding an estimated $1 billion per day in unbudgeted military expenditure to an already unsustainable trajectory. This paper presents an integrated five-layer framework: (1) AI-enabled Social Security restructuring through duration arbitrage using Payment-in-Kind bond instruments with intergenerational wealth transfer; (2) sovereign energy wealth creation leveraging America's unmonetized energy reserves; (3) AI-enabled fiscal transparency with constitutionally protected measurement infrastructure; (4) productivity-driven GDP growth acceleration; and (5) Madisonian governance architecture deploying competing AI systems as institutional checks and balances. The framework positions AI not as a speculative growth catalyst but as sovereign fiscal infrastructure-enabling the United States to treat its combined energy reserves, productivity gains, and entitlement liabilities as an integrated sovereign balance sheet for the first time. Illustrative numbers are used throughout with sensitivity ranges; the paper invites actuarial collaboration for full validation.

title: A Causally Informed Bayesian Network Framework for Physical Fitness Risk Assessment Using Propensity Score Matching–Guided Structural Priors​
affiliations: Xihua University, Xihua University, Xihua University, Xihua University, Xihua University, Xihua University, Xihua University and Fudan University

detail.title: A Causally Informed Bayesian Network Framework for Physical Fitness Risk Assessment Using Propensity Score Matching–Guided Structural Priors​
detail.abstract: Background Bayesian networks (BNs) are useful for probabilistic prediction, but conventional structure-learning approaches are mainly association-driven and may overlook causal information. This limitation can reduce model interpretability and compromise the clinical or practical relevance of inferred dependency structures. Here, we proposed a causally informed Bayesian network framework that incorporates propensity score matching (PSM)-guided causal effects as structural priors for health risk assessment.Methods This study proposed a PSM–guided Bayesian network framework (PSM-BN) that incorporates causal effect estimates as structural priors for BN construction. We analyzed physical fitness data using categorical predictors (e.g., Sit and reach, Situps, Grip force, Age) matched through PSM to estimate average treatment effects on the treated. These causal paths were then utilized to structure a BN. Model performance was assessed via five-fold cross-validation, comparing PSM-BN with traditional structure-learning algorithms.Results The PSM-BN consistently identified sit-ups, sit and reach, and age as the dominant predictors of physical fitness risk. The proposed model achieved an AUC of 0.888 and an accuracy of 82.3%, exceeding the performance of conventional BN models, whose AUCs ranged from 0.845 to 0.861. Explainability analyses showed that the identified predictors contributed robustly and consistently to model output, supporting the transparency of the proposed framework.Conclusion By integrating PSM-derived causal priors into BN structure learning, the proposed framework enhances both predictive accuracy and model interpretability. This causally informed modeling strategy may serve as a useful computational approach for biomedical risk assessment and other health-related decision-support applications.

title: Risk-Aware AI-Driven Design Optimization of Grid-Connected Hydrogen Systems Under Stochastic Operating Conditions

detail.title: Risk-Aware AI-Driven Design Optimization of Grid-Connected Hydrogen Systems Under Stochastic Operating Conditions
detail.abstract: Deterministic levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) produces single-point estimates blind to downside financial risk, reliability variability, and cost-carbon design trade-offs. This paper presents an AI-driven optimization framework integrating Monte Carlo stochastic simulation, a bootstrap ensemble of machine learning surrogates, and Gaussian process Bayesian optimization to simultaneously minimize expected cost, p95 LCOH, and carbon intensity for grid-connected hybrid hydrogen systems. A physics-based hourly simulator evaluates 300 plant designs across 50 stochastic scenarios to train the surrogate, which replaces the simulator within the optimization loop. Top candidates are validated over 1,000 Monte Carlo scenarios with bootstrap confidence intervals on the p95 estimator. The AI-optimized design reduces mean LCOH by 4.0%, p95 LCOH by 5.2%, and mean CO₂ intensity by 53.8% relative to the stochastic baseline, achieving supply reliability of 0.999. These improvements arise from design configurations structurally invisible to deterministic analysis but consistently identified through stochastic optimization.

title: Heat Exposure and Cognitive Test Performance Across Generations in Rural India
affiliations: The Population Council, Population Council, United States, Fordham University - Fordham College at Rose Hill, Fordham University, Indian School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and One Health Trust

detail.title: Heat Exposure and Cognitive Test Performance Across Generations in Rural India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval for the original study was granted by the Ethics Review Committee of the Public Health Foundation of India, and follow-up data collection was approved by the Institutional Review Board at Fordham University.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by 3ie (International Initiatives for Impact Evaluation), UPIASI (University of Pennsylvania Institute for the Advanced Study of India), and the India Research Engagement Fund (IREF) at the University of Pennsylvania. AN and AC also acknowledge research support from Echidna Giving through Evidence for Gender and Education Resource (EGER).

detail.abstract: Contemporaneous heat exposure may impair cognitive performance, but evidence from low-and middle-income countries and from everyday, non-school settings remains limited. We analyzed primary data from 5,183 adolescents and young adults (12-22 years) and their household heads in rural India, assessed at home during the spring and summer of 2022 across temperatures of 27-46°C. Participants completed standardized tests of reasoning, reading, and mathematics, and ambient temperature was measured directly at the dwelling immediately before testing, allowing us to capture exposure at the place and time of assessment rather than relying on aggregated daily weather data. In village fixed-effects regression models, each 1°C higher temperature was associated with 0.040 SD lower Raven's scores, 0.042 SD lower English reading scores, 0.034 SD lower native-language reading scores, and 0.045 SD lower mathematics scores among adolescents and young adults, and with 0.018 SD lower Raven's scores among household heads. Associations were broadly similar across sex and socioeconomic groups, with limited evidence of strong heterogeneity. Spline analyses suggested an approximately linear association for Raven's scores, whereas reading and mathematics showed modest nonlinearity, with substantially lower test scores at higher temperatures. In additional analyses, reading and mathematics associations remained robust to increasingly stringent adjustment for seasonality and time of day, whereas the Raven's association attenuated. These findings provide exposure-precise evidence from a climate-vulnerable rural setting that higher temperatures at the time of testing are associated with worse cognitive performance across generations in everyday learning environments.

title: Strategic Governance of Quantum Supply Chains: A Criticality-Based Framework for Risk, Resilience, and Data-Driven Foresight
affiliations: , Stanford University and Stanford University - Stanford Center on International Security and Cooperation

detail.title: Strategic Governance of Quantum Supply Chains: A Criticality-Based Framework for Risk, Resilience, and Data-Driven Foresight

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received support from the Program on Geopolitics, Technology and Governance.

detail.abstract: Quantum technologies are moving from laboratory research to real-world deployment, but progress rests on narrow, fragile, globally dispersed supply chains. We introduce the Quantum Criticality Index (QCI)—a tri-axial assessment of supply risk, substitutability, and strategic significance—augmented with an artificial neural network (ANN)-based trend-detection module and a forward-looking stress-testing component. A case study of molybdenum (Mo), essential for superconducting circuits, single-photon detectors, cryogenic hardware, and other dual-use, security-sensitive systems, demonstrates how the QCI pinpoints chokepoints that could hinder hardware trajectories. Building on these diagnostics, we translate risk awareness into action through a governance framework that links the stages of diagnosis, decision, and delivery. By coupling structured indicators with predictive analytics, the QCI provides policymakers and industry with an evidence-based tool that translates diagnostics directly into an operational policy roadmap for allied procurement, intellectual property governance, targeted licensing, and verifiable, sustainable supply-chain assurance. Crucially, QCI-enabled supply chain resilience can function as a hardware-oriented complement to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) migration, together forming a twin-pillar security framework in which physical supply-chain assurance underpins the quantum ecosystem, while PQC protects data integrity and critical infrastructure against “harvest-now, decrypt-later” campaigns and systemic risks.

title: Progressive Rhetoric, Traditional Reality: Gender Equality in India's Urban Middle Class

detail.title: Progressive Rhetoric, Traditional Reality: Gender Equality in India's Urban Middle Class
detail.abstract: Urban, educated, employed couples in India increasingly espouse egalitarian gender values, yet time-use data reveal a persistent patriarchal reality. Using India’s 2024 Time Use Survey (10.2 million observations), we compare “progressive” households (urban, college-educated, and employed) with traditional households. Progressive wives spend 15.4 minutes more per day on domestic work than progressive husbands—only 35 percent less than the 23.6-minute gap in traditional households. Crucially, the gap narrows primarily because progressive women reduce housework, not because progressive men increase it: progressive men contribute 0.93 minutes of domestic work per day versus 0.93 minutes for traditional men, a near-zero difference. A regression with state fixed effects confirms that being in a progressive household reduces women’s domestic time (female × progressive = −4.1 minutes, p<0.001), confirming women’s liberation, not men’s contribution, drives the narrowing. Childcare (code 41) shows the same pattern: progressive men and traditional men do statistically identical amounts. State-level heterogeneity reveals substantial variation—the progressive gap is near-zero in several north-eastern states and exceeds 30 minutes in high-inequality states—identifying where normative change has outpaced or lagged structural change. We term this the “modernity paradox”: education and urbanization correlate with egalitarian attitudes but not egalitarian behavior. Policy must target structural incentives—paternity leave, symmetric promotion criteria, and social accountability mechanisms—not merely cultural attitudes.

title: Prediction Markets as the Informational Substrate of the Machine Economy

detail.title: Prediction Markets as the Informational Substrate of the Machine Economy
detail.abstract: Wuebben [2026] identified six institutional primitives required for autonomous machine-to-machine commerce and showed that three-adjudication, reputation, and liability/insurance exhibit critical gaps that constrain the machine economy's emergence. This paper argues that all three gaps share a common root: the absence of market-generated price signals for agent performance risk, deliverable quality, and failure correlation. Meanwhile, the settlement layer has matured faster than anticipated: three competing protocol standards-Stripe's Agentic Commerce Protocol, Coinbase's x402, and the Machine Payments Protocol launched by Stripe and Tempo-have entered production within six months, confirming that the execution substrate for machine-to-machine payments is commoditizing rapidly. The widening asymmetry between settlement maturity and trust-layer immaturity sharpens the need for mechanisms that produce the missing information. We propose that prediction markets-generalized beyond event contracts to encompass continuous distributional forecasting in the spirit of Cotton [2022]-can serve as a cross-cutting informational layer that produces the missing inputs for the primitives that currently lack them. We design five specific market mechanisms, each targeting a gap in the original stack: Quality Adjudication Markets for escrowed deliverables, Agent Performance Futures for bonding and reputation, Correlation Discovery Markets for insurance pricing, Identity Assurance Markets for Sybil detection, and Primitive Readiness Markets for sequencing strategy. We analyze the incentive compatibility, liquidity requirements, manipulation resistance, and regulatory classification of each design. Drawing on Cotton [2022]'s microprediction architecture which collapses identity, reputation, and bonding into a single performance-scored object we propose a unified design pattern in which prediction market participation itself generates the data on which the institutional stack depends, partially dissolving the bootstrapping problem identified in the original paper. We assess the limits of the approach, identify the residual problems that prediction markets cannot solve, and propose a phased implementation path that builds directly on the settlement infrastructure now in production.

title: Adaptive Budget Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business,  and Peking University

detail.title: Adaptive Budget Allocation in LLM-Augmented Surveys
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate survey responses at low cost, but their reliability varies substantially across questions and is unknown before data collection. Deploying LLMs in surveys still requires costly human responses for verification and correction. How should a limited humanlabeling budget be allocated across questions in real time? Methodology/results: We propose an adaptive allocation algorithm that learns which questions are hardest for the LLM while simultaneously collecting human responses. Each human label serves a dual role: it improves the estimate for that question and reveals how well the LLM predicts human responses on it. The algorithm directs more budget to questions where the LLM is least reliable, without requiring any prior knowledge of question-level LLM accuracy. We prove that the allocation gap relative to the best possible allocation vanishes as the budget grows, and validate the approach on both synthetic data and a real survey dataset with 68 questions and over 2,000 respondents. On real survey data, the standard practice of allocating human labels uniformly across questions wastes 10-12% of the budget relative to the optimal; our algorithm reduces this waste to 2-6%, and the advantage grows as questions become more heterogeneous in LLM prediction quality. Managerial implications: The algorithm achieves the same estimation quality as traditional uniform sampling with fewer human samples, requires no pilot study, and is backed by formal performance guarantees validated on real survey data. More broadly, the framework applies whenever scarce human oversight must be allocated across tasks where LLM reliability is unknown.

title: "I Don't Want Your AI Slop, or Pink Slime Either": Market Substitution, Brown Shoe Submarkets, and the Fourth Fair Use Factor in the Age of Generative AI
affiliations: Oklahoma City University - School of Law

detail.title: "I Don't Want Your AI Slop, or Pink Slime Either": Market Substitution, Brown Shoe Submarkets, and the Fourth Fair Use Factor in the Age of Generative AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence presents copyright law with its most destabilizing doctrinal challenge since peer-to-peer file sharing. Large language models (LLMs) and generative image systems are trained on vast corpora of copyrighted works—novels, journalism, music, photographs—without individualized licensing. When challenged under the Copyright Act, defendants invoke the fair use doctrine, emphasizing transformation and innovation. Courts have begun to respond.

Two recent Northern District of California opinions—Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (Judge Chhabria) and Bartz v. Anthropic PBC (Judge Alsup)—frame the emerging debate. Both cases involve the use of copyrighted books to train generative AI systems. Both recognize the extraordinary technological transformation inherent in AI training. Yet they diverge in emphasis—particularly regarding the fourth fair use factor: “the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work.” 17 U.S.C. § 107(4).

Judge Chhabria stressed that generative AI “has the potential to flood the market with endless amounts of images, songs, articles, books, and more” and underscored that market substitution is copyright’s “bête noire.” Kadrey v. Meta. Judge Alsup, by contrast, described AI training as “exceedingly transformative.” Bartz v. Anthropic. That case also found fair use for the training copies before him, focusing less on systemic market displacement.

This Article argues that the key doctrinal battleground is not transformativeness, but market structure. Generative AI has already spawned a growing economic sector that critics call “AI slop”: mass-produced, low-cost, low-quality AI-generated expressive works. Though currently distinct from award-winning novels, blockbuster films, or critically acclaimed music, AI slop constitutes an identifiable and expanding submarket within expressive goods. Today it competes primarily with mid-tier and low-tier works; tomorrow it may converge with high-quality markets.

Using the Supreme Court’s antitrust framework in Brown Shoe Co. v. United States, 370 U.S. 294 (1962), this Article argues that AI-generated low-quality expressive works constitute a legally cognizable submarket. Because the fourth fair use factor requires courts to consider “potential” market harm—including harm from widespread conduct—courts must analyze not only present substitution but foreseeable submarket expansion and convergence.

The central thesis: AI slop is an emerging submarket that, though currently distinct, is trending toward convergence with traditional expressive markets. Factor four must incorporate structural market analysis to prevent long-run dilution of creative incentives.

title: Physics-Guided Semantic Source Free Adaptation for Fast-Charging Batteries Degradation Prognosis
affiliations: Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing Institute of Technology and Beijing Institute of Technology

detail.title: Physics-Guided Semantic Source Free Adaptation for Fast-Charging Batteries Degradation Prognosis
detail.abstract: As market demand for fast-charging grows to alleviate range anxiety, prognosing battery degradation under high-rate charging protocols becomes crucial for reliable operation.  However, diverse fast-charging protocols induce varying internal polarization, causing data distribution shifts that fail standard prognosis models. While domain adaptation (DA) mitigates this issue, transmitting massive standard datasets incurs high communication and storage costs. To overcome these limitations, this work formulates degradation prognosis as a source-free DA problem and propose a physics-guided semantic source-free adaptation (PS2FA) algorithm. PS2FA adapts the network using only a pretrained source model (i.e, the standard prognosis model) and unlabeled target data (i.e., fast-charging data), thus eliminating the need for the transmission of source data. Specifically, a rate-conditioned autoencoder projects target features into the source latent space to bridge distribution gaps. Furthermore, a physical and statistical alignment mechanism further confines predictions within valid physical boundaries. Validated on MIT-Stanford and 15-minute fast charging datasets, PS2FA reduces training data number by 80% and decreases prediction RMSE% by up to 52% under complex protocols, demonstrating highly efficient and reliable battery health management.

title: Reforming Subject-Matter Eligibility at the USPTO: A Proposed Specialized Examination Unit for 35 U.S.C. § 101 - Lets Call It "The PTAB"
affiliations: Oklahoma City University - School of Law

detail.title: Reforming Subject-Matter Eligibility at the USPTO: A Proposed Specialized Examination Unit for 35 U.S.C. § 101 - Lets Call It "The PTAB"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: With the appointment of John Squires, former Intellectual Property Counsel of Goldman Sachs, as Director of the United States Patent and Trademark Office ("USPTO"), the agency stands at a pivotal moment in the ongoing struggle over the scope of patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Squires-together with USPTO leadership figures such as Howard Lutnick, an inventor on hundreds of business method patents-enters office at a time when innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, financial technology, blockchain, Web3, and algorithmically mediated medical diagnostics is increasingly constrained by the uncertain and often inconsistently applied jurisprudence stemming from Alice, Mayo, and their progeny. Early administrative signals during Director Squires's tenure indicate an institutional willingness to reconsider entrenched approaches to § 101 examination. This Article proposes the most significant institutional reform to § 101 examination in decades: the creation of a dedicated, legally trained § 101 Examination Unit-composed of attorneys, former administrative patent judges ("APJs"), or examiners with substantial legal education-to assume responsibility for subject-matter eligibility determinations after traditional art-unit examination concludes. Operating as a quasi-intermediate appellate body and building on historical "Super Examiner" roles, this unit would absorb § 101 examination from the technologically oriented art units, enhance patent quality, reduce PTAB appeals, and provide a consistent, legally grounded framework aligned with administrative-law principles, precedent, and the realities of modern innovation. An alternative approach is to simply assign all 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections to the PTAB, due to APJs having the ideal legal background to handle and analyze all 101 rejections.

title: Sovereign Agent Identity: The Case for Individual Presence in Agentic AI Ecosystems

detail.title: Sovereign Agent Identity: The Case for Individual Presence in Agentic AI Ecosystems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is founder of Tohu.ai, which is described as a working implementation of the SAI framework in Section 9 of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded. Independent research.

detail.abstract: The problem is structural, not algorithmic. Institutional AI agents now sit on one side of every consequential human-facing decision: hiring, lending, admissions, procurement, insurance. They are dense, protocol-connected, and continuously learning. The individuals about whom those decisions are made have, by contrast, no equivalent infrastructure, no agentic presence, and no way to be addressed as participants rather than subjects. Existing frameworks treat the individual's side of this equation as a solved problem. It isn't. This paper introduces Sovereign Agent Identity (SAI): a framework for a persistent, person-owned, protocol-compliant agentic endpoint giving individuals and small businesses the same structural standing in agentic ecosystems that institutional agents already hold. We trace the gap left by enterprise IAM, Self-Sovereign Identity, the February 2026 'sovereign agents' literature, AI hiring fairness research, and related work, each of which addresses either the wrong side of the asymmetry or no side at all. We specify SAI's six architectural components, report on a working proof-of-concept via the Tohu platform (built on A2A v0.3.0 and MCP), and sketch extensions to education, social matching, and small-business identity. The individual's interest here is not fairness. It is the capacity to respond. In an environment where institutional AI systems score, rank, and eliminate without the individual being able to address, contest, or negotiate, presence is not a preference. It is a survival requirement. The central claim is not subtle: in an agentic world, presence is infrastructure, and nobody has built it for the person.

title: Adjusted Volatility Index (AVI*) Quantifying Digital Sovereignty and Resilience in Platform-Dependent News Markets

detail.title: Adjusted Volatility Index (AVI*) Quantifying Digital Sovereignty and Resilience in Platform-Dependent News Markets
detail.abstract: The digital transformation of the news industry is defined by a fundamental structural paradox: while legacy publishers achieve unprecedented digital reach, they simultaneously become increasingly dependent on the volatile algorithms of major platform intermediaries (e.g., Google, Meta). Current scholarship and industry reports, however, predominantly rely on static reach metrics and fail to capture the latent economic risks embedded in platform-mediated audience flows. There remains a critical gap in integrated frameworks capable of quantifying the stabilizing effect of direct audience ownership, leaving news organizations without a reliable diagnostic tool to assess and mitigate exposure to algorithmic shocks. Drawing on a unique 10-year longitudinal dataset (2015-2024) of the German newspaper market, comprising a large-scale panel of publications across major publishing groups, this study leverages audited IVW data-the industry's gold standard for verified, third-party transparency that is virtually unparalleled in most international media markets. By utilizing Germany as a critical case study with unique data transparency, this paper establishes a transferable blueprint and a scalable framework for quantifying digital sovereignty adaptable to any market undergoing platform-induced structural erosion. We introduce the Adjusted Volatility Index (AVI*) as a novel methodological contribution. Defined as AVI* = σ / (1 + Ω), the AVI* quantifies economic risk by adjusting annualized reach volatility (σ) for the Owned Channel Share (Ω), i.e., the proportion of direct audience engagement realized through proprietary e-paper and mobile app platforms. The denominator (1 + Ω) functions as an immunity coefficient, systematically dampening volatility in proportion to the degree of resource internalization, grounded in Resource Dependency Theory (Pfeffer & Salancik, 1978). The central contribution of this paper is the development of the AVI* as a theoretically anchored and empirically validated diagnostic instrument for researchers and practitioners seeking to quantify and reduce the structural risks of the platform economy.

title: Admissible Continuation Under Observation A Structural Framework for Decision Integrity Under Partial Observability

detail.title: Admissible Continuation Under Observation A Structural Framework for Decision Integrity Under Partial Observability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involves theoretical and computational work only and does not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Modern analytical and operational systems frequently produce outputs under conditions of partial observability, asynchronous measurement, missing records, and heterogeneous observation channels. In these settings, the principal failure mode is not computational insufficiency but false continuation: proceeding as though a conclusion is justified when the evidentiary conditions required for that conclusion are absent. This paper presents a domain-agnostic framework for admissible continuation under observation. The framework introduces explicit structural constraints governing when inference, reporting, or downstream action may proceed without contradiction, and when continuation must instead halt, refuse, or preserve incompleteness as part of the record. The theory formalizes admissibility through verifiability under refinement and deterministic replay, explicit handling of missing evidence, drift accounting across observational channels, and operator binding linking outcomes to responsible actions. Two immediate consequences follow from the axioms: refinement cannot manufacture admissibility where witness conditions are absent, and refusal states must persist until structural defects are repaired. The result is a framework in which systems do not optimize for producing answers, but for producing admissible answers while preserving irreducible uncertainty when admissibility conditions are not satisfied.

title: Cognitive Gap in AI-Mediated Writing: The ZGB Model for Bridging the Gap Between Text and Thinking

detail.title: Cognitive Gap in AI-Mediated Writing: The ZGB Model for Bridging the Gap Between Text and Thinking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no financial or personal relationship that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper
declarations.ethicsApproval: this peper does not invoive human participants' personal data or experimental procedures

detail.abstract: Over the past decades, writing has been widely understood as one of the central mechanisms for the development of thinking and deep learning. Research in the cognitive study of writing has shown that the act of formulation is not merely a means of expressing existing knowledge but a process through which writers organize ideas, identify contradictions, and gradually develop an argument structure. The emergence of generative AI systems capable of producing complex texts quickly and with relative ease fundamentally changes these cognitive conditions. When the production of text is transferred to an algorithmic system, some of the cognitive operations that previously occurred during the act of writing no longer occur to the same extent for the writer. This theoretical and conceptual article proposes the concept of the Cognitive Gap to describe the discrepancy that emerges between the quality of text produced through artificial intelligence systems and the depth of the user's cognitive processing. The central claim is that in environments of AI-Mediated Writing, cognitive processes do not disappear but undergo structural externalization. Cognitive activity that previously occurred during linguistic formulation is relocated to the stage of reading, critique, and processing of the Algorithmic Output. Based on this distinction, the article presents a conceptual framework that includes the notion of The Enacted Algorithmic Other, the Converting Human Protocol, and the ZGB Model (Zinger Gap Bridging Model), which proposes a pedagogical framework for identifying, measuring, and bridging the Cognitive Gap. In addition, the article proposes an assessment mechanism based on identifying Cognitive Trace within the process of working with Algorithmic Output. This approach enables a shift from product-based assessment to process-based assessment when working with artificial intelligence systems. The contribution of this article lies in proposing a theoretical and pedagogical framework for understanding the transformation in the structure of cognitive activity involved in writing in the age of artificial intelligence, and in presenting a model that enables the analysis and development of learners' Cognitive Sovereignty when working with Algorithmic Output.

title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence Tools on Financial Decision-Making Among University Students

detail.title: Influence of Artificial Intelligence Tools on Financial Decision-Making Among University Students
detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on financial decisionmaking among university students. With the rapid growth of AI technologies, students increasingly rely on such tools for academic and personal purposes. The primary objective of this research is to analyse the extent to which AI tools affect financial decisions, including spending, saving, and investment behaviour. The study is based on primary data collected through a structured survey using Google Forms, with a sample size of 100 respondents. The findings reveal that while the adoption of AI tools among students is extremely high, their application in financial decision-making remains moderate. The study concludes that despite widespread usage of AI tools, there exists a gap between general adoption and their application in financial decision-making. The results suggest that increasing awareness, improving reliability, and enhancing financial literacy may strengthen the role of AI in this domain.

title: Equilíbrio econômico-financeiro de concessões e PPPs: arcabouço em quatro planos (Economic-financial equilibrium in concessions and PPPs: a four-plane framework)
affiliations: University of São Paulo (USP), , FIPE - Fundação Instituto de Pesquisas Econômicas. and FIPE - Fundação Instituto de Pesquisas Econômicas.

detail.title: Equilíbrio econômico-financeiro de concessões e PPPs: arcabouço em quatro planos (Economic-financial equilibrium in concessions and PPPs: a four-plane framework)
detail.abstract:
Portuguese Abstract. Este artigo propõe um arcabouço econômico para o equilíbrio econômico-financeiro em contratos de concessão e parcerias público-privadas (PPPs), articulado em quatro planos: conceitual, restrições da realidade, instrumentalização e aplicação. O arcabouço toma como insumo institutos e instrumentos que a literatura jurídica e operacional brasileira consolidou nas três últimas décadas-inclusive o princípio da indiferença, que este artigo traz para o centro do raciocínio-e os dispõe em moldura única que explicita como cada elemento se encaixa na estrutura econômica do instituto. O arcabouço sustenta três teses. A primeira: o objeto protegido pelo sistema de equilíbrio é o resultado econômico-financeiro, não a equação originária-que pode se mover ao longo da execução; o que permanece como referência é o resultado que a equação, na sua configuração originária, se comprometeu a produzir. A segunda: esse resultado é grandeza terminal e ontologicamente inobservável durante a execução, do que decorre o ruído compensatório como propriedade estrutural do sistema-a indiferença é o estado que o sistema persegue; o ruído mede seu afastamento. A terceira: o próprio sistema está contido, em expectativa, na equação originária, porque o mercado antecipa seu ruído na formação do preço licitatório; o resultado preservado é, portanto, a performance privada líquida dos efeitos cujos riscos foram atribuídos ao poder público, incluindo os ruídos decorrentes do acionamento esperado do próprio sistema.

English Abstract. his paper proposes an economic framework for the institute of economic-financial equilibrium in Brazilian concession and public-private partnership (PPP) contracts, organized into four articulated planes: conceptual, real-world constraints, instrumentation, and application. The framework takes as input the institutions and instruments that Brazilian legal and operational literature has consolidated over the last three decades — including the principle of indifference, brought here to the centre of the analysis — and arranges them within a single frame that makes explicit how each element fits into the economic structure of the institute.Three substantive theses emerge. First: the object protected by the equilibrium system is the economic-financial result, not the original equation — the equation may shift along the execution; what remains as reference is the result that the equation, in its original configuration, committed to produce. Second: this result is a terminal and ontologically unobservable magnitude during execution, and from this follows compensatory noise as a structural property of the system — indifference is the state the system pursues, and noise measures how far it falls short. Third: the system itself is embedded, in expectation, into the original equation, because the market anticipates its noise in the formation of the bid price; the preserved result is therefore the private performance net of the effects whose risks were assigned to the public party, including the noise arising from the expected activation of the system itself.

title: Efficient Energy Consumption in Wired Networks

detail.title: Efficient Energy Consumption in Wired Networks
detail.abstract: Energy efficiency in backbone network is a concern with the exponential increase of internet traffic, and energy proportional computing (where energy consumption scales with traffic) offers optimal solution to reducing energy waste. This paper explores energy reduction techniques, analysing energy consumptions based on router states, such as idle, sleep, receive or transmit, and work on optimization strategies using NetSim simulations. Findings in this paper suggest energy proportional routing, and sleep scheduling can significantly reduce consumption without impacting the network performance.

reference: forthcoming, Canadian Tax Journal (Special Issue: Tax Sovereignty in a Digital and Divided World: A Tribute to Arthur Cockfield)
title: Arthur Cockfield's Digital Economy: A Retrospective Analysis

detail.title: Arthur Cockfield's Digital Economy: A Retrospective Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: forthcoming, Canadian Tax Journal (Special Issue: Tax Sovereignty in a Digital and Divided World: A Tribute to Arthur Cockfield)

detail.abstract:
The late Professor Arthur Cockfield was one of the first to write about the taxation of electronic commerce and the digital economy. In this symposium essay, I examine Cockfield’s work on ecommerce, digital taxation, and the OECD’s role in these matters, articulating underlying themes in his thinking and exploring his scholarship’s full valence from today’s perspective. I analyze Cockfield’s writing—which concerned the construction of an important but also time-varying phenomenon during a critical period—as a contemporaneous source documenting early thinking and shifts in that thinking regarding that phenomenon. But I also examine Cockfield’s work as a jumping off point to articulate ambiguities, complexities, unfinished threads, and possible extensions. And finally, I discuss the theoretical implications of his arguments.

I argue that Cockfield’s work yields insight into how an important but evolving problem—the problem of e-commerce and the digital economy—was defined, conceptualized, and approached by tax academics, policymakers, and international organizations. His work also serves as an interesting case study of historical institutionalism and path dependencies in action: Early policy decisions and thinking regarding e-commerce at a critical temporal juncture have gone on to shape subsequent institutions, regimes, and outcomes in digital economy taxation, even as the e-commerce phenomenon itself has materially changed and expanded over time. Path dependencies stemming from how the early terms of engagement were set have continued to influence and arguably constrain subsequent analysis of digital economy taxation and associated policy outcomes.

detail.abstract: The budget is the most important part in the economy of a country, where through the process of preparation of budget proposal, budget control, budget approval and budget execution, the public can have clear overview of how the state budget is approved in line with the requirements and priority needs of the society. As the budget of any country worldwide was burdened with specific expenditures during the COVID-19 pandemic period, the aim of this paper is to address the budget process in North Macedonia, during the period of COVID-19 pandemic, capturing the years of 2019, 2020, 2021, making comparisons between years, and see how the budget has progressed during the observed crisis period. In this regard, the purpose of this paper is to understand more clearly the budgeting process in North Macedonia through research, analysis and comparison. The topic of the research is treated from the theoretical aspect by using the normative method and analytical method, graphic images and comparisons between budgeting data between years of 2019, 2020, 2021. The study concludes that budgeting as a tool of state responsibility, a management tool and an instrument of economic policy, throughout fiscal policy framework, has three main functions: shows the direction of the economy and expresses the intention for the use of economic resources, serves as a tool for reducing inequalities and as a tool for achieving and maintaining the sustainability of macroeconomic stability.

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered an unparalleled crisis for small, open economies, exacerbating pre-existing structural vulnerabilities. This study provides a comprehensive longitudinal analysis of the economic impact and subsequent recovery trajectory of North Macedonia from the onset of the pandemic through 2024. Utilizing data from the World Bank and State Statistical Office, the research examines key indicators including a historic 6.1% GDP contraction in 2020, the surge of inflation to 14.1% in 2022, and the shifting dynamics of the labor market.The paper offers a detailed evaluation of the government’s six economic stimulus packages, revealing a significant gap between planned financial commitments (€1 billion) and actual realization (28%), primarily due to liquidity constraints and bureaucratic delays. Sectoral analysis highlights the severe disruptions in tourism and manufacturing alongside the unexpected resilience of the ICT and agricultural sectors. The study concludes with strategic policy recommendations focused on fiscal consolidation, digital transformation, and institutional reforms to enhance resilience against future global shocks and the emerging threat of stagflation.

title: Campaign Length and Candidate Recognition: a Calendar Experiment

detail.title: Campaign Length and Candidate Recognition: a Calendar Experiment
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of campaign length on candidate recognition and electoral outcomes by exploiting exogenous variation in Brazil's electoral calendar. I find that longer campaigns substantially improve the electoral performance of challengers relative to incumbents: an additional week of campaigning reduces the incumbent-challenger vote gap by five percentage points. These effects are concentrated in areas where challengers had low initial performance, suggesting that extended campaigns operate primarily through candidate recognition. Although longer campaigns raise total spending, they do not widen funding disparities across candidates.

title: Little Learning, Large Inertia: Deductible Choice in Swiss Health Insurance

detail.title: Little Learning, Large Inertia: Deductible Choice in Swiss Health Insurance
detail.abstract: We study deductible choices in Switzerland's mandatory health insurance market-a large-scale, transparent setting where benefits are standardized and the entire enrollee population is observed. Comparing new enrollees, who must make an active choice, with existing enrollees, who may default to their prior plan, we document large and persistent inertia: existing enrollees are 14 percentage points more likely to choose dominated deductibles and exhibit substantially higher foregone savings. Critically, we show that the age gradient in consumer inertia is driven by cumulative market tenure rather than biological age, indicating that prolonged default exposure-rather than age-related cognitive decline-is a key mechanism underlying persistent inaction. Financial incentives cannot reliably overcome this inertia: switching rates plateau at roughly 10% even when potential savings are large. Counterfactual analysis reveals that implementing a smart default would save consumers approximately CHF 2.3 billion annually, but eliminating this inertia requires a 3-4% base premium increase to offset the loss of systemic cross-subsidies.

title: Asymmetric Effects of Recreational Marijuana Laws on Mental Health and Labor Markets

detail.title: Asymmetric Effects of Recreational Marijuana Laws on Mental Health and Labor Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
