detail.abstract: This draft chapter discusses the main features and development of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) from a law and economics perspective. The EU ETS is analysed in terms of environmental effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, while also paying some attention to fairness and solidarity. Although the EU ETS operates successfully in meeting the emissions caps at relatively low cost, it has also become a hybrid instrument with some inefficient design elements.

title: Labour Law Reforms and Industrial Relations in India

detail.title: Labour Law Reforms and Industrial Relations in India
detail.abstract: Parliament sought to simplify compliance, promote ease of doing business, enhance labour market flexibility and expand social security coverage. However, these reforms have triggered substantial debate concerning their long-term implications for collective bargaining, trade union autonomy, job security and industrial peace. This article critically examines the structural, constitutional and institutional implications of India's labour law reforms on industrial relations. It evaluates statutory provisions relating to retrenchment thresholds, strike regulations, fixed-term employment, union recognition and gig worker inclusion. Drawing upon key judicial pronouncements such as Bangalore Water Supply, Excel Wear, Maneka Gandhi, and Rina Devi, the paper situates labour reform within constitutional principles of dignity, equality and the right to livelihood under Articles 14, 19, and 21. The article argues that while the Labour Codes modernise regulatory architecture and enhance administrative efficiency, their ultimate success depends on balanced implementation, institutional accountability and judicial oversight. Industrial harmony requires not merely flexibility but a sustained commitment to social justice.

title: Escaping the Malacca Dilemma: How China's Chokepoint Vulnerability Shapes Its Foreign Policy and Security Behavior in the Indo-Pacific

detail.title: Escaping the Malacca Dilemma: How China's Chokepoint Vulnerability Shapes Its Foreign Policy and Security Behavior in the Indo-Pacific

keywords: China's reliance on the Malacca Strait
China's Chokepoint Vulnerability Shapes Its Foreign Policy and Security Behavior in the Indo-Pacific

detail.abstract: The Strait of Malacca is one of the most important waterways in the modern world. Geographically, it is a short strip of water that connects the Malay Peninsula and the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It shares borders with Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore. Connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea, it serves as the major passage for almost 80% of China's imported crude oil and two-thirds of its total marine trade. This research proposal gives a focused and theoretically supported examination of how China's reliance on the Malacca Strait influences its foreign policy and security actions in the Indo-Pacific region. The study combines two complementary frameworks. Offensive Realism outlines China's power-maximizing and security-oriented behavior. Supply Chain Risk highlights the economic and logistical basis for its infrastructure plan. Together, they provide a more comprehensive explanation than any framework could provide separately. The key strength of the research is its cross-disciplinary approach. It treats the Malacca Dilemma as both a supply chain vulnerability and an international relations security problem. This opens new explanatory pathways that existing literature has not explored. The qualitative single case study design is appropriate because the research question is interpretive and requires depth rather than generalizability. Overall, this study contributes to both academic scholarship and policy debate. It offers a systematic and evidence-based explanation for one of the most consequential strategic tensions in the contemporary Indo-Pacific order.

title: The Economics of Belonging: Institutions, Participation, and a Structural Reinterpretation of the Capability Approach

detail.title: The Economics of Belonging: Institutions, Participation, and a Structural Reinterpretation of the Capability Approach
detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Economics of Belonging as a structural extension of the capability approach, integrating insights from institutional economics, social choice theory, mechanism design, and game theory. While the capability approach expanded the evaluative space of economics, it remains grounded in methodological individualism.

The paper argues that capabilities are not primary units of analysis but outcomes of institutional belonging, defined as effective participation within institutional structures. It shows that aggregation from individual states is structurally infeasible in environments characterised by multidimensionality, incomplete information, and multiple equilibria. In such contexts, equilibrium selection depends on institutions, expectations, and patterns of belonging.

A dynamic framework is proposed in which belonging underpins effective demand and sustained growth through middle-class expansion. The paper concludes that the capability approach is best understood within a broader institutional and relational perspective centred on belonging.

title: Zero Trust Computing Models for Modern Computer Networks

detail.title: Zero Trust Computing Models for Modern Computer Networks
detail.abstract: The high rate of development of digital infrastructures and distributed computing environments has aggravated network security risks such as advanced persistent attacks, insider threats, and massive data breaches. The conventional perimeter-based security models are becoming more ineffective with regard to the changing risks. The paper examines the efficiency of the Zero Trust computing models as a modern approach to network security improvement in dynamic and complicated settings. This study discusses empirical and theoretical recent research in the area of Zero Trust architectures and implementation plans through the systematic literature analysis approach and a comparative evaluation framework. The results indicate that the Zero Trust models can enhance organizational security posture dramatically by using the mechanisms of continuous authentication, least-privilege access control, and adaptive risk assessment. Moreover, these models are highly adaptable and scalable on cloud, enterprise, and hybrid network platforms. The researchers conclude that Zero Trust computing is an urgent and long-term model of the next-generation cybersecurity architecture, especially to counter the growing system decentralization and complex threat landscapes (Ike et al., 2021; Shore et al., 2021).

title: Secure Software Supply Chain Engineering and Dependency Risk Management

detail.title: Secure Software Supply Chain Engineering and Dependency Risk Management
detail.abstract: Organizations today must ensure that their digitally connected infrastructures are safe and secure. The software that organizations use relies on third-party software and open-source repositories. When these open-source repositories are compromised or when software systems are dependent on vulnerable third-party components, organizations expose themselves to significant cyber risks and operational disruptions. Recent incidents demonstrate how weaknesses in ecosystems can spread and increase the financial, reputational, and security risks (Ivanov, 2018; Fan & Stevenson, 2018). The synthesis of the literature and risk assessment frameworks in this study focuses on the supply chain of software and the security challenges therein. This study builds on the existing theories of cyber risk and supply chain management to inform the governance and control structures, vulnerability management frameworks, and the interdependencies of digital ecosystems (Kure et al., 2018). The results indicate that there are many vulnerabilities in software supply chains-including third-party compromise, poor visibility across networks of dependencies, and inadequate assurance processes. Additionally, the analysis highlights several unaddressed areas in dependency governance, including oversight regulation gaps, inconsistent risk assessment, and poor stakeholder collaboration. Current security measures, the author argues, are mostly reactive and uncoordinated, which results in their being unable to address systemic risks. For the study, in order to strengthen resilience, a holistic approach to intertwined risk governance that incorporates cybersecurity, supply chain governance, and operational continuity is needed. This holistic approach is key to building confidence, increasing transparency, and reducing cascading disruptions in software supply chains.

title: MARKET SUFFOCATION HYPOTHESIS A Practitioner's Guide to Diagnosing Quality Upgrading Failure Producer Decision Model | Suffocation Index

detail.title: MARKET SUFFOCATION HYPOTHESIS A Practitioner's Guide to Diagnosing Quality Upgrading Failure Producer Decision Model | Suffocation Index
detail.abstract: Agricultural quality upgrading programs in developing-country commodity markets have followed the same logic for decades: raise the price for high-quality products, provide training and inputs, and producers will comply. The results have been mixed. High-quality tiers emerge, but they typically serve specific channels, like exports, where rules are enforced. Domestic markets continue to buy low-quality products with few consequences, and "quality sinks" persist alongside high-quality goods. Systemic transformation-a shift in what the average consumer buys-has not been achieved in the cases the Market Suffocation Hypothesis (MSH) examines. The MSH proposes that when producers have reliable access to buyers who accept low-quality products, upgrading is an optional choice rather than a structural necessity. Standard programs try to pull producers toward high-quality channels. The MSH argues it is just as important to ask if the producer faces structural pressure to change. As long as the low-quality route remains open, upgrading stays optional regardless of the price premium. This guide applies the MSH for practitioners using two models. The Producer Decision Model identifies if upgrading is rational for a typical producer and which constraint-such as testing reliability, the price gap, or low-quality market access (θ)-is blocking it. The Suffocation Index (SI) turns the market access variable (θ) into a score. It combines four indicators to separate policy factors (regulatory reach and enforcement) from market responses (price differences and market share). Used together, these models ask key questions: Is access to low-quality markets high? Which channels maintain it? Which mechanism-such as regulatory closure, trade enforcement, buyer consolidation, premium market expansion-could limit these markets? The guide provides step-by-step tables, ordinal rating guidance for data-scarce settings, a fully worked example using Uganda's maize sector, and conclusions to support programme design. The guide does not cover how the equations are derived. For theoretical foundations see: Nsonzi, F.

title: Information and Environmental Inaction under Voluntary Compliance: Heterogeneous Responses among Non-Recyclers

detail.title: Information and Environmental Inaction under Voluntary Compliance: Heterogeneous Responses among Non-Recyclers
detail.abstract: Public policies increasingly rely on non-coercive instruments such as information provision to promote pro-environmental behavior, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains mixed. We develop a simple framework in which informational interventions affect perceived net benefits of participation, implying heterogeneous responses across individuals. We test these predictions using survey data on pharmaceutical waste recycling in France, where all non-participants receive the same standardized message. Our results show that non-participants are not a homogeneous group. Individuals who report an intention to change behavior after receiving information exhibit valuations of environmental and health benefits comparable to those of participants. In contrast, non-participants who do not express such intentions display significantly lower valuations and remain largely unresponsive. These findings indicate that environmental inaction reflects different underlying mechanisms: some individuals face informational constraints, while others attach low value to the associated environmental and health benefits. title: Who Is Open to AI Financial Advice? Consumer Profiling, Advice Access, and Advisory Configuration in the United States

detail.title: Who Is Open to AI Financial Advice? Consumer Profiling, Advice Access, and Advisory Configuration in the United States

detail.abstract: This paper profiles the retail consumer who expresses openness to AI-generated financial advice and examines how such openness relates to existing human advisory relationships. Using the 2024 National Financial Capability Study (N ≈ 18,476), merged with the companion Investor Survey (N ≈ 1,802), I estimate binary probit models and a multinomial logit specification across a fourcategory advisory-configuration taxonomy. Prior FinTech adoption is the single strongest predictor of AI-advice openness. Decomposition of the FinTech index reveals that speculative technologies carry the largest individual effects, with cryptocurrency ownership at 9.4 pp, followed by online trading platforms and mobile payments (each approximately 8.0 pp), and buy-now-pay-later usage at 6.2 pp. Once the index is decomposed, objective financial literacy loses significance at conventional levels (p = 0.083), suggesting that much of the literacy-AI-openness association operates through the FinTech adoption channel. Buy-now-pay-later usage, a proxy for financial constraint, is independently associated with AI openness across every advisory configuration (RRR = 2.4-4.5), consistent with an advice-access-gap interpretation. A negative income gradient (AME =-4.3 pp for the highest bracket) reinforces this pattern. Among investors, two distinct AI-open segments emerge: those who already use a human advisor and express concurrent AI openness ("Human + AI Open") are characterised by high overconfidence (RRR = 2.07) and institutional trust (RRR = 1.34); those outside the advisory channel ("AI Open / No Advisor") are knowledgeable, sceptical, and hold smaller portfolios. A matched-comparison analysis yields a positive conditional association between human-advisor experience and AI openness (+6.8 pp, p = 0.014), though this likely reflects a general advice-seeking propensity rather than a causal effect. Scam susceptibility does not predict AI openness in any segment. These findings carry implications for the pricing, distribution, and regulation of AI-enabled advisory services.

title: AGES: Algorithmic Global Equilibrium System for International Governance

detail.title: AGES: Algorithmic Global Equilibrium System for International Governance
detail.abstract: In an increasingly interconnected global environment, existing mechanisms of international governance struggle to ensure balanced and sustainable development 1,2 , as well as a level of stability commensurate with such interdependence. Current models rely on fragmented indicators and largely non-binding agreements, often proving insufficient to counteract competitive dynamics that exacerbate inequalities and systemic risks. This paper proposes an integrated algorithmic framework based on the Systemic Reliability Index (SRI), designed to assess the relative positioning of states in real time and to introduce feedback mechanisms that incentivize more stable systemic configurations. Unlike traditional indicators, the proposed model is not limited to describing reality. Rather, it embeds a logic of systemic stabilization directly into decision-making processes. The paper outlines the theoretical foundations, operational structure, and potential implications of the model, here defined as AGES (Algorithmic Global Equilibrium System), while also addressing the limitations and critical challenges associated with its implementation. To ensure robustness and adaptability, the system incorporates periodic updates and audit mechanisms aimed at improving data reliability and supporting continuous evolution. The objective is not to provide a definitive solution, but to open a research trajectory on the use of algorithmic systems in global governance as instruments for fostering long-term cooperation and systemic stability.

title: A Non-Activation Theorem for Platforms

detail.title: A Non-Activation Theorem for Platforms
detail.abstract: We identify the conditions under which every economic field (including platforms) is behaviorally equivalent to a pure field. The conditions hold if and only if every searcher either has complete information, or has incomplete information with an infinite attention budget (λ j = ∞) and zero opportunity cost (K j = 0) (Non-Activation Theorem).

title: Top-3 Reasons for Conflicts and Top-3 Conflict Resolution Techniques Used by Employees at All Levels in Organizations

detail.title: Top-3 Reasons for Conflicts and Top-3 Conflict Resolution Techniques Used by Employees at All Levels in Organizations
detail.abstract: Conflict is inevitable in an organizational environment. The paper finds the Top-3 Common Reasons for Conflicts at Employees, Project Managers, Top Management levels; Top-3 Common Conflict Resolution Techniques used by Employees, Project Managers, Top Management at their levels. The common findings present the Top Reasons for Conflicts and Top Conflict Resolution Techniques used by Employees at all levels in the Organization. In Each of these earlier research works Top-5 Reasons for Conflicts, Top-5 Conflict Resolution techniques used are found based on Secondary Research/Literature Review at different levels of employees, such as Employee Level, Project Manager Level, and Top Management Team Member Level.

These studies include both Secondary Research and Primary/Empirical Research Studies. The Top-3 CSFs Commonly found in all 4 different research works Contributing to Software Project Success include Having Clear Project Goal and Objectives, Having Proper Project Planning and Having Effective Communication.

title: Who Needs Wall Street? The Role of Private Capital in the Adoption of Dual-Class Share Structures

detail.title: Who Needs Wall Street? The Role of Private Capital in the Adoption of Dual-Class Share Structures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, commercial, or personal relationships that could be perceived to influence the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data and databases accessed under institutional academic licences (Ritter IPO dataset; WRDS/Compustat; PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor). It involves no human subjects, no primary data collection, and no individually identifiable information. Ethics approval was therefore not required.

The research was conducted as part of the author's undergraduate thesis at Renmin University of China's School of Business, within the ACE triple-degree programme (LUISS Guido Carli University / Renmin University of China / The George Washington University).

detail.abstract: The empirical literature on dual-class structures in U.S. IPOs traces their adoption primarily to firm-level determinants, leaving underexplored the role of macro-financial conditions in the private capital market that shape founders' bargaining power at the moment of listing and, within that environment, the distinction between potential capital (dry powder) and realized investment activity (deal volume). This study estimates, by logistic regression on 3,199 operating-company U.S. IPOs over 2000 through 2023, the association between aggregate annual late-stage venture capital deal volume and the probability of dual-class adoption, with year-clustered standard errors, 2-digit SIC industry fixed effects, and a linear time trend. The coefficient on late-stage deal volume is positive and statistically significant (β = 0.0038, p < 0.001); when deal volume and dry powder enter jointly, deal volume retains significance at the 5% level while dry powder attenuates to marginal significance, a pattern consistent with a bargaining power channel operating through realized deal-making rather than through the latent stock of uncommitted capital. The association survives alternative measurement, functional form, profitability controls, subsample restrictions, and a wild cluster bootstrap appropriate to the 24-cluster regime; the design is associative, not causal. The thesis specifies realized late-stage deal-making as the upstream driver through which the Berle-Means separation of ownership and control is inverted at the moment of listing, upstream of the public-market instruments built to discipline it.

title: Multi-Scale Stress Signal (MSSS) Multi-Scale Stress Accumulation as a Predictor of Elevated Volatility Across Financial Markets

detail.title: Multi-Scale Stress Signal (MSSS) Multi-Scale Stress Accumulation as a Predictor of Elevated Volatility Across Financial Markets
detail.abstract: We introduce a multi-scale stress accumulation framework for identifying regimes of elevated future volatility in financial time series. The model constructs a binary stress signal based on extreme return events and aggregates it using exponential weighting across fast, intermediate, and slow temporal scales. To ensure adaptability across changing market conditions, stress regimes are defined using rolling quantile-based thresholds. We evaluate the relationship between stress regimes and future realized volatility using Bitcoin (BTC-USD) as a primary case study, with additional validation across Ethereum (ETH-USD), U.S. equities (SPY), and foreign exchange (EUR/USD). Across all assets, periods classified as high stress are consistently associated with elevated short-term volatility. Out-of-sample testing demonstrates stable performance with minimal degradation between training and test periods. Across all tested asset classes, stress regimes are associated with a 20-60% increase in forward realized volatility. Unlike traditional volatility models that directly estimate variance dynamics, the proposed framework identifies a structural signal based on the accumulation of extreme events across time scales. The results suggest that multi-scale stress accumulation captures a generalizable property of financial markets related to volatility clustering and regime transitions. All computations and empirical results were obtained using a Python-based implementation of the proposed framework.

detail.abstract:
This monograph provides an integrated, evidence‑based framework for estimating return‑to‑work outcomes, worklife expectancy and lifetime earnings following injury or disability in Australia. Drawing on the Australian Bureau of Statistics Survey of Disability, Ageing and Carers (2022) and updated actuarial tables, the book documents the persistent educational, vocational and income disadvantages experienced by people with disabilities and outlines their implications for medico‑legal assessment.

The first chapter synthesises two decades of national data demonstrating the structural nature of disability‑related disadvantage across education, labour force participation, occupational access, income and discrimination.

The second chapter presents updated Australian worklife expectancy and lifetime earnings calculations by age, sex and disability category, using a transparent three‑step actuarial method based on career duration, employment probability and median earnings.

The third chapter introduces the Return‑to‑Work Likelihood Profile, a structured 14‑factor assessment tool designed to support consistent, defensible vocational opinions in rehabilitation and legal contexts.

Across these sections, the document emphasises that population‑level statistics represent mean outcomes and must be interpreted alongside individual medical, psychological, social and labour‑market factors. The work is intended as a practical reference for lawyers, insurers, vocational assessors, rehabilitation professionals and researchers seeking a coherent, empirically grounded approach to estimating vocational loss following injury or disability.

title: Predicting the impact on Stock Market with Current Trade Tariff Announcements
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Southern California, University of Southern California and University of Southern California

detail.title: Predicting the impact on Stock Market with Current Trade Tariff Announcements
detail.abstract: This study investigates how financial news related to the Trump tariffs, from March 31 to April 19, 2025, influences the direction of short-term stock market returns (positive or negative) at both the company and ETF levels. Using a dataset of 706 financial news articles collected from reliable sources such as Yahoo Finance and CNN, we apply FinBERT to extract 768-dimensional semantic embeddings that capture latent textual signals. At the company level, we align these embeddings with minute level stock return data for 14 firms across various sectors. We use LASSO as a filtering method to select the most predictive features, which are then used as input variables for XGBoost classification to predict stock return directions at the company level. Model performance is evaluated using accuracy, AUC, and ROC analysis. In parallel, we analyze three ETF markets-DIA, SPY, and XLI-using minute-level data to compare model performance across modeling approaches, including XGBoost and Random Forest. Models are assessed based on out-of-sample accuracy, AUC, F1 score, and other metrics. Results show that specific FinBERT dimensions-particularly finbert_59-consistently contribute to return prediction across companies. However, the accuracy of predicting company-level stock return directions is lower than that at the ETF level. This may be due to the greater complexity and heterogeneity of individual companies, which are influenced by a wider range of firm-specific factors. In contrast, ETF-level performance is notably stronger, with both XGBoost and Random Forest models demonstrating high predictive power in forecasting ETF return directions.

title: Section 11 Standing After Slack v. Pirani

detail.title: Section 11 Standing After Slack v. Pirani
detail.abstract:
This symposium marks thirty years since the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act reshaped securities litigation in the United States.  In June 2023, the Supreme Court’s decision in Slack Technologies v. Pirani brought to the surface longstanding tensions in Section 11 doctrine.  The Court unanimously reaffirmed that Section 11 plaintiffs must trace their securities to the allegedly defective registration statement—a requirement that, according to conventional wisdom, cannot be satisfied in modern securities markets where registered and unregistered shares trade together in commingled pools.

In the wake of Slack, many commentators questioned whether Section 11 litigation remained viable for initial public offerings (IPOs).  Mandatory minimum lock-ups emerged as a possible solution: if the SEC were to require that issuers prevent unregistered shares from entering the market for a brief window, purchasers during that period could establish standing. The SEC’s Investor Advisory Committee endorsed this approach, and a working group of academics and former officials petitioned for regulatory action in that direction. But lock-ups only solve part of the problem. Tracing remains an issue for seasoned offerings, direct listings, or SPACs, and so lock-ups are a partial remedy at best.  

The legal landscape post-Slack provides an opportunity to reexamine the conventional wisdom about tracing. For one, the oft-repeated claim that securities held in “fungible bulk” at the Depository Trust Company cannot be traced is a red herring.  Transfer agents maintain issuance-level records, allowing for identifying deposits and transfers of registered shares to identifiable purchasers without the use of any LIFO, FIFO or any other accounting methodology which apply to commingled pools of shares.  And notwithstanding that issuers could eliminate even the slightest question about tracing by adopting separate CUSIPs or registering every share, they have not done so. This sort of private ordering (or lack thereof) raises interesting questions about the economics of Section 11 liability.

title: FINANCIAL ANALYSIS OF ADANI ENTERPRISES: A Systematic Review of Fifty Peer-Reviewed Studies

detail.title: FINANCIAL ANALYSIS OF ADANI ENTERPRISES: A Systematic Review of Fifty Peer-Reviewed Studies
detail.abstract: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL) has emerged as India's most consequential diversified infrastructure conglomerate, spanning ports, airports, coal trading, agribusiness and renewable energy. This study presents a systematic review of 50 peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2024, structured across five thematic clusters: profitability and revenue growth; capital structure and leverage; valuation and market dynamics; governance, ESG and segment performance; and efficiency, machine learning and technical analysis. AEL's revenue expanded over twenty-fold in a decade, driven by aggressive, debt-financed infrastructure investment. Persistently high leverage-with a debt-equity ratio of 2.1 against an estimated optimal of 0.45 combined with the January 2023 Hindenburg Research crisis and chronically low board independence (30%) constitute the firm's principal structural risks. Methodological approaches reviewed include GARCH volatility modelling, event study methodology, panel data regression, structural equation modelling, LSTM-based machine learning, and NLP sentiment analysis. Three original contributions extend prior reviews: a five-theme bibliometric framework with original visualisations; a Python-based automated DCF, NPV, IRR and Payback Period model; and candlestick technical chart analysis of AEL equity. Policy implications are identified for SEBI, institutional investors including LIC and SBI, and for Adani Enterprises corporate management. Future research directions concerning governance reform and renewable energy financial sustainability are discussed.

title: Researcher-Induced Estimation Uncertainty at Scale Using Agentic AI

detail.title: Researcher-Induced Estimation Uncertainty at Scale Using Agentic AI
detail.abstract: Reported standard errors capture sampling uncertainty conditional on one set of researcher decisions, but defensible alternatives in sample construction and specification can shift estimates substantially. I use repeated, independent AI-agent runs, implemented with large language models (LLMs), as stochastic replicators that receive the same prompt and dataset but generate different research choices. Applying the method to the immigration policy-employment question studied by Huntington-Klein et al. (2025), AI agents generate 139 specifications with an interquartile range of [-0.042, 0.046]. The results support AI agents as scalable proxies for multi-analyst designs that characterize researcher-induced estimation uncertainty.

detail.abstract: El sedentarismo prolongado ha sido identificado como un factor de riesgo independiente asociado a enfermedades cardiovasculares, metabólicas y deterioro cognitivo, incluso en individuos físicamente activos. En México, la alta prevalencia de inactividad física en población adulta evidencia una problemática de salud pública que no ha sido completamente abordada por los marcos normativos vigentes en seguridad y salud en el trabajo. El presente estudio analiza el vacío existente en regulaciones como la NOM-035, NOM036 y la denominada Ley Silla, las cuales, si bien atienden aspectos psicosociales y ergonómicos, no contemplan la inmovilidad metabólica como riesgo crítico. Desde un enfoque conductual, se integran la Teoría de la Acción Planificada, el Modelo de Creencias sobre la Salud, la Autoeficacia y el Modelo de Adopción de Precauciones para explicar la persistencia del comportamiento sedentario. Se propone un modelo de intervención basado en micro-interrupciones del sedentarismo como estrategia viable, accesible y alineada con evidencia científica actual. Palabras clave: sedentarismo, inmovilidad metabólica, comportamiento, salud laboral, micro-pausas, prevención.

title: Digital Trade and Structural Transformation in Developing Economies: Opportunities, Constraints, and Policy Implications

detail.title: Digital Trade and Structural Transformation in Developing Economies: Opportunities, Constraints, and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: Digitalization has fundamentally reshaped the architecture of global trade. Unlike previous waves of globalization driven by industrial capacity and physical infrastructure, the current transformation is powered by data, platforms, and digital connectivity (Ahmadova & Mammadov, 2025b; UNCTAD, 2021). For developing countries, digital trade presents both an unprecedented opportunity and a structural challenge. This paper examines the relationship between digital trade and economic development, focusing on productivity growth, export diversification, labor market transformation, financial inclusion, and institutional adaptation. It argues that digital trade can become a strategic development tool, but only if supported by coherent policy frameworks, infrastructure investment, and human capital development (Mammadov et al., 2026; World Bank, 2022). Without such foundations, digital integration may reinforce inequalities rather than reduce them.

title: Institutional Actor Modeling in Dodona: A Central Bank Rate Policy Case Study, 2024-2026

detail.title: Institutional Actor Modeling in Dodona: A Central Bank Rate Policy Case Study, 2024-2026
detail.abstract:
We present early test results for Dodona, a general cognitive reasoning system currently under development. Notably, Dodona incorporates the abilities to acquire symbolic knowledge from various sources, model actors and institutions that shape events, and reason formally over evidence to produce calibrated forecasts with auditable reasoning chains. 

This paper reports test results from a 27-month hindcast study covering 72 central bank rate decisions across the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), European Central Bank (ECB), Bank of England (BoE), and Bank of Japan (BoJ) from January 2024 through March 2026. 

For this test scenario, using only public data, the system models named institutional actors (committee members, governors, and senior officials) from their public communications, aggregates stance probabilities through a culturally-calibrated equilibrium model grounded in committee decision-making theory, and produces direction forecasts with calibrated confidence scores. Strict temporal holdout is enforced at the data layer: no evidence dated after each decision's announcement is accessible during forecast generation. 

The hindcast achieves 80.6% direction accuracy (58/72 decisions correct) against verified ground truth outcomes. By institution: FOMC 94.4% (17/18), ECB 88.9% (16/18), BoJ 77.8% (14/18), BoE 61.1% (11/18). Cut detection is 95.0% (19/20).

Furthermore, we selected five marquee cases, decisions where market consensus was split or significantly wrong, and called them all correctly, including the Bank of Japan's July 2024 surprise hike, and the Bank of Japan's NIRP exit in March 2024.

title: TRADE, TARIFFS, SANCTIONS AND SECURITY: A FRAMEWORK FOR JUDICIAL REVIEW

detail.title: TRADE, TARIFFS, SANCTIONS AND SECURITY: A FRAMEWORK FOR JUDICIAL REVIEW
detail.abstract:
National security and international trade, and their intersections, have become critical focuses for recent administrative action. It was once rare to invoke national security as a justification for tariffs and restriction on foreign investment, but it has now become increasingly common. Courts reviewing these measures have largely defaulted to deferential approaches developed in an earlier era—one in which such actions were infrequent and rarely litigated. But in an era where assertions of national security are more common, this dogmatic jurisprudential approach lacks coherence. A new framework is needed to better guide judicial review. 

This Article proposes that new framework. It identifies a distinction between two categories of justifications: Category I restraints, which seek to prevent adversaries from acquiring strategic advantages; and Category II restraints, which aim to shore up perceived weaknesses in the domestic industrial base. Category I restraints are more likely to involve classified information and fall within the President’s core foreign affairs authority, thus warranting substantial judicial deference. Category II restraints, by contrast, often resemble conventional economic regulation and rely on publicly available information, thereby falling more squarely within the judiciary’s competence to assess under established administrative law principles. 

The framework introduced in this Article provides a doctrinally grounded and judicially administrable approach that allows courts to calibrate deference in national security cases. This Article thus helps to clarify the proper legal structure of this rapidly evolving area of law and provides guidance for the growing number of cases that are now making their way through the courts.

detail.abstract: Bangladesh's agricultural sector employs 40.6 percent of the national workforce and contributes 11.5 percent of GDP, yet remains governed by a legislative framework that was last substantively reformed in the colonial era. This paper advances a focused argument: that five identifiable 'institutional voids' in Bangladesh's agri-business legal architecture systematically prevent the emergence and scaling of circular economy-based livestock enterprises. Drawing on New Institutional Economics, specifically Douglass North's framework of formal institutional constraints, and on doctrinal analysis of primary Bangladeshi legislative instruments, the paper maps each void to a specific operational constraint faced by circular agri-enterprises integrating biogas, vermicompost, livestock genetics, and Islamic investment instruments. Comparative analysis of regulatory innovations from the European Union, Malaysia, India, and Kenya identifies practical legislative solutions that are directly transposable to Bangladesh's statutory context. The paper concludes with five targeted model provisions and a reform sequencing strategy prioritising short-horizon interventions with the highest return on regulatory investment. The paper is the Sheikh, A. (2025). title: ENHANCING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURE ON CORPORATE PERFORMANCE IN THE PUBLIC TRANSPORT SECTOR IN ZIMBABWE: A PAPER FROM MY MBA DISSERTATION

detail.title: ENHANCING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURE ON CORPORATE PERFORMANCE IN THE PUBLIC TRANSPORT SECTOR IN ZIMBABWE: A PAPER FROM MY MBA DISSERTATION

keywords: Zimbabwe transport systems JEL Classification: M12

detail.abstract: This study examines the influence of organizational culture on corporate performance in the public transport sector in Zimbabwe, a context characterized by persistent operational inefficiencies, weak governance, and declining service quality. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and complementary cultural frameworks, the study conceptualizes organizational culture as a multidimensional construct comprising leadership, organizational values, and employee recognition systems. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining quantitative data from structured questionnaires administered to 240 employees with qualitative insights from semi-structured interviews with managerial staff. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation, and multiple regression analysis, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. The findings reveal a statistically significant and positive relationship between organizational culture and corporate performance, with organizational values emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by leadership and employee recognition. The results further demonstrate that culture influences performance through behavioral alignment, employee motivation, and enhanced service delivery. This study contributes to the literature by providing context-specific evidence from a developing economy and advancing a process-oriented understanding of the culture-performance relationship. The findings offer practical implications for managers and policymakers seeking to improve institutional effectiveness through culture-driven strategies.

title: Global Energy Consumption and the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF): A Unified Systems Theory of Energy, Stability, and Sustainable Civilization

detail.title: Global Energy Consumption and the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF): A Unified Systems Theory of Energy, Stability, and Sustainable Civilization
detail.abstract: Global energy consumption has exceeded 620 exajoules per year, sustaining a continuous civilizational power demand of approximately 20 terawatts-a system governed by nonlinear dynamics, multi-scale feedback, and deep structural imbalance. This paper presents the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF) as a rigorous axiomatic system for analyzing and correcting these imbalances. We formally derive the UBFF operator algebra from four foundational laws-the Law of Balance, the Feedback Loop Mechanism, the Law of System Integrity, and the Interconnected Nodes Principle-and demonstrate that each admits a precise mathematical formulation: a Lyapunov stability condition on energy-state trajectories, a transfer function characterizing demandresponse dynamics, a thermodynamic efficiency functional, and a graph-Laplacian flow conservation law, respectively. Applying this framework to the global energy system, we derive conditions under which fossil-fuel-driven imbalance propagates as systemic instability. We further develop a Philippine energy case study, quantifying the coalinduced feedback deficit and proposing an UBFF-optimal renewable transition pathway. Finally, we analyze the rapidly growing energy footprint of artificial intelligence infrastructure, model it as a high-gain nonlinear node amplifier, and derive the critical feedback threshold beyond which AI energy demand destabilizes the broader grid system. The UBFF provides a unified diagnostic and prescriptive apparatus that subsumes thermodynamic, network-theoretic, and control-theoretic constraints within a single coherent structure.

title: Co-Creating Sustainable Enterprises through Open Innovation: Strengthening Africa-Europe Collaboration in Technology-Enabled Entrepreneurship

detail.title: Co-Creating Sustainable Enterprises through Open Innovation: Strengthening Africa-Europe Collaboration in Technology-Enabled Entrepreneurship
detail.abstract: Collaborative open innovation and technology-enabled entrepreneurship have emerged as pivotal drivers of sustainable development across Africa and Europe. Despite growing policy attention, limited empirical synthesis exists on how such partnerships translate into measurable business and social impact. This study aimed to analyse the mechanisms through which open innovation ecosystems enhance entrepreneurial performance and inclusivity in cross-regional collaborations. Using qualitative content analysis of secondary data from peer-reviewed research and policy reports, the study identified that digital co-creation significantly strengthens business agility, innovation diffusion, and socioeconomic resilience. Findings revealed that enterprises engaging in Africa-Europe collaborative innovation frameworks achieved increased R&D productivity, market expansion, and digital sustainability alignment. The paper concludes that integrating technology-enabled entrepreneurship within open innovation networks fosters systemic competitiveness and shared prosperity, provided that institutional, policy, and digital capacity barriers are systematically addressed.

title: A Commentary on the Competition Commission of India's Market Study on Artificial Intelligence and Competition

detail.title: A Commentary on the Competition Commission of India's Market Study on Artificial Intelligence and Competition
detail.abstract: This commentary critically examines the Market Study on Artificial Intelligence and Competition published by the Competition Commission of India (CCI). While acknowledging the study's comprehensive overview of the AI ecosystem, its applications across Indian industries, and its identification of key competition concerns, this commentary highlights significant gaps in the study's analysis. These include its failure to adequately address India-specific enforcement challenges, the limitations of the current Competition Act in tackling algorithmic collusion, the absence of Indian case studies, and the study's tendency to present an overly optimistic picture of AI adoption without sufficiently addressing risks to smaller businesses and consumers. This commentary also evaluates the study's action plan and argues that it lacks the specificity and boldness needed to meaningfully address the competition concerns identified

title: Regulatory Credit Supply Shocks, Reallocation, and Real Economic Outcomes
affiliations: University of Virginia, , Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning and Indian School of Business

detail.title: Regulatory Credit Supply Shocks, Reallocation, and Real Economic Outcomes
detail.abstract: We study how regulatory interventions targeting weak banks affect credit allocation and real economic outcomes. Using staggered bank-level exposure to regulatory restrictions and the universe of collateralized corporate loans matched with firm-level financial data, we find that affected banks reduce lending disproportionately to high-risk firms, which subsequently experience persistent declines in sales and investment and are largely unable to substitute toward non-bank financing. In contrast, low-risk firms in exposed industries receive relatively more credit and expand investment and employment. The results are robust to controlling for firm-quarter fixed effects, which help isolate supply-side effects, employing recent advances in DiD estimators with heterogeneous treatment effects, and using an instrumental variables approach that relies on bank regulatory thresholds to predict PCA entry. We further document a decline in output prices in PCA-exposed industries. The price reduction is smaller for low-risk firms, indicating heterogeneous competitive adjustments. These patterns align with the "zombie-congestion mechanism", whereby continued lending to weak firms depresses prices and weakens competitive discipline. Overall, our findings show that regulatory enforcement restricting credit to high-risk firms improves competitive discipline in output markets and is accompanied by modest gains in productivity.

title: AI Meets Antitrust: How Large Language Models Reshape Market Concentration
affiliations: University of Verona - Department of Economics

detail.title: AI Meets Antitrust: How Large Language Models Reshape Market Concentration
detail.abstract: Large language models are rapidly becoming a primary interface for consumer product discovery, yet little is known about how their recommendations relate to real-world market structure. This paper provides the first empirical benchmark of LLM brand recommendations against actual market shares. Using 1,429 responses from three frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) across sixteen U.S. consumer categories, I compare the implied concentration of LLM recommendations to retail-value shares from Euromonitor Passport 2024. In fragmented markets such as skincare, LLMs concentrate their recommendations on fewer brands than the market share distribution would suggest; in highly concentrated markets such as headphones, they distribute recommendations across more brands than the market share distribution reflects. Both patterns reflect a single phenomenon: LLM recommendations live in a narrow concentration band roughly one third the width of the real market's, regardless of where the real market sits. A second pattern tilts top recommendations toward specialist and premium brands that hold only two-thirds of the market share of actual category leaders. Findings are stable across the three models studied.
