detail.abstract: Social Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA) is a century-old method for evaluating policy proposals in terms of financial and non-financial effects. As a consequence, CBA may help to steer government investments and other policy beyond GDP and towards the notion of well-being. CBA may also help meeting Sustainable Development Goals (SDG). This paper investigates how CBA practice can better measure the impact of policy proposals in view of well-being. This amounts to four general recommendations: a more comprehensive overview of effects, more attention to future generations, more attention to distributional effects and more attention to effects on the rest of the world. These recommendations are illustrated by examples from Dutch and Japanese CBA practice. This paper stresses that the notion of well-being is useful for improving the measurement and policy relevance of CBA practice. It also warns of the downside of mechanical decision-making rules based on a CBA, e.g. the benefits of a policy measure should be larger than the costs in monetary terms. Such rules imply that major dimensions of well-being will be ignored, e.g. negative impacts on vulnerable households or effects that are hard to put into monetary terms like biodiversity.

title: Who Sets Housing Prices? Marginal Buyers and Demand Heterogeneity

detail.title: Who Sets Housing Prices? Marginal Buyers and Demand Heterogeneity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Housing prices in many urban markets appear increasingly disconnected from local income levels. This paper develops a theoretical framework to explain this phenomenon based on heterogeneous demand and inelastic housing supply.

The key insight is that prices are determined by marginal buyers—those with the highest willingness to pay—rather than by average demand conditions. The model distinguishes between local buyers, whose willingness to pay is tied to local income, and global buyers, whose willingness to pay is driven by external wealth and largely independent of local economic conditions.

When supply is constrained, shifts in the upper tail of the willingness-to-pay distribution determine which segment sets prices. As global buyers increasingly dominate the marginal position, housing prices become progressively less sensitive to local income, generating an endogenous transition from locally anchored to globally determined price formation.

The framework provides a tractable explanation for the decoupling of housing prices from local economic fundamentals in supply-constrained markets, highlighting the role of demand composition and marginal competition in price formation.

title: EARNING THEORY: Kill a Mouse or an Elephant, Choice is Yours.

detail.title: EARNING THEORY: Kill a Mouse or an Elephant, Choice is Yours.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical analysis based on existing literature and established economic and behavioural frameworks. It does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures. Therefore, no ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Every professional, entrepreneur, and earner recurrently faces a structurally identical choice: pursue small, low-barrier, immediately rewarding opportunities, or invest concentrated effort in large, high-barrier opportunities that yield disproportionate and compounding returns. This paper proposes the Earning Theory — a conceptual framework for understanding, categorising, and acting on this choice. The framework posits that many earning opportunities can be understood as belonging to one of two categories: Mice (low-barrier, low-visibility tasks providing immediate but limited income with no leverage or enduring reputation) and Elephants (high-barrier, high-visibility engagements yielding potentially exponential returns, permanent reputation, and self-perpetuating future opportunity). Drawing on prospect theory, hyperbolic discounting, human capital theory, and labour market signalling, the paper argues that most earners default to Mouse work not for lack of Elephant opportunities but due to well-documented cognitive biases. The central doctrinal proposition — Elephant work is not risk; it is art — reframes high-barrier opportunity pursuit as a learnable, skilled craft rather than a gamble. A four-phase operational framework (Identification, Preparation, Execution, Leverage) is developed, along with an 80/20 time-allocation heuristic. The paper is explicitly theoretical and conceptual; all examples are analytical illustrations. No primary empirical dataset is presented; quantitative validation is identified as a priority for future research. Organisational implications for law firms, consulting practices, and freelance platforms, and educational implications for professional schools, are developed. Limitations, including survival constraints, structural inequality, gatekeeping barriers, and the possibility of Elephant failure, are acknowledged. Conditions under which the theory could be falsified or revised are specified.

title: A Multi-Channel AI-Mediated Civic Engagement Architecture for Low-Resource Government Contexts

detail.title: A Multi-Channel AI-Mediated Civic Engagement Architecture for Low-Resource Government Contexts

declarations.ethicsApproval: his paper presents an architectural framework and illustrative evidence from government-initiated platform deployments. No primary data collection involving human participants was conducted by the author. The Nairobi deployment described draws on program documentation and publicly available materials. No ethics approval was required for this pape

keywords: Social Policy Global Practice civic technology

detail.abstract: Governments in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) do not need to build new civic engagement platforms from scratch. A rich ecosystem of mature, openly licensed platforms (CONSUL Democracy, Decidim, DIGIT, and CitizenOS) already exists, is free to fork, and has been deployed in hundreds of jurisdictions. Yet these platforms, in their current form, consistently fail to deliver meaningful institutionalized citizen engagement in LMIC contexts. This paper diagnoses three specific architectural failures that account for this gap, drawing on the World Bank Digital Citizen Engagement Stocktake (124 country cases) and field deployments in Kenya and India. First, the intake layer is exclusive: platforms are designed for broadband-connected, web-literate users, systematically excluding citizens who interact via SMS, voice calls, WhatsApp, USSD, or in-person intermediaries. The exclusion extends to authentication: mainstream platforms require email-based account verification, a mechanism that is structurally inaccessible to the majority of low-income citizens in LMIC contexts who authenticate all consequential digital interactions through SMS or WhatsApp. Second, closing the loop is broken: feedback is collected but citizens receive no channel-matched response, destroying the trust that sustains future participation. Third, analytical capacity is absent: government civic engagement teams, typically two to five staff, face data volumes that are impossible to analyze meaningfully without AI assistance, meaning feedback is collected and not used. This paper proposes a design framework that addresses all three failures by adding three architectural layers to any forkable open-source civic platform: (1) an inclusive multi-channel intake layer with a per-channel closing-the-loop mechanism; (2) an AI-powered sensemaking layer anchored by Jigsaw Sensemaking Tools, an open-source library that enables small teams to listen at scale without requiring governments to build or fine-tune large language models; and (3) a phased AI enrichment roadmap calibrated to LMIC institutional capacity. This paper illustrates the framework through two implementation patterns: a CONSUL Democracy-based participatory platform deployed in a multi-stakeholder governmentinitiated consultation context, and a DIGIT-based citizen feedback system (CivicBridge) prototyped with India's CPGRAMS. The paper draws on a 124-country stocktake for cross-cutting evidence. This paper explicitly positions this as a design science contribution: a rigorously grounded architectural pattern intended to guide implementation and generate testable hypotheses, rather than an empirically validated causal model (Hevner et al., 2004). The framework's contribution is to provide a replicable, evidence-informed architectural pattern that practitioners and future evaluation studies can implement, test, and extend.

title: Carbon Risk and Firm Valuation in an Emerging Market Emissions Trading System: Evidence from Kazakhstan

detail.title: Carbon Risk and Firm Valuation in an Emerging Market Emissions Trading System: Evidence from Kazakhstan

keywords.keywords: carbon risk; emissions trading system; firm valuation; Tobin's Q; difference-in-differences; Kazakhstan; emerging market

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether carbon exposure systematically depresses firm valuation following the introduction of Kazakhstan's national Emissions Trading System (KazETS) in 2013. Using an unbalanced panel of 52 publicly listed industrial firms observed over 2008–2022, we estimate a difference-in-differences (DiD) model that exploits cross-sectional variation in pre-policy carbon intensity to identify a causal effect on Tobin's Q. Firms in the upper tercile of pre-regulation carbon intensity experienced a statistically significant reduction in Tobin's Q of approximately 0.39 percentage points relative to low-intensity peers after KazETS implementation (t = −3.44; p < 0.01), a finding that is robust to the inclusion of firm and year fixed effects, industry-by-year interaction effects, and a battery of alternative specifications including staggered DiD estimators, propensity score matching, and placebo tests. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the valuation discount is largest in the mining and energy sectors and is amplified for firms with lower institutional ownership. Our results contribute to a growing body of evidence that financial markets price regulatory climate risk in emerging economies, and they carry implications for investors, corporate managers, and policymakers in the Central Asian region and comparable commodity-exporting economies.

title: What if Britain solved its housing crisis? IEA Discussion Paper No.123

detail.title: What if Britain solved its housing crisis? IEA Discussion Paper No.123
detail.abstract:
This paper presents a forward-looking, scenario-based analysis of the United Kingdom's housing shortage by imagining a future (set in 2035) in which the crisis has been successfully resolved. Written as a retrospective from that future vantage point, the report first outlines the structural causes of the crisis, including a chronic undersupply of housing, restrictive planning regulations, and political resistance to development. It highlights how these constraints led to high house prices, limited living space, reduced labour mobility, and broader economic inefficiencies.

The study then explores a hypothetical policy shift beginning after 2024, in which a reform-oriented government liberalises planning laws, incentivises local development, and significantly expands housebuilding. These changes trigger a significant housing boom that improves housing affordability, increases home ownership, and reduces rental costs. Beyond the housing market, the analysis emphasises wider economic and social benefits, including higher productivity, improved fiscal outcomes, enhanced labour mobility, and reduced political polarisation. 

By combining economic analysis with speculative narrative, the report argues that Britain's housing crisis is largely a result of policy choices rather than structural inevitability, and that comprehensive supply-side reforms could deliver substantial long-term gains.

title: The UIL Triad: Three Laws of Information Linking Entropy, Truth, and Cost Across Complex Systems

detail.title: The UIL Triad: Three Laws of Information Linking Entropy, Truth, and Cost Across Complex Systems
detail.abstract: We introduce a universal information cost theory-the UIL Triad-comprising three fundamental principles that constrain information processing, entropy dynamics, and change costs across all complex decision systems[1]. The First Law establishes that no decision-relevant information emerges from structureless states without external input, grounded in Kolmogorov complexity and algorithmic information theory[5]. The Second Law presents the Universal Information Law (UIL): , stating that any local ∆𝑆 𝑡ℎ + λ∆𝑆 𝑖𝑛𝑓𝑜 ≥ 0 gain in usable information must be compensated by entropy or energy elsewhere-a generalization of Landauer's principle to semantic and decision-theoretic contexts[1][3]. The Third Law proves that as systems approach complete, truthful, shared information (), the cost of further changes diverges with convex acceleration: 𝐼 𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑡ℎ → 𝐼 𝑚𝑎𝑥

title: Universal Information Law Unifying Quantum Thermodynamics and Biological Aging Through Entropic Constraints

detail.title: Universal Information Law Unifying Quantum Thermodynamics and Biological Aging Through Entropic Constraints
detail.abstract: This comprehensive monograph proposes a Universal Information Law (UIL) that unifies disparate observations across quantum physics, thermodynamics, and biological aging under a single informational framework. We argue that information represents a primary physical quantity subject to universal constraints analogous to thermodynamic laws, with domain-specific manifestations emerging from different physical encodings and measurement procedures.

title: Imperial Measurement: A Cost–Benefit Analysis of Western Colonialism

detail.title: Imperial Measurement: A Cost–Benefit Analysis of Western Colonialism
detail.abstract: This paper reassesses the economic significance of Western colonialism for the development of European economies, with particular reference to Britain. Revisiting Eric Williams's thesis, we evaluate the extent to which colonial exploitation and the transatlantic slave trade contributed to industrialisation. Drawing on quantitative evidence on trade shares, fiscal costs, and investment patterns, the study finds that colonial activities accounted for only a small proportion of national income and growth. While certain private actors realised substantial gains, these were offset at the aggregate level by the fiscal and military costs of empire. Comparative evidence across European powers further suggests the absence of a systematic relationship between colonial possession and long-run economic performance. The paper concludes that colonialism played a limited and non-decisive role in Western economic development.

title: The Voluntary Disclosure Patterns of Firms with Negative Net Debt
affiliations: Auburn University - School of Accountancy, Indiana University, Indianapolis, Texas A&M University - Lowry Mays College & Graduate School of Business and University of Connecticut

detail.title: The Voluntary Disclosure Patterns of Firms with Negative Net Debt
detail.abstract: We examine the voluntary disclosure patterns of firms with negative net debt (NND), i.e., firms whose financial assets exceed their financial liabilities, and the associated capital market consequences. NND, an increasingly common capital structure, enhances firms' financial flexibility by reducing their reliance on external financing and weakening creditor oversight. However, these same features heighten agency conflicts, particularly for firms with limited capital market experience. We explore how NND firms address these agency frictions through management guidance and how this behavior evolves with listing age. Using a large sample of U.S. public firms, we find that newly listed NND firms provide significantly more guidance than their positive net debt (PND) peers, consistent with efforts to build market credibility and reduce information asymmetry. In contrast, established NND firms issue less guidance than PND firms, suggesting diminishing marginal benefits to disclosure over time. This pattern is most pronounced for sales guidance and holds across other guidance types except capital expenditure guidance, which NND firms of all listing ages tend to withhold. Non-guiding NND firms face higher cost of capital than PND firms, and guidance is associated with lower cost of capital for newly listed, but not established NND firms. Our findings highlight the dynamic role of voluntary disclosure and listing age in mitigating agency costs for NND firms.

title: Demographics and the Trilemma: How Population Aging Shapes Exchange Rate Regime Choice

detail.title: Demographics and the Trilemma: How Population Aging Shapes Exchange Rate Regime Choice
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how demographic structure influences the resolution of the monetary policy trilemma. Using panel data for 140+ countries from 1970 to 2020 with income-conditioned controls that replace the KAOPEN-based specification, we test whether population aging systematically reshapes trilemma configurations. Income conditioning fundamentally changes the picture: aging remains strongly associated with greater financial openness (Z₁ = 2.55, p < 0.01), attenuated 25% from the unconditional estimate but robust, while the exchange rate stability result collapses entirely once income is controlled (Z₁ =-0.12, NS; log_gdp_pc = +0.201, p < 0.01), revealing that the prior ERS finding was confounded with income level. The effect on monetary independence remains null (Z₁ = 0.37, NS). Income interactions are pervasive: Z₁ x log_gdp_pc is positive and significant for both FO (+0.035, p < 0.01) and ERS (+0.054, p < 0.01), and negative for MI (-0.040, p < 0.01), indicating that all three demographic-trilemma relationships are income-conditioned. Logit models confirm that aging increases peg probability (Z₁ = 0.69, p < 0.01), with the income interaction positive (+0.011, p < 0.05). The eurozone amplification survives income conditioning but is halved: Z₁ =-101.5 (p ~ 0.054) vs.-189.8 in the baseline, suggesting that roughly half the earlier estimate reflected income-correlated heterogeneity. The CFA Franc Zone strengthens (Z₁ = +139.0, p < 0.05). The KAOPEN mediation first stage is halved (Z₁ = 3.14, p < 0.01, vs. 7.28 baseline), consistent with the income-KAOPEN confound. The CA mediation test yields Z₁ =-39.0 (p < 0.01) in the baseline, attenuating to-30.3 (p < 0.01) when trilemma indices are added-a 22.3% attenuation, modest but larger than the zero attenuation in the unconditional specification, suggesting income conditioning reveals a small but genuine mediation channel. Bilateral gravity evidence from approximately 100,000 country-pair-year observations confirms that demographic divergence predicts portfolio positions 2.6 times more strongly within monetary unions than across floating-rate pairs (dZ₁ x same_union =-0.786, p < 0.001), while FDI is null. The findings reframe the trilemma-demographics nexus: demographics reshape financial openness and peg choice, but the prior ERS result was an income confound; EMU amplification is real but more modest than originally estimated; and the CFA result is robust to income conditioning.

title: Fashion as Political Discourse: An Analysis of Clothing as a Medium of Sociopolitical Expression

detail.title: Fashion as Political Discourse: An Analysis of Clothing as a Medium of Sociopolitical Expression
detail.abstract:
This paper examines fashion as a form of political discourse, investigating whether changes in U.S. political climate are reflected in mainstream clothing trends from 1952 to 2020. Drawing on the concept of fashion as a visual language, the study hypothesizes that conservative political environments align with more traditional and gender-normative styles, while liberal environments correspond with more expressive and inclusive aesthetics.

Using archival Sears and JCPenney catalogs, the analysis codes key garment attributes, including hemlines, necklines, color palettes, and gender presentation, to construct a yearly fashion index for presidential election years. These data are compared to presidential vote share as a measure of political climate.

The results reveal a strong positive relationship between the overall fashion index and Democratic vote share, indicating that more liberal political periods are associated with less traditionally modest and more expressive fashion trends. While dress-specific results are not statistically significant, both top and bottom categories demonstrate significant positive relationships.

These findings suggest that fashion operates as a measurable reflection of broader ideological shifts, contributing to an expanded understanding of cultural artifacts as indicators of political and social change.

title: Stocks versus Bonds: What Are the Odds?
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Stocks versus Bonds: What Are the Odds?
detail.abstract:
In this short case, a Wall Street Journal article indicating that bond returns exceed stock returns about a third of the time motivates Deja Williams, an accountant and individual investor, to gather data and explore the issues on her own. Annual data on stock indexes and bond yields is provided. Despite the rather modest data set, the case provides an excellent foundation upon which to build a compelling class exploring risk and return and, with a modest amount of added work, introduce bond pricing basics. The context is nonthreatening to those new to finance, who tend to enjoy the discussion.This fictional case has been used at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business in the pre-matriculation program, where it is taught in a regular class format. It has also been used with executive programs. It would be appropriate for MBA or undergraduate classes as an introduction to financial markets. The case is particularly appropriate for audiences new to finance.

Excerpt

Stocks Versus Bonds: What Are the Odds?

Deja Williams was a devoted reader of The Wall Street Journal. It was not just the business coverage she enjoyed, but the cultural coverage as well. As she sat down to read the June 7, 2020, issue, an article in the “Mutual Funds and ETFs” section caught her attention. With the COVID-19 pandemic still raging across the globe, she had been focused less on the future and more on surviving the present. But the title of this article, “Will Stocks Trail Bonds over the Next Decade?,” had surprised her. She had always believed, as the first sentence of the article stated, that stocks would beat bonds as investments over the long run. This made sense since stocks were riskier than bonds. To even ask whether this would be true over the next 10 years seemed ridiculous, especially given that yields on government bonds were extremely low at the time.

As a senior accountant with a major paper products manufacturing company, Williams was no stranger to the world of business and had witnessed many a stock market gyration. She typically followed standard practice for financial planning: She saved all she could, took advantage of tax breaks, invested in low-fee diversified funds, and selected a level of acceptable risk by choosing the appropriate balance of stocks and bonds in her portfolio. Most importantly, she ignored what might be going on in the market at any moment and stuck to her plan—she was quite some years away from retirement and focused on building her nest egg rather than on how to live off it.

As she read the article, she began to wonder just how much she actually knew about stock and bond returns. The advice she had always followed made good sense, and she was not about to change her plans, but the article made her wonder a bit more about what was “under the hood.” What were stock and bond returns really like? How much did they vary over different time horizons? The article's main observation was that bonds proved to be better investments than stocks surprisingly often. Was this true? Could this make sense? Williams was not one to blindly accept statements that went against her instincts. She resolved to see for herself.

. . .

title:
Competiție și bipolarizare. Noi tendințe în sistemul politic românesc

Competition and Bipolarization: New Tendencies in the Romanian Political System

detail.title:
Competiție și bipolarizare. Noi tendințe în sistemul politic românesc

Competition and Bipolarization: New Tendencies in the Romanian Political System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: his article analyses the results and political implications of the June 2004 Romanian local elections, arguing that they marked a significant turning point in the structure of the Romanian party system. The article identifies three new forms of electoral behaviour that emerged prominently in this cycle: the useful vote, the sanction vote, and the protest vote, all of which functioned as instruments of citizen pressure directed primarily against the governing Social Democrat Party (PSD). Drawing on electoral data at the county and municipal levels, the article demonstrates that the 2004 local elections initiated a structural shift from a dominant-party multiparty system towards a democratic bipolar system, with PSD and the newly formed Justice and Truth Alliance (Alianța DA) as the two central poles of competition. The article further reveals two distinct electoral geographies: an urban versus rural Romania, and a western versus south-eastern Romania, each displaying markedly different patterns of party preference and electoral mobilization. The analysis shows that while PSD retained strong control in Moldavia, Oltenia, and Muntenia, the Alliance consolidated its position in Transylvania, Banat, and major urban centres. The article concludes that the local elections of 2004 served as a critical pre-parliamentary test, reconfiguring inter-party alliances, delegitimizing the dominant party through the sanction vote, and revealing an electorate increasingly capable of autonomous, strategic political behaviour.Romanian local elections 2004

title: Algorithmic Debiasing: Is There Really a Low-Cost Accuracy-Fairness Trade-off?

detail.title: Algorithmic Debiasing: Is There Really a Low-Cost Accuracy-Fairness Trade-off?
detail.abstract: This paper challenges a central premise of algorithmic debiasing (AD) for consumer credit scoring models-that less discriminatory alternative (LDA) models can deliver materially improved fairness at minimal accuracy cost. Using a simplified logisticregression credit scoring model, I show that this conclusion depends critically on how model accuracy is measured. Specifically, when a relative or rank-order accuracy metric (such as the area under the ROC curve (AUC)) is used, an LDA Model may exhibit only a modest decline in accuracy for a given improvement in fairness-a result consistent with the low-cost narrative adopted by AD proponents. However, when an absolute calibration accuracy metric is used, the LDA Model underpredicts realized default rates for approved loans by a material magnitude-significantly compromising the model's accuracy for credit portfolio risk management, loss forecasting, and capital allocation. I trace this miscalibration to the mechanics of fairness regularization which systematically lowers estimated default probabilities for credit profiles correlated with the protected class status while raising them for other credit profiles, thereby producing non-monotonic calibration curves that cannot be remediated by traditional scorecard re-calibration approaches without unwinding the fairness gain. I conclude with implications for lender due diligence of AD methodologies and argue that LDA Models claiming "low-cost" fairness improvements warrant independent evaluation of calibration accuracy within the model's operational approval region before adoption.

title: Euler and the Boundaries the Observable

detail.title: Euler and the Boundaries the Observable
detail.abstract: This micro-essay explores two of Euler's celebrated formulas through the conceptual framework of "The Eye of Superreality." The static model V-E + F = 2 and the dynamic model e iπ + 1 = 0 are examined as profound representations of perception's dual nature: closed structure and cyclical process. These mathematical expressions reveal universal principles applicable to both human and artificial intelligence interactions with reality. The essay demonstrates how these formulas illuminate the architecture of perception, the role of blind spots, and their philosophical implications for understanding observable reality.

title:
Democrația low cost în minunata lume iliberală

Low-Cost Democracy in the Wonderful Illiberal World

detail.title:
Democrația low cost în minunata lume iliberală

Low-Cost Democracy in the Wonderful Illiberal World

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This article examines the confluence of illiberalism, populism, and post-democracy as defining features of contemporary political life, arguing that liberal democracy is facing an unprecedented challenge from within. The new populism, oriented towards an assumed illiberalism and invoking the authentic "needs" of the so-called popular sovereign, is systematically matched by the dissemination of "fake news" and "alternative facts," a process facilitated by the perverse effects of new media and search engine manipulation. Drawing on the concept of post-democracy developed by Colin Crouch, the article traces the structural conditions under which democratic institutions are hollowed out while their formal appearance is preserved.

The article identifies two main actors of illiberalism: an "uncivil society" rooted in pre-modern nationalist and xenophobic traditions, and a neo-nationalist post-democratic movement that exploits the crises of post-modernity. These forces, exemplified by the illiberal turns in Hungary, Poland, and Romania, combine populist mobilization with authoritarian consolidation of power, following models pioneered by Vladimir Putin and later adapted by Viktor Orbán, Jarosław Kaczyński, and Donald Trump.

Populism is analysed both as a "thin ideology" — defined by the anti-elitist distinction between a "pure people" and a "corrupt elite" — and as a political instrument that becomes explosively dangerous when fused with illiberalism. This fusion enables the systematic dismantling of constitutional rights and civil liberties under the banner of popular sovereignty, transforming democracy into a low-cost plebiscitary ritual stripped of its liberal substance. The article concludes that the post-democratic condition represents a transitional regime in which institutional forms survive but the political nation, as the source of sovereignty, loses any real influence over those in power.

keywords: cross-section of stock returns JEL Codes: G12

detail.abstract: Short-term reversal appears to have weakened in international equity markets because standard measures mix firm-specific and industry-wide returns. When evaluated relative to industry peers, the reversal persists. Using data from 64 countries, the conventional strategy delivers negligible returns, whereas an industry-adjusted strategy earns 0.53% per month with a Sharpe ratio of 0.74. The effect reflects the reversal of firm-specific shocks masked by persistent industry components. A regret-based signal captures the same industry-relative variation and adds no independent return. Reversal did not disappear; it was mismeasured.

title: SOCIAL SYSTEMS AS PERCEPTUAL ENTITIES: A DEVELOPMENTAL THEORY OF SOCIETAL VIABILITY UNDER STRUCTURAL CHANGE

detail.title: SOCIAL SYSTEMS AS PERCEPTUAL ENTITIES: A DEVELOPMENTAL THEORY OF SOCIETAL VIABILITY UNDER STRUCTURAL CHANGE
detail.abstract: Social theory has produced powerful accounts of how societal systems function and reproduce themselves within established frameworks of meaning but has not specified the developmental dynamics through which those frameworks generate their own limits and require reconstruction. This gap — the untheorized foundation beneath institutionalism, autopoietic systems theory, communicative action theory, and structural functionalism alike — has moved from peripheral to central as artificial intelligence introduces new interpretive logics faster than any societal system can consolidate them. This paper extends the Integrating Structure and Life Energy (ISLE) framework to the societal level, treating societies as perceptual entities: emergent interpretive configurations sustained by the distributed meaning-making activity of populations, irreducible to any of their constituent institutions or actors. Drawing on the ISLE mechanism — in which consolidation of governing premises progressively compresses interpretive elasticity, accumulates misalignment, and drives the system toward a coherence horizon at which reconstruction becomes necessary — the paper derives three conditions that are necessary and jointly sufficient for societal viability under structural change: material viability, interpretive capability, and social meaning coherence within the ISLE mechansim. It introduces premise regulation architecture as the structural variable governing the rate at which these conditions are maintained or eroded as consolidation deepens. Five developmental pathways — reconstruction, false alignment, fragmented recognition, constrained oscillation, and breakdown — specify the outcomes produced across different condition configurations. The framework reframes the central problem of societal analysis: not which institutional configuration produces optimal performance within a given structural plane, but what determines whether a societal system can reconstruct its governing premises as the conditions of viability change.

title: RECONCILING AFFIRMATIVE ACTION AND MERIT: EVIDENCE AND DESIGN FROM INDIA

detail.title: RECONCILING AFFIRMATIVE ACTION AND MERIT: EVIDENCE AND DESIGN FROM INDIA
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes India's affirmative action system through the lens of market design, identifying a fundamental conflict between the Indra Sawhney (1992) and Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008) Supreme Court rulings. While the former established the "over-and-above" principle and within-category fairness, the latter introduced a specific cutoff mandate and de-reservation recommendation. We establish that these legal requirements are jointly incompatible, as no assignment rule can simultaneously satisfy all the resulting axioms. By exploring alternative relaxations, we identify a family of rules that support soft reservations and prove that the Forward Transfer rule is merit-dominant. Finally, we propose a reinterpretation of the cutoff policy that resolves legal inconsistencies and eliminates endogenous feedback, offering a superior meritocratic rule ready for immediate institutional implementation.

reference: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 26-2
title: The Price-Change Statistics We’ve Weighted For
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: The Price-Change Statistics We’ve Weighted For

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 26-2

detail.abstract: The real effects of monetary policy depend on price stickiness. Existing studies that measure aggregate stickiness using US consumer price index microdata hold the consumption basket fixed. This yields a lower level of stickiness in 2024 compared with 1978. We show instead that stickiness is unchanged. Although individual products now change prices more frequently, the effect is largely offset by shifts in consumer spending, notably toward services with stickier prices. These consumption-basket shifts reduce the estimated decline in monetary non neutrality by 25 percentage points, suggesting that monetary policy remains far more effective than methods used in existing studies imply.

title: Evolutionary Pathways to Female Labor Force Participation in India and the United States

detail.title: Evolutionary Pathways to Female Labor Force Participation in India and the United States
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes India's chronic low Female Labor Force Participation Rate (FLFPR),
indicative of poor institutional responsiveness, deleterious norms, and scarce labor demand puts
the economy in a self-reinforcing trap of very underutilized human capital. Unlike the sharply
different path of the United States, where policy, legal reforms, and social movements produced
sustained female labor force integration. Through an evolutionary comparative paradigm, of
variation selection and retention, paper follows the way the U.S. transformed social movements
and legislative punctuations into long-lasting institutional retention, whereas India's incremental
advances are precarious and uneven. The paper argues that India cannot replicate U.S. reforms
verbatim but recommends pursuing an adaptive policy transfer through contextual learning and
institution building. This strategy can break the equilibrium of low participation, which would lead
to inclusive growth and transform gender parity as a welfare objective into an economic productive
strategy.

title: The 72-Hour Shock? Preliminary Evidence from 52 Token Unlock Events on Binance A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Unlock Events and Their Asymmetric Impact on Cryptocurrency Prices

detail.title: The 72-Hour Shock? Preliminary Evidence from 52 Token Unlock Events on Binance A Cross-Sectional Analysis of Unlock Events and Their Asymmetric Impact on Cryptocurrency Prices

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has written a Web3 and blockchain column for The Electronic Times (Etnews), one of Korea’s leading technology newspapers, for over eight years.
