detail.abstract: This paper advances a conceptual framework explaining how predictive statementsoriginating from sources as diverse as fortune-tellers, informal advisors, and contemporary analytical systems-shape human cognition, behaviour, and agency through processes of internalisation. While prediction is typically understood as a tool for reducing uncertainty, this paper argues that predictive authority functions performatively: it does not merely anticipate the future but actively participates in constructing it. Drawing on insights from cognitive psychology, anthropology, and neuroscience, the paper introduces the Predictive Authority Internalisation Model (PAIM), which outlines how externally delivered forecasts are cognitively encoded, emotionally stabilised, and incorporated into self-narratives, subsequently guiding perception, decision-making, and action. The framework demonstrates how predictive statements can produce both adaptive and maladaptive outcomes. In adaptive contexts, prediction may support meaning-making and emotional regulation; however, under conditions of heightened uncertainty and reduced perceived control, it may foster deterministic drift, whereby probabilistic information is reinterpreted as fixed destiny. This process can result in behavioural constraint, dependency, and self-fulfilling outcomes. By distinguishing between prediction as informational input and prediction as internalised script, the paper contributes a unifying theoretical account of how human beings transform uncertainty into lived reality. The analysis concludes by outlining pathways for reclaiming agency while retaining the functional benefits of predictive thinking.

title: COLLATERAL DAMAGE: THE STRUCTURAL CASE FOR EXEMPTING SMALL BUSINESSES FROM BROAD-BASED TARIFFS

detail.abstract: Tariffs are taxes, and like all taxes, their constitutional legitimacy depends on whether Congress has exercised its Article I power with awareness of the consequences it produces. When applied uniformly to firms of radically unequal financial capacity, broad-based tariffs function as regressive levies on liquidity-imposing costs that large corporations absorb as rounding errors while destroying small firms that lack the balance-sheet depth, supply-chain flexibility, and contractual leverage to survive them. Congress has long recognized the particular vulnerability of small enterprises through a comprehensive statutory framework anchored in the Small Business Act, yet trade law has never been brought within that commitment. This Article argues that this isolation is a failure of legislative coherence, not constitutional necessity, and that Congress has clear authority-grounded in Article I and confirmed by its own declared statutory commitments-to correct it. This Article proceeds in five Parts. Part II establishes the economic predicate, demonstrating through Transaction Cost Economics, Agency Theory, and Contract Theory that uniform tariff incidence on unequal firms is a structurally determined outcome: small importers are captive to the full incidence of tariffs because their financial constraints foreclose absorption,

title: Real or Nominal? Interest Rate Illusion in International Remittances
affiliations: and Saint Cloud State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Real or Nominal? Interest Rate Illusion in International Remittances
detail.abstract: Due to their size, steady, and upward trajectory relative to other sources of international capital flows, remittances have emerged as the largest and most stable source of scarce foreign exchange to the developing world. This paper revisits some key drivers of remittance inflows, including the two policy variables: the interest rate and the exchange rate. In their panel estimations including 21 major remittance destinations for the 1980-2017 time period, Ratha and Kang (2020) found that the nominal interest rate was significant, but the real interest rate was not. In the present study, we reexamine if indeed such a money illusion exists. Replacing deposit interest rates with lending interest rates in the same model on updated data (1980-2020), we were able to recover the significance of the real interest rate and thus, rule out the presence of the said money illusion. Moreover, our results indicate that currency devaluation may help boost remittance inflows in most cases. We also demonstrate that results based on panel studies may not necessarily agree with those based on country-specific time-series studies and therefore, policy formulation calls for both exercises.

title: Agreeing to Lose: Why Rituals Bind and Algorithms Won't

detail.title: Agreeing to Lose: Why Rituals Bind and Algorithms Won't
detail.abstract: Why do people accept losses when they could fight and expect to win? Existing accounts trace compliance to fairness perceptions, social signaling, or the shadow of the future. We propose an alternative mechanism requiring none of these. Building on Bénabou and Tirole's intrapersonal signaling framework, we model a procedural ritual as a game played between an agent's earlier and later selves. The ritual creates a behavioral record the agent cannot fully reconstruct as strategic in hindsight, producing a self-image the agent will pay to protect. The model yields three results. The mechanism produces behavioral signatures the standard procedural justice empirical toolkit cannot structurally distinguish from the voice effect. Poorly designed rituals actively erode compliance through a dilution effect on the defector pool. And institutions face strictly diminishing returns driven by demographic depletion rather than psychological fatigue. The framework illuminates a vulnerability in modern institutional design: the current push to automate dispute resolution risks removing structural features that make voluntary compliance possible.

title: Structural Equation Modeling of Motorcycle Risk Perception and Crash Exposure in Urban Bangladesh

detail.title: Structural Equation Modeling of Motorcycle Risk Perception and Crash Exposure in Urban Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Bangladesh has the highest global death rates for motorcycle accidents, which make up the majority of all traffic accidents in Bangladesh. For the last couple of years, the rate has been rising. According to data from the BUET Accident Research Institute (ARI), in 2022, motorbikes accounted for 62% of all vehicles on the road, with 26 accidents occurring for every 10,000 motorcycles. This is due to their accessibility, affordability, and ride-sharing use. Hence, it is essential to investigate the risk factors that contribute to motorcycle accidents, how they affect risk assessment, and how to develop the necessary policy implications. Data on perceived risk was gathered for this study from 1,559 participants in offline and online questionnaire survey. Age, gender, occupation, residence division, usage classifications, ride sharing app usage criteria together with ratings on the perceived risk of 40 precursors to motorcycling accidents in the setting of Dhaka were gathered . Ranking and Contributions of different precursors on safety status and accident exposure have been demonstrated by structural equation modelling. Lastly, policy implications have been analysed in this study. In conclusion, any developing country's urban context will benefit greatly from the provided SEM tools for accident analysis and prevention.

title: SnowPole-VehicleLoc: An Open-Source Software Framework for Vehicle Localization Using Georeferenced Snow Poles

detail.abstract: Reliable vehicle localization remains challenging in GNSS-limited and GNSSdenied environments, particularly under harsh Nordic winter conditions where visual cues are frequently obscured by snow. This paper presents SnowPole-VehicleLoc, an open-source, end-to-end software framework for vehicle localization using georeferenced snow poles and LiDAR-GNSS data fusion. Snow poles are treated as stable, machine-perceivable roadside infrastructure landmarks that remain detectable under snow-covered conditions using LiDAR-based perception. SnowPole-VehicleLoc is motivated by the need for a reproducible and softwareoriented realization of infrastructure-assisted vehicle localization. While the underlying localization methodology has been presented previously, the present work focuses on the software implementation of the approach. In particular, it provides a complete and modular realization of the localization pipeline, together with dynamic visualization and demonstration tools, as well as the datasets and source code required to develop, reproduce, and extend the system. The framework integrates LiDAR-based snow pole detection, GNSS-LiDAR fusion for landmark anchoring, and incremental LiDAR-based vehicle navigation to enable continuous vehicle pose estimation under varying levels of GNSS availability. SnowPole-VehicleLoc is validated using real-world LiDAR and GNSS data collected on Norwegian highways under Nordic winter conditions.

title: A Complete Taxonomy of Black-Scholes Greeks: Closed-Form Solutions for First, Second, and Third-Order Sensitivities

detail.title: A Complete Taxonomy of Black-Scholes Greeks: Closed-Form Solutions for First, Second, and Third-Order Sensitivities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: We present the most complete unified taxonomy of Black-Scholes option price sensitivities (Greeks) available in the literature, encompassing 21 distinct measures through third order: first-order (Delta, Vega, Theta, Rho), second-order (Gamma, Vanna, Charm, Vomma, Veta, Vera, Dual Delta, Dual Gamma), third-order (Speed, Zomma, Color, Ultima, DvannaDvol, DvommaDspot), and portfolio-level (Dollar Delta, Dollar Gamma, Lambda). For each Greek we provide: (i) a fully explicit derivation from the dividend-adjusted Black-Scholes formula showing every application of the chain rule and product rule, (ii) alternative derivation paths including risk-neutral expectation differentiation and heat equation Green’s function representations, (iii) closed-form expressions for both European calls and puts, (iv) identification of put-call parity equivalences, (v) complete asymptotic analysis (deep ITM/OTM, short/long-dated, zero/high vol limits), (vi) monotonicity and convexity properties with extrema locations, (vii) dimensional analysis for practitioner interpretation, and (viii) practical trading context. We derive the Black-Scholes PDE from first principles via Itô’s lemma and the replicating-portfolio argument, establish the risk-neutral pricing connection, and prove the key symmetry lemma that simplifies every Greek derivation. The Gamma-Theta tradeoff is proved directly from the PDE with trading implications. The Vanna-Volga pricing method is derived from smile replication principles. We provide a complete treatment of sticky-strike versus stickydelta hedging conventions, delta hedging theory with continuous and discrete P&L analysis, Greeks under stochastic volatility (Heston model), numerical methods for Greeks computation (finite differences, pathwise, likelihood ratio, and adjoint algorithmic differentiation), and the behavior of Greeks near expiry including pin risk. A differential-geometric interpretation frames the Greeks as gradient, Hessian, and third-order tensor components on the six-dimensional Black-Scholes parameter manifold, with the PDE as a constraint surface. Fourth-order Greeks are derived and a convergence analysis of the Taylor price expansion justifies the third-order truncation for perturbations up to 10% of spot. Publication-quality three-dimensional surface visualizations for all 21 Greeks reveal the topology of each sensitivity across its natural parameter space. Formal proofs of all 12 put-call parity equivalences, a complete 21 Greek formula reference card, and a comprehensive monotonicity and extrema table are provided as appendices. A Python implementation with numerical verification against finite differences accompanies the paper, with over 50 figures. To our knowledge, this constitutes the most comprehensive rigorously derived reference for Black-Scholes Greeks in a single document.

detail.abstract:
This study examines the integration of F-35 and Rafale aircraft within the Hellenic Air Force and its implications for network-centric warfare in the Eastern Mediterranean and Aegean region.
The evolving security environment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Aegean Sea has accelerated the transformation of air power doctrines, shifting from platform-centric to network-centric warfare models. This paper examines the integration of fourth-and-a-half generation Rafale F3R aircraft with fifth-generation F-35A stealth fighters within the Hellenic Air Force, analyzing how their combined operational use reshapes the balance of power in the region. The study explores the technological, operational, and strategic implications of this integration, focusing on sensor fusion, low observability, data-link interoperability, and multi-domain coordination. Particular emphasis is placed on how information superiority, rather than numerical strength, increasingly determines air dominance outcomes. Through a case study of the Aegean operational environment, this research highlights the unique geographical and tactical conditions that amplify the effectiveness of network-centric systems. The findings suggest that the combined deployment of Rafale and F-35 platforms creates a layered and adaptive air combat architecture, significantly enhancing situational awareness, response time, and strike precision. The paper concludes that the integration of these platforms represents not merely an upgrade in capabilities, but a fundamental transformation in the nature of air warfare, with broader implications for regional deterrence, NATO interoperability, and future conflict scenarios.

title: Strengthening Hurricane-Resilient Infrastructure Delivery in the United States Through Procurement Governance, Contract Risk Management, and Delivery Controls

detail.title: Strengthening Hurricane-Resilient Infrastructure Delivery in the United States Through Procurement Governance, Contract Risk Management, and Delivery Controls

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
The United States faces increasing pressure to modernize and protect its infrastructure systems against hurricanes, flooding, severe weather events, and related climate-driven disruptions. Public and private assets; including roads, bridges, hospitals, schools, logistics hubs, utilities, housing stock, and coastal developments-are exposed not only to physical damage, but also to prolonged operational interruption, escalating repair costs, insurance stress, and delayed economic recovery. In response, resilience policy has traditionally concentrated on engineering design standards, structural hardening, emergency preparedness, and post-event funding mechanisms. While these responses remain essential, they do not fully address a critical and frequently overlooked determinant of infrastructure performance: the governance systems through which projects are procured, contractually structured, commercially controlled, and operationally delivered. 

This paper argues that many infrastructure failures stem not solely from engineering deficiencies, but from procurement inefficiency, poor contractor selection, weak contractual risk allocation, fragmented oversight, cost overruns, avoidable disputes, and delayed recovery systems. These governance failures can significantly undermine otherwise sound engineering outcomes and are particularly consequential in hurricane-prone jurisdictions such as Florida, Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, and the Carolinas. 

The paper proposes a governance-based resilience model built upon five interrelated pillars: resilient procurement systems, contract risk management, cost governance, dispute avoidance mechanisms, and rapid recovery delivery frameworks. It is submitted that integrating these disciplines into U.S. infrastructure delivery systems can materially reduce economic loss, improve accountability, accelerate reconstruction, and strengthen long-term national resilience. The article concludes that governance-led resilience should be recognized as a core component of modern infrastructure policy in the United States.

title: Unknown Rational Expectations: Evidence from NFL Prediction Markets
affiliations: Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Oregon State University and Texas Tech University

detail.title: Unknown Rational Expectations: Evidence from NFL Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: Rational expectations are well-supported in financial markets. Evidence that traders are also rationally inattentive, however, runs through a single channel: the business cycle. Whether inattention binds independently of cyclical variation-as a primitive cognitive friction mapping objective events into subjective beliefs-remains open. We answer using NFL prediction markets: binary contracts traded on Polymarket against a cash-like safe asset, benchmarked against ESPN's continuous win probability, in an environment that trends but does not cycle. Using 2025-26 season data and a dynamic program nesting FIRE and cognitive discounting, we reject FIRE three ways: U-shaped pre-game volatility drifting with competitiveness, a persistent state-dependent wedge unaltered by concurrent market load, and precisely zero cross-game spillovers. These collapse to a cognitive discount of 80%, validated by a reinforcement-learning agent reproducing the inaction and panic-liquidation patterns. The result isolates acyclical, purely-cognitive rational inattention, locating the friction at the state-to-probability mapping rather than the attention-across-assets margin.

title: Efficiency and Market Power: The Two Faces of the Multinational Enterprise
affiliations: Dept of Management, Mays Business School, Texas A&M University

detail.title: Efficiency and Market Power: The Two Faces of the Multinational Enterprise

keywords: two faces of the Janus MNE

contentType.other: Accepted by the editors but the manuscript has not been branded, typeset or copyedit by the publisher in any way.

detail.abstract: International business (IB) scholars have historically treated efficiency and market power as separate explanations for the existence, growth, and success of multinational enterprises (MNEs). This paper argues that efficiency and market power must be considered together, and that their separation has left internalization theory ill-equipped to distinguish value-creating from value-extracting MNE behavior. In addition, the bundling of different types of market imperfections has inadvertently provided an efficiency-enhancing rationale for MNE misconduct such as abusive transfer pricing and BEPS (base erosion and profit shifting). The paper first revisits two foundational contributions to the theory of the MNE: Hymer's (1960) dissertation and Dunning and Rugman's (1985) commentary. The paper next revisits Rugman and Eden (1985), which connects internalization theory to transfer pricing and the efficiency versus market power debate. The costs of jurisdictional arbitrage through BEPS activities illustrate the real-world costs of an efficiency-only framing. The paper then proposes the AMOR (Advantage, Motivation, Opportunity, and Rationalization) framework, which unbundles three types of market imperfections (natural, structural, and jurisdictional) within internalization theory to show that efficiency and market power are not competing but complementary explanations for internalizationboth manifest in the two faces of the Janus MNE. The paper concludes by discussing how AMOR can guide IB scholars in building more complete theories of the MNE and better equipping scholars and policymakers to identify and address rent-extracting MNE behavior.

title: "And here's what I think about tariffs…": What happens when politics enters supply chain decisions?
affiliations: Portland State University and Arizona State University (ASU)

detail.title: "And here's what I think about tariffs…": What happens when politics enters supply chain decisions?

keywords: "And here's what I think about tariffs…": What happens when politics enters supply chain decisions?"

detail.abstract: As supply chain topics like tariffs have become increasingly prominent in public and political discourse, the influence of potential biases from politics has also grown. This study investigates how differences in political ideology influence supply chain management decisions. We use a between-subjects vignette experiment with a final sample of 216 supply chain professionals who evaluated a new sourcing plan proposed by a manager in response to tariffs. Participants were randomly assigned to conditions where the proposal by the manager included statements that were conservative (pro-Trump), liberal (anti-Trump), or politically neutral. These statements influenced participants' view of the manager's political ideology and resulted in different levels of support for a tariff-related plan and the manager. Our findings include three key insights. First, conservatives were more likely to support a tariff-related sourcing plan. Second, a manager including a political statement did not significantly impact employee support for the plan, but it did decrease employee support of that manager. Third, ideological dissimilarity between an employee and their manager strongly decreased the support of both the plan and manager-even in the neutral condition. Overall, political ideology biases supply chain decision making, suggesting an important new stream of research.

title: Cybersecurity Risk and the Protection of U.S. Financial Infrastructure: A Strategic Framework for Cooperative Financial Institutions

detail.title: Cybersecurity Risk and the Protection of U.S. Financial Infrastructure: A Strategic Framework for Cooperative Financial Institutions
detail.abstract: The increasing digitization of financial services has fundamentally reshaped the operational landscape of financial institutions, introducing both efficiency gains and significant vulnerabilities. Cybersecurity risk has emerged as a central concern, with cyberattacks targeting financial infrastructure, consumer data, and institutional operations at an unprecedented scale. While large financial institutions have invested heavily in cybersecurity frameworks, cooperative financial institutions such as credit unions often operate with comparatively limited resources despite serving a critical role in the U.S. financial system. This article examines cybersecurity risk within credit unions and its broader implications for national economic stability and financial infrastructure protection. It develops a leadership-driven framework integrating cybersecurity governance, enterprise risk management, and organizational resilience. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature in cybersecurity, financial regulation, and organizational leadership, the study argues that strengthening cybersecurity capabilities in credit unions is essential for protecting consumer trust, ensuring operational continuity, and safeguarding systemic stability. The findings highlight that leadership-driven cybersecurity innovation represents a matter of substantial merit and national importance, contributing directly to U.S. economic security and resilience.

detail.abstract: Digital transformation failure is widely attributed to technological and organizational factors, yet a substantial proportion of mid-market digital transformations in founder-led firms stall before deployment completes. This paper argues that in founder-led enterprises, the founder personally constitutes both the most powerful enabler and the most powerful constraint on digital transformation. It introduces the Founder Readiness Framework (FRF-4), a conceptual model organized around four dimensions: strategic aperture, structural decoupling, learning orientation, and identity plasticity. The framework is situated within the literature on founder-led firms, digital maturity, and organizational change, and is illustrated through three stylized archetypes of founder readiness profiles and the distinct transformation trajectories each produces. The paper contributes a diagnostic vocabulary and decision aid for boards, investors, and transformation consultants working with founder-led firms. It identifies empirical calibration of the framework, longitudinal tracking of transformation trajectories, and sector-specific validation as priority directions for future research.

title: The Path to Quiet Authority: A Brief on Leadership Beyond Performance and the Gaze

detail.title: The Path to Quiet Authority: A Brief on Leadership Beyond Performance and the Gaze

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
This brief extends prior analysis of leadership power and its differential cost, examining what leadership requires once those patterns are recognized and their consequences understood. It builds on Brief 1, Positional Aggression and Discursive Distancing (Adams-Qualtiere, 2026), and Brief 2, Who Bears the Cost of Organizational Power (Adams-Qualtiere, 2026).

It advances a formation-based model of leadership structured across four movements: Unaware Impact, Discerned Leadership, Intentional Formation, and Quiet Authority. The central argument is direct: leadership does not change through awareness alone. It changes when power is governed through discipline, restraint, and accountability to the conditions it produces.

The brief shifts leadership evaluation from intention and expression to observable impact. It positions self-governance as the mechanism through which power is disciplined, the deliberate ending of misaligned behaviors as the test of integrity, and intentional formation as the work of building environments in which authenticity does not carry disproportionate risk. Trust is reframed as an outcome of consistent leadership practice rather than a strategy, and restraint is established as the defining discipline of mature authority.

Drawing on the SHAPE framework as an accountability architecture, this brief presents Quiet Authority as an observable leadership standard, evidenced in environments where ownership is sustained, participation does not require self-protection, and leadership presence no longer depends on continuous intervention. It concludes by interpreting Micah 6:8 as a practical standard for the use of power in organizational life. The brief also includes a Quiet Authority profile and SHAPE self-assessment to support reflection and application.

title: THREE ESSAYS ON APPLIED ETHICS
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Centre for Development Studies

detail.title: THREE ESSAYS ON APPLIED ETHICS
detail.abstract:
Essay 1. Meritocracy: A Modern Misconception

This essay argues that the problematic and distorted notion of meritocracy is an expression of a deeper human propensity to hubristic pride and self-love. Drawing on Augustinian and Kantian notions of self-pride, it shows how secularization, Enlightenment individualism, and market society reinforced a view that connects success with moral deservingness while subordinating moral obligation to self-interest. The essay argues that this distorted meritocratic ethos undermines social cohesion, demonizes the unsuccessful, and crowds out the public good. Against this, it advances a broader humanistic conception of meritocracy grounded in self-reflection, acknowledgment of privilege, recognition of luck and wider humanity, and a balanced approach that promotes collaboration, reciprocity, and the common good.

Essay 2. Migrants: Overcoming the Obstacle of Difference Identity

This essay argues that populist movements in the Global North have created a new cultural monster: “migrants" as a contextual response to socio-cultural anxieties. Drawing on Cohen’s seven theses of monster culture, Said’s account of Orientalism, and broader empirical evidence, the essay shows how migrants are cast as embodiments of difference, disorder, and threat, fueling xenophobic cultures of exclusion. At the same time, it argues that the immigrant “monster” can provoke reflection on identity, responsibility, and moral obligation. Through utilitarian, Rawlsian, and collective responsibility arguments, the essay develops philosophical justifications for openness toward migrants while recognizing legitimate tensions of acculturation and difference. It concludes that the obstacle of difference identity can be overcome through a more reflective understanding of otherness, shared humanity, and responsibility.

Essay 3. Should Liberal Feminists Support Hijab Ban in the West?

This essay investigates the philosophical and ethical arguments on both sides of the debate over hijab bans, asking whether liberal feminists have justification to support such bans. Drawing on different strands of liberal feminism, the essay evaluates whether a hijab ban can increase gender empowerment or contribute to a more gender-just society. Using the concepts of resources, agency, and achievements, and a conception of gender justice centered on reducing the costs of gendered lifestyles, the essay examines tensions between autonomy, secularism, multicultural accommodation, and substantive equality. It argues that the question is not whether hijab is “just a cloth,” but whether bans improve women’s empowerment and advance gender justice more than the baseline. The essay concludes by assessing whether liberal feminist support for hijab bans is philosophically defensible.

title: Outsourcing Decision in the Presence of Supplier Copycatting
affiliations: ,  and University of Western Ontario - Ivey Business School

detail.title: Outsourcing Decision in the Presence of Supplier Copycatting
detail.abstract: Supplier copycatting occurs when the supplier to a manufacturer copies the manufacturer's original product and encroaches into the market with a copycat product. This increasingly common phenomenon poses challenges to both manufacturers and suppliers worldwide. Unlike conventional supplier encroachment, supplier copycatting changes both the current market competition as well as the future manufacturer-supplier relationship. When a supplier copycats, it risks losing the manufacturer's future wholesale business, while the manufacturer may respond by switching future production to an alternative supplier. Previous research has not considered the impacts of these realities.  To fill this gap in the literature, we propose a two-period game-theoretic approach to supplier copycatting. We investigate a setting where an original manufacturer outsources the production of its product to a high-quality supplier with copycatting capabilities. If this supplier decides to produce a copied product, it will lose the manufacturer's wholesale contract in the second period, and the manufacturer will outsource the production to an alternative, lower-quality supplier. We examine how the parties' optimal decisions are influenced by the presence of the manufacturer's future production alternatives and the repercussions awaiting the copycatting supplier. Our results indicate that (a) the manufacturer can be worse off upon an improvement in the quality of the alternative supplier's production, (b) under certain conditions, upon an improvement in the quality of the copycat product, the copycatting supplier's profit is reduced. Furthermore, an increase in the quality of the copycat product can convince the supplier against copycatting; (c) an increase in copycatting cost can improve the supplier's profit; and (d) the copycatting supplier's tendency to encroach is reduced upon a fall in the net present value of the future profits. These results are driven by the manufacturer's future production alternatives and the supplier's future repercussions; and have strong implications for manufacturers that outsource production, as well as the suppliers to original manufacturers.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the achievement of a new world record in offset printing as the outcome of a rigorous and deeply structured application of Lean Manufacturing principles in a high-productivity industrial environment. The central objective is to demonstrate that the systematic elimination of waste, combined with process standardization and data-driven performance management, can substantially redefine operational limits in the graphic industry while maintaining strict quality requirements.

The project is grounded in core Lean methodologies, including continuous improvement (Kaizen), setup time reduction (SMED), standard work, visual management, and Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) as a primary performance indicator. A strong emphasis was placed on identifying and eliminating micro-stoppages, reducing variability, and stabilizing production flows. The integration of intelligent automation and real-time monitoring systems enabled precise control over process deviations, reinforcing a culture of operational discipline and accountability.

title: Social Media Algorithm and political polarization
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Chitkara University, Chitkara University and Chitkara University

detail.title: Social Media Algorithm and political polarization
detail.abstract: The algorithms that rule your social media feeds determine what content you'll be able to see on platforms and apps. The ultimate goal of these algorithms is to keep users engaged by surface more relevant content, i.e. content you are likely to like, comment on, or share. But when it comes to political discourse online, this system can have its downsides. Since emotional, shocking, or contentious content drives engagement, that kind of content is what typically gets promoted to users. This can result in a "filter bubble," a feed full of information that agrees with and reinforces the user's current beliefs. Research has found that algorithms may be perpetuating personalisation of content online-and exacerbating political polarization. To address these challenges, our research calls for greater algorithmic transparency, the development and enforcement of new regulations for online intermediaries and enhanced digital literacy to better equip citizens to negotiate and critically consume online information.

title: Intel Corporation Case Study

detail.title: Intel Corporation Case Study
detail.abstract: This is a peak at Gordon Moore, the co-founder and emeritus CEO of Intel, who has been noted as one of the most prominent and successful managers today. Intel company, under the strategic leadership of Moore Group, has become the largest manufacturer of computer chips in the world. This company is now one of the most admired companies in America and one of the most profitable companies on the "Fortune 500" list. Gordon Moore coined the phrase "strategic turning point." Moore argues that at the magic point of a strategic turning, all rules change. Moore owes most of his victories to his strategic leadership philosophy revealed in this article. We recount the experience of his victories and failures and show how he has controlled events and turned threats into opportunities at Intel. title: Multipolarity, AI, and the Reordering of Global Business

detail.title: Multipolarity, AI, and the Reordering of Global Business
detail.abstract: The paradigm of frictionless globalization, which anchored multinational enterprise (MNE) strategy for three decades, is undergoing a structural rupture. The global economy is not deglobalizing but rather reconfiguring into a multipolar system characterized by selective interdependence and fragmented regulatory regimes. This paper examines why global business strategy must be fundamentally rethought as artificial intelligence (AI) and data transition from operational byproducts to tightly regulated, sovereign strategic assets. As nations increasingly weaponize geoeconomic instruments” such as export controls, data localization mandates, and identity-linked trust barriersâ” firms can no longer rely on singular, globally integrated operating models. Instead, this paper posits that survival in the AI-driven multipolar order requires the adoption of "federated enterprise" architectures. Through a multi-stack approach to technology, jurisdiction-sensitive governance, and policy-aware product design, MNEs must build duplicative resilience across competing techno-blocs. The analysis identifies five emerging business archetypes poised to thrive in this environment and explores the profound sectoral implications of this transition. Finally, it outlines three plausible scenario trajectories for the global economy, demonstrating that the future belongs not to the most centralized firms, but to the most geopolitically adaptable and architecturally modular organizations.

title: The BASIT Framework: A Multiplicative Model for System-Level Value Generation in Integrated Logistics Systems

detail.title: The BASIT Framework: A Multiplicative Model for System-Level Value Generation in Integrated Logistics Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, personal, or organizational relationships that could be perceived as having influenced the content of this manuscript, and no external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Bajahnon Adaptive Strategic Integration Theory (BASIT), a formally propositioned, multiplicatively structured framework for understanding and improving the performance of complex, multi-entity logistics systems. Despite extensive research on data quality, decision-making, and supply chain coordination as independent performance drivers, the literature lacks an integrative framework that formally specifies how these dimensions interact at the system level. BASIT addresses this gap by positing that system-level value generation is a multiplicative — not additive — function of Data Intelligence (DI), Decision Quality (DQ), and Coordination Effectiveness (CE), governed by an Operational Cost denominator (OC/F). This multiplicative structure, expressed through the Bajahnon Multiplier Model (BMM) equation SVG = (DI × DQ × CE) / OC, generates empirically distinguishable predictions from additive competitor models and prescribes integrated, simultaneous investment across all three constructs. We further introduce the BASIT Readiness Index (BRI) and the BASIT Impact Assessment Tool (IAT) as validated diagnostic instruments for measuring system readiness. Preliminary application to a logistics corridor case demonstrates a BRI improvement from 36 to 68 following a coordination-based intervention, providing initial evidence of the framework's diagnostic and prescriptive utility. The paper concludes with a research agenda for empirical validation and the framework's position within the broader BASIT Research Ecosystem.

title: What a journal is for: a proposal for AI-born journals, twenty-five years after Editorial Manager

detail.title: What a journal is for: a proposal for AI-born journals, twenty-five years after Editorial Manager
detail.abstract: Editorial Manager is twenty-five years old this year. ScholarOne, its older cousin, is somewhat older. A quarter of a century is time enough to ask whether we are doing the right thing, and whether we are doing it rightly. This letter argues that we are not, and that the technology for a better answer has now arrived. The online submission apparatus that grew up around these two systems now absorbs, on my best estimate, around one billion researcher-hours of cumulative labour since 2001-the equivalent of roughly half a million personyears of dedicated work, comparable in magnitude to the direct labour of the Human Genome Project. The case I make here is not a criticism of publishers, who in building these systems solved real problems at the time, nor of the editorial community, which has trusted them in good faith. It is a proposal. I argue that what scholarly communication needs now is a class of AI-born journals: venues designed around AI-enabling architecture from first principles, freed from the incremental accretion of procedural layers that no one now remembers why we added. The philosophical claim that supports the proposal is a claim about editorial identity: a journal's brand is carried by its editor's

title: Redefining the Architecture of Choice: Voluntary Agreements as Institutional Nudges and the Limits of Behavioral Public Policy Theory

detail.title: Redefining the Architecture of Choice: Voluntary Agreements as Institutional Nudges and the Limits of Behavioral Public Policy Theory

declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Behavioral public policy has generated an extensive literature on nudging, yet the theoretical conceptualization of nudging as an instrument class remains contested and underdeveloped. This paper argues that the framework has a structural blind spot: nearly all nudge theory is built around individual-level interventions, leaving behavioral instruments that operate at the institutional level largely untheorized. Voluntary agreements (VAs)-formalized non-coercive commitments between public authorities and private actors-make this gap visible. Their sixtype typology, as mapped by Croci (2005), corresponds to distinct behavioral mechanisms including reputational salience, commitment effects, and anticipatory loss framing, all operating on organizational rather than individual decision-makers. Using the thematic synthesis approach of Xiao and Watson (2019), this paper traces the evolution of nudge theory from Thaler and Sunstein (2003) through Tor's (2026) mechanism-based definition-the most theoretically rigorous formulation to date-and argues that even Tor's advance leaves the meso-level of behavioral governance unaccounted for. The paper concludes by identifying this as a productive theoretical gap and proposing a future research agenda.

title: The Standard Model of Complex Economic Systems: A Unified Framework for Bayesian Signal Integration in Financial Markets

detail.title: The Standard Model of Complex Economic Systems: A Unified Framework for Bayesian Signal Integration in Financial Markets

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive theoretical framework termed "The Standard Model of Complex Economic Systems" that bridges econophysics, signal processing, and portfolio theory using Hilbert space methods. We develop a unified approach that integrates fundamental analysis with sophisticated quantitative methods, applying Bayesian inference in function spaces to signals extracted from spectral analysis, wavelet decomposition, and operator-theoretic analysis of financial time series. The primary objective is to optimize the Omega ratio for leveraged liquid assets that have passed specific fundamental screening criteria. This dual-methodology approach addresses a significant gap in current practice: fundamental analysis establishes intrinsic value baselines while Hilbert space methods identify market signals that enable predictive modeling of period total returns. We introduce the Summers Total Risk-Adjusted Performance Measure (S Ω) with functional extensions that provide improved interpretability while preserving higher-moment sensitivity. Empirical testing demonstrates that our approach significantly outperforms traditional optimization techniques, particularly during market regime transitions and periods of high volatility. The framework contributes to the theoretical understanding of financial markets as complex adaptive systems while offering practical applications for investment management. By providing a physically interpretable model of market dynamics grounded in functional analysis, this paper establishes a foundation for a new paradigm in quantitative finance.

title: Impact of Hyperinflation on IAS 29 Financial Reporting in Nigeria: A Comparative Analysis

detail.title: Impact of Hyperinflation on IAS 29 Financial Reporting in Nigeria: A Comparative Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: UMYU Journal of Business Administration and Management, Volume 1, No. 1 & 2, Pp. 167-181

detail.abstract: Although Nigeria has not formally met the 100% three-year cumulative inflation benchmark, it exhibits several qualitative characteristics of a hyperinflationary economy, including severe currency devaluation, widespread dollarization, inflation-linked contracts, and declining purchasing power. This studyexamines therelevance and applicability of IAS 29: Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies in the Nigerian context,focusing on how these hyperinflationary conditions affect the reliability and comparability of financial statements prepared under historical cost accountingUsing a qualitative methodology based on recent macroeconomic data and regulatory literature, the study findings reveal that while IAS 29 is not yet mandated by Nigerian regulators, some multinational subsidiaries are voluntarily applying inflation-adjusted models for internal and group reporting purposes. Challenges identified include the absence of regulatory guidance, limited technical capacity, lack of consistent inflation data, and disconnects between tax and accounting frameworks. Comparative insights from Zimbabwe, Argentina, and Lebanon underscore the importance of early intervention, policy coordination, and professional guidance to avoid systemic financial distortions. The findings confirm that continued reliance on historical cost accounting undermines the reliability, comparability, and decision-usefulness of financial statements in high-inflation contexts. The study concludes that Nigeria is transitioning from high inflation to a hyperinflation-risk economy and recommends proactive regulatory guidance on IAS 29 implementation, enhanced access to credible inflation indices, alignment of tax policies with inflation-adjusted reporting, and the development of inflation monitoring and forecasting frameworks. It further calls on reporting entities to strengthen auditor collaboration, adopt early inflation-adjusted disclosures, and build resilience through scenario planning, while investors are urged to interpret financial information cautiously and demand transparency. Without decisive action, Nigeria risks deeper macroeconomic deterioration and erosion of financial reporting credibility.

title: Bunching at the Floor: Minimum Pay Compliance in NYC Ride-Hail, 2024

detail.title: Bunching at the Floor: Minimum Pay Compliance in NYC Ride-Hail, 2024
detail.abstract: I use the public High-Volume For-Hire Services (HVFHS) trip record dataset to document how Uber and Lyft responded to New York City's minimum per-trip driver pay rule during 2024. Across 218 million non-shared in-city trips, 54.8% of Uber trips and 67.5% of Lyft trips paid drivers within 2% of the contemporaneous minimum implied by the Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) pay formula. Under the retrospective utilisation rate that the TLC adopted in June 2025 to address platform lockout behaviour, these bunching shares fall to 31.6% and 39.1% respectively, implying that a substantial share of 2024 trips would have fallen below a non-manipulated minimum. Bunching is heavily concentrated in outer-borough (Boro Zone) pickups: Uber's Yellow Zone bunching is 44.2% but its Boro Zone bunching is 59.8%; Lyft's gradient is flatter at 64.4% and 69.0%. The two platforms also bunch with different distributional shapes: Lyft's above-floor mass is sharply concentrated, while Uber's is dispersed across a wider range of above-floor payments. An unpaid-time decomposition using Uber's onscene timestamps shows that 22.9% of per-trip minutes are unpaid approach or boarding on average per trip (19.0% as an aggregate ratio across all Uber-sample minutes). The findings establish a baseline for subsequent work on surplus allocation, the effect of the June 2025 rule changes, and the introduction of congestion pricing.

title: Operationalising NCSC CAF 4.0 in UK Building Societies A Sector-Specific Implementation Framework for Small-to-Medium Mutuals

detail.title: Operationalising NCSC CAF 4.0 in UK Building Societies A Sector-Specific Implementation Framework for Small-to-Medium Mutuals
detail.abstract: The National Cyber Security Centre published version 4.0 of its Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) on 6 August 2025. The revision is the most substantial since the framework's introduction in 2018. The architecture of four objectives, fourteen principles and forty-one contributing outcomes is preserved, but the indicators of good practice now place noticeably greater weight on threat intelligence, behavioural monitoring, threat hunting, secure software development, and the governance of automated decision-making technologies including artificial intelligence. UK financial services firms are increasingly being asked, directly or indirectly, to express their cyber resilience in CAF terms. For the country's roughly 42 building societies, this creates a practical difficulty. CAF was written for operators of essential services under the NIS Regulations, and its indicators carry assumptions about scale, functional separation and in-house capability that simply do not hold in most mutuals. The result is that a competent small mutual can read the IGPs literally and conclude that it is failing-when the underlying outcome is being delivered through an outsourced or supplier-mediated arrangement. This paper sets out a sector-specific way of applying CAF 4.0 in the building society context. It identifies six recurring tensions between CAF's default assumptions and the operating reality of small-tomedium mutuals; offers a reading of each of the four objectives that takes those tensions seriously; proposes a maturity pathway that sits alongside CQUEST, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and Cyber Essentials Plus rather than competing with them; and introduces a four-artefact evidence pattern for outcomes that are delivered through suppliers. An anonymised illustrative case shows the framework in use. The intended audience is information security managers, chief risk officers and board cyber subcommittees in the mutual sector. The paper is offered as a working draft to invite refinement through sector consultation.

title: Product-Customer Coupling: Why Product-Market Fit Happens When It Happens

detail.title: Product-Customer Coupling: Why Product-Market Fit Happens When It Happens

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper based on theoretical analysis; it involves no human subjects, empirical data collection, or primary research requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The paper was developed independently by the author.

detail.abstract: We present Product-Customer Coupling (PCC), a cybernetic account of when and why product-market fit emerges. Grounded in Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety (Ashby, 1956, 1958) and the Good Regulator theorem (Conant and Ashby, 1970), PCC treats adoption as a coupling problem between a product firm and a customer that is already regulating its own essential variables. The framework is organised around one definitional claim and three mechanism claims. The customer is an incumbent regulator, not a blank slate; switching cost decomposes into destruction cost (variety lost from the customer's existing toolkit) and exposure cost (harm while essential variables sit transiently unregulated); shifts in the disturbance landscape open structural entry windows, making timing a theorised condition rather than luck; and teams converge on viable couplings through model-based search under an exposure budget, not through undirected iteration. Together these address four questions left under-specified by Jobs-to-Be-Done, Lean Startup, the resource-based view, and disruption theory: why iteration works when it works, why timing matters, why switching costs are hard to predict ex ante, and why some pivots succeed and others fail. Product-market fit, on this account, is the segment-level reproducibility of a viable product-customer coupling sustained by economic density sufficient for the product firm's own viability. PCC yields five falsifiable predictions and concrete design implications for product, pricing, and organisation.

title: Latent Human Capital and the Immigrant Mobility Advantage: A General Equilibrium Analysis

detail.title: Latent Human Capital and the Immigrant Mobility Advantage: A General Equilibrium Analysis
detail.abstract: Children of low-income immigrants in the United States systematically out-earn children of comparable natives. I develop a dynastic general-equilibrium model to explain this "immigrant mobility advantage" and quantify the macroeconomic costs of the institutional frictions underlying it. The central mechanism is a wedge between latent human capital and realized earnings: immigrants are positively selected on ability but face institutional frictions that decay at rate λ. Calibrated to U.S. data, the model fits key empirical patterns and reveals that immigrant frictions cost the U.S. economy 4.94% of GDP. This loss is split between a static labor-misallocation loss (1.57 pp) and dynamic effects on intergenerational investment in human and physical capital (3.37 pp). I find that friction decay (assimilation) accounts for 87% of the second-generation advantage, with positive selection contributing the remainder. Finally, the model identifies a "sign-flip" threshold at λ ≈ 0.25, beyond which frictions persist too strongly for the mobility advantage to appear. Calibrating λ across ten OECD destinations recovers a distribution of friction values that straddles this threshold, consistent with the heterogeneous mobility gaps documented in the empirical literature.

title: Retail Strategy and Customer Loyalty in Bangladesh's Modern Grocery Sector: A Theoretical Framework for Shwapno's Sustainable Market Leadership

detail.title: Retail Strategy and Customer Loyalty in Bangladesh's Modern Grocery Sector: A Theoretical Framework for Shwapno's Sustainable Market Leadership
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding customer loyalty in Bangladesh's organized grocery retail sector, using Shwapno-the country's dominant grocery chain-as its empirical anchor. Drawing on the research methodology framework of Sekaran and Bougie (2016), the study identifies service quality, service innovation, and brand trust as independent variables; perceived value-for-money (PVM) as a mediating variable; and socioeconomic status (SES) as a moderating variable. Six hypotheses are proposed and grounded in established retail theory, including SERVQUAL (Parasuraman, Zeithaml & Berry, 1988), Zeithaml's value model (1988), and Morgan and Hunt's Commitment-Trust Theory (1994). The framework extends Western retail theory to an emerging-market context characterized by SES heterogeneity, high price sensitivity, and a transitioning retail landscape. Findings from this theoretical analysis suggest that the mediated pathway-service innovation driving loyalty through perceived value-is likely the most consequential, with SES amplifying this relationship among lower-and middle-income consumers. Theoretical and practical contributions for emerging-market retail management are discussed.

title: Who Likes Tracking? Evidence on Institutional Feedback in Education Policy *

detail.title: Who Likes Tracking? Evidence on Institutional Feedback in Education Policy *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Commission of the University of Lausanne (CER-UNIL; Project No. C_FDCA_052024_00017). Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to survey participation: the consent form was presented at the beginning of the online questionnaire, and only respondents who actively agreed to participate were able to proceed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), Grant Number 212258.

detail.abstract: Education is recognized as a core component of the welfare state, yet we know little about how existing institutional arrangements shape public support for education policies. We test policy feedback theory in compulsory education, a policy domain where empirical evidence is still limited. Drawing on 4,382 Swiss citizens from eight cantons, we field an innovative visual vignette experiment using directed graphs that mirror official schematics of school structures. Respondents rate their support (0-10 scale) for fictitious education systems varying across seven policy dimensions that affect educational inequality. We focus on tracking, the fundamental structuring principle of education systems and find that, first, tracking is indeed the most consequential attribute, raising support by 1.05 points. Respondents exposed to tracking in their own canton assign an additional 0.53 points to tracked systemsconsistent with self-reinforcing policy feedback theory. Second, as suggested by this theory, different subgroups support tracking for distinct reasons, linked to interpretive effects (beliefs, values) and resource effects (income, education). Third, other institutional features have comparatively modest effects, if at all. Our results highlight citizens' attachment to familiar policy designs and its implications for education reform, with broader implications for the study of education as social policy.

title: Climate-Friendly Choices in Online Grocery Retail: Evidence from Recipes and Delivery Decisions
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN and Norwegian University of Life Sciences (NMBU) - Department of Economics and Resource Management

detail.title: Climate-Friendly Choices in Online Grocery Retail: Evidence from Recipes and Delivery Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Ekaterina Kuzmina was employed as a data scientist at Oda Norge AS for most of the time this paper was written. This employment is declared as it may be considered a relevant financial activity outside the submitted work. The remaining authors did not have any conflict of interest to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Research Council of Norway under the projects “VOM: Incentives for Measures for Food System Transition”, Grant No. 319892.

detail.abstract:
Retailers are increasingly implementing climate communication initiatives to encourage more sustainable consumer choices, yet little is known about how customers respond to such initiatives across different stages of the online shopping journey. This study analyzes transaction data from 50,000 customers of a Norwegian online grocery retailer that implemented climate labels on delivery time slots and one-click recipes. Using behavioral data from the full year of 2023, we examine how frequently customers choose climate-friendly options and whether green consumer behavior is consistent within and across these two retail decision domains.

The results show substantial differences between the domains. While most customers select climate-friendly delivery slots at least occasionally, relatively few choose climate-friendly one-click recipes. This suggests that consumers are more willing to make climate-friendly choices when these relate to how groceries are delivered than when they influence what they buy and ultimately eat. Moreover, we find limited consistency in green behavior across the two domains: only a small segment of customers consistently makes climate-friendly choices in both recipe and delivery decisions.

These findings indicate that green consumer behavior in online grocery retail is highly context dependent. For retailers, the results suggest that climate communication may be most effective when targeted toward customers who have previously demonstrated consistent climate-friendly behavior within the same decision domain, providing practical insights for the design of sustainability initiatives in online food retail.

title: The Mixed Approach of Knowledge Management: The Best Strategy for Managing Knowledge

detail.title: The Mixed Approach of Knowledge Management: The Best Strategy for Managing Knowledge

detail.title: Impact of Social Media and Digital Marketing on Brand Engagement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on secondary data, industry analysis, and publicly available information. No human or animal subjects were involved; therefore, ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The growing digitalization of communication has brought about a paradigm shift in the way brands engage with consumers, making social media and digital marketing the key drivers of brand engagement. This paper investigates the strategic use of digital media to increase brand visibility, customer interaction, and relationship-building in a competitive marketing environment. Through the analysis of social media usage patterns, digital marketing tools, and strategies for executing marketing campaigns in a digital media agency setting, the paper assesses the impact of targeted online communication on consumer awareness, traffic, and brand perception. The paper combines industry analysis, strategic models such as Porter's Five Forces Model and SWOT analysis, and practical insights from marketing campaigns to examine the efficacy of content marketing, search engine optimization, social media advertising, and data-driven marketing in influencing consumer engagement. The results show that a consistent digital presence, personalized content messaging, and interactive communication can greatly improve customer reach, engagement levels, and brand trust. Moreover, data analytics and attribution modelling allow organizations to track the performance of marketing campaigns in real-time, enabling strategic optimization of marketing investments. The paper emphasizes that digital marketing not only increases brand awareness but also enables the development of long-term customer relationships through sustained interaction, feedback, and valuebased communication. The paper adds to the body of knowledge on how integrated digital strategies can drive measurable business outcomes and sustainable competitive advantage. The results of this paper have significant implications for marketers interested in using digital ecosystems to enhance brand engagement in a dynamic marketing environment.

title: Working Paper: Measuring Assortment-Specific Unique-Demand Contributions from Assortment and Sales Data

detail.title: Working Paper: Measuring Assortment-Specific Unique-Demand Contributions from Assortment and Sales Data
detail.abstract: Firms often need to know whether a product adds demand to a category or mainly shifts sales from other items in the assortment. In many settings, however, they observe only the assortments that were offered, available covariates, and product-level sales. They do not observe total category demand, the no-purchase option, or full substitution patterns. We develop an assumption-lean framework that uses these limited data to measure assortment-specific unique demand. Unlike approaches that impose a specific distribution family for sales, our framework does not require that restriction. The method approximates expected product sales with a tractable exponential-index model estimated from included-product observations only. This gives one framework for both forecasting and measuring product-and assortment-level effects without requiring a fully specified choice model. We show that, under mild regularity conditions, the objective is strictly convex, the solution is unique when it exists, and the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. The fitted model also provides practical measures of unique demand, cannibalization, sales halo effects, and assortment redundancy, helping managers rank products by incremental assortment value rather than observed sales alone. The framework is useful for assortment evaluation, SKU retention and deletion, and new-product forecasting when demand-system data are limited.

title: AI in Pricing Strategies: Dynamic Pricing Models and Revenue Management

detail.title: AI in Pricing Strategies: Dynamic Pricing Models and Revenue Management
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming pricing strategies by enabling businesses to adopt dynamic pricing models and optimize revenue management. Traditional pricing methods often fail to respond to real-time market changes, whereas AI-driven pricing systems use data analytics, machine learning, and predictive modeling to adjust prices dynamically based on demand, competition, and customer behavior. This research paper explores the role of AI in pricing strategies, focusing on its applications, benefits, and challenges in dynamic pricing and revenue management. The study is conceptual and based on existing literature. Findings indicate that AI enhances profitability, improves customer targeting, and ensures competitive advantage, though concerns such as ethical pricing, data privacy, and implementation complexity persist.

title:
Luxury Brands Need Silence, Not Content

Strategic Refusal, Scarcity, and the Politics of Absence in the Attention Economy

detail.title:
Luxury Brands Need Silence, Not Content

Strategic Refusal, Scarcity, and the Politics of Absence in the Attention Economy
detail.abstract: This paper argues that luxury branding is being weakened not only by macroeconomic pressure, price fatigue, and platform volatility, but also by a cultural overreaction inside marketing itself: the belief that visibility must be constant, friendliness must be scalable, and relevance must be proven every day. In ordinary categories, content abundance can sustain attention. In luxury, however, communicative overproduction may erode the very conditions that make desire possible. Luxury has historically depended on distance, asymmetry, selectivity, opacity, and controlled access. The attention economy rewards the opposite traits: speed, reply culture, perpetual disclosure, platform conformity, and algorithmic presence. Building from the author's February 2026 essay "Luxury Brands Need Silence, Not Content," this paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding silence not as passivity but as a strategic act of refusal. It proposes that, in luxury, absence can carry symbolic force: refusing to discount, refusing to speak incessantly, refusing to chase every platform, refusing to flatten authority into relatability, and refusing to let engagement metrics determine cultural posture. The paper draws on current industry reporting, consumer-behavior literature on psychological distance and inconspicuous consumption, and selected public cases including Hermès, Rolex, Bottega Veneta, and Burberry.

title: Informal Ties and Sales Agent Turnover: Evidence from Randomized Dormitory Assignment
affiliations: University of Utah, University of Rochester - Simon Business School, Simon School of Business – University of Rochester and Nanjing University

detail.title: Informal Ties and Sales Agent Turnover: Evidence from Randomized Dormitory Assignment
detail.abstract: Sales agent turnover poses significant challenges for firms that rely on sales agents to maintain customer relationships and generate revenue. This paper studies how informal ties (e.g., shared hometowns) among agents affect turnover. We develop a conceptual framework that distinguishes between the effect of informal ties while tied peers remain present and the incremental effect of losing a tied peer. The framework helps clarify whether informal ties reduce turnover overall and whether they operate primarily through support or competition. Partnering with a leading Chinese medical equipment company, we assemble a unique panel dataset tracking roughly 2,000 agents over 20 months. New hires are randomly assigned to company dormitories, generating exogenous variation in exposure to peers who share background traits such as hometown, dialect, or alma mater. We document three main findings. First, agents assigned to dorm rooms with more same-background roommates stay with the firm longer on average. Second, tied peers reduce early quit risk while they remain with the firm. Third, the departure of a tied peer raises the remaining agent's quit risk. Together, these findings suggest psychological support as the operative mechanism, supported by survey evidence and the absence of productivity spillovers. A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that improving social matching among new hires could generate economically meaningful savings in recruiting and training costs.

title: Identity-Anchored Scaling in Multi-Vertical Markets: An Empirical Analysis

detail.title: Identity-Anchored Scaling in Multi-Vertical Markets: An Empirical Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available data and does not involve human participants. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Universal Niche Theory into a testable empirical framework for understanding identity-anchored scaling across multiple markets. The central claim is that certain user identities generate recurring demand across adjacent verticals, allowing firms to reuse engagement, trust, and data beyond a single product category. The study evaluates three core questions: whether engagement intensity predicts monetization density, whether observable behavioral proxies help explain this relationship, and whether identity-anchored platforms exhibit stronger engagement–monetization dynamics.

To test these mechanisms, the paper integrates behavioral research, official statistical data, and public firm disclosures. It replaces earlier conceptual constructs with measurable variables, including identity-anchored total addressable market (ITAM), engagement intensity, cross-vertical scope, and monetization density. Using a firm-quarter panel of disclosed platform data alongside a within-firm time-series analysis, the results show a consistent positive relationship between engagement intensity and monetization density, supporting the proposed mechanism.

The findings suggest that identity anchors enable scalable cross-vertical expansion when four conditions hold: the identity is large and recurrent, needs extend across adjacent domains, repeated interaction creates habit, and expansion preserves identity coherence. The paper also identifies clear boundary conditions, showing that the framework fails when firms expand without maintaining identity consistency or when addressable populations are too narrow. The result is a more rigorous, falsifiable, and economically grounded formulation of the Universal Niche Theory.

title:
The Synthetic Influencer Is the Brand’s Wet Dream

Control, Disclosure, and the Elimination of Human Friction in Influencer Marketing

detail.title:
The Synthetic Influencer Is the Brand’s Wet Dream

Control, Disclosure, and the Elimination of Human Friction in Influencer Marketing
detail.abstract: This paper examines the rise of synthetic influencers as a revealing development in contemporary brand culture. It argues that their importance lies not primarily in their novelty as computer-generated endorsers, but in what their adoption discloses about the institutional preferences of modern marketing. Synthetic influencers promise brands what human creators cannot reliably provide at scale: control without negotiation, intimacy without biography, beauty without labor unpredictability, and relevance without the risk of a person exceeding the brief. In that sense, they should be read less as a technological breakthrough than as an organizational confession. They reveal a market that has grown increasingly uncomfortable with the volatility, contradiction, and social cost attached to real human influence. Building from the author's April 21, 2026 essay "The Synthetic Influencer Is the Brand's Wet Dream," this working paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding synthetic influencers as instruments of friction reduction in an economy that publicly praises authenticity while operationally rewarding manageability. Combining close reading of current industry developments, official company materials, regulatory guidance, and recent academic research, the paper shows that virtual and synthetic influencers occupy an unstable position in the influencer economy. They can attract attention, signal uniqueness, and in some circumstances support positive consumer responses; yet they also intensify unresolved problems around disclosure, trust, labor, representation, and the replacement of human unpredictability with programmable performance. The paper contributes in three ways. First, it reframes synthetic influencers as a governance issue rather than a mere creative tactic. Second, it proposes a compact typology of syntheticinfluencer use, ranging from symbolic novelty to full-spectrum brand controllability. Third, it offers a practical governance ladder for brands deciding whether synthetic influence can be deployed without collapsing credibility. Its central claim is simple: synthetic influencers are not the future because they are culturally superior to people. They are the future because, for many brands, they are easier.

title: The Credentialing Apparatus: How Social Work's Institutional Gatekeeping Filters Out Lived Experience Knowledge

detail.title: The Credentialing Apparatus: How Social Work's Institutional Gatekeeping Filters Out Lived Experience Knowledge

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial conflicts of interest. This paper extends a prior body of theoretical work by the same author, cited throughout, and the author's positionality as a practitioner-researcher is addressed in the Limitations section.

detail.abstract:
Professional social work claims a foundational commitment to epistemic justice: centering lived experience, dismantling structural barriers, and amplifying the voices of system-impacted communities. This paper argues that the profession's own institutional infrastructure systematically contradicts these commitments through mechanisms that, taken together, function as a credentialing apparatus filtering lived experience knowledge out of the profession at every stage of entry and participation.

Drawing on primary organizational documents, peer-reviewed research, federal workforce data, and IRS disclosures, this analysis applies credentialing sociology (Weber, 1978; Collins, 1979) and epistemic injustice theory (Fricker, 2007; Okoroji et al., 2023) to four interlocking mechanisms maintained by the Association of Social Work Boards (ASWB), the Council on Social Work Education (CSWE), the National Association of Social Workers (NASW), and accredited MSW programs. These mechanisms include: a racially stratified licensure examination that ASWB's own leadership has attributed to structural racism yet has not structurally reformed; accreditation standards that formally prohibit crediting lived experience while invoking it as pedagogical value; conference participation policies that require presenters to absorb an undisclosed financial cost as a condition of contributing to professional discourse; and a debt-to-income structure in MSW education that disproportionately burdens Black and Hispanic practitioners with the highest average debt loads against the lowest starting salaries in the graduate degree landscape.

The paper's central theoretical contribution is locating the origin of the epistemic erosion spiral (Wernau, 2026a) upstream, in institutional design rather than downstream clinical drift. Where prior work identified the spiral as a self-reinforcing process through which clinical dominance erodes professional legitimacy in marginalized communities, this analysis demonstrates that the spiral is structurally engineered by the very institutions charged with sustaining the profession. It extends document analysis of MSW field education manuals (Wernau, 2026b) by showing that the gap between stated equity commitments and structural practice is not isolated to field education but pervades the profession's entire institutional architecture. The analysis concludes by identifying the accountability mechanisms these organizations lack and the specific structural reforms necessary to interrupt the gatekeeping cycle.
