title: Does Channel Regulation Matter for EV Subsidy Design? Implications for Market Share and Social Welfare
affiliations: School of Business Administration, South China University of Technology,  and Soochow University

detail.title: Does Channel Regulation Matter for EV Subsidy Design? Implications for Market Share and Social Welfare
detail.abstract: Regulations on EV direct sales create heterogeneous regional channel structures, yet most subsidy programs are still designed as if the underlying sales channel were irrelevant. We study how a government should allocate a fixed per-unit EV subsidy between consumers and manufacturers when EVs are sold either through retail intermediation or through direct sales. We develop a game-theoretic model under the dual policy objectives of maximizing EV market share and social welfare, and derive closed-form threshold rules for the optimal beneficiary and allocation rate. The central result is that channel regulation changes the optimal subsidy target because it changes subsidy pass-through, consumer acquisition frictions, and firms' selling costs. As a result, direct-sales deregulation does not mechanically justify shifting support upstream. Under the market-share objective, tight budgets require bifurcated subsidies that support both consumers and manufacturers, whereas sufficiently large budgets justify fully consumer-side subsidies. Across channel structures, more manufacturer-oriented support in direct-sales markets is optimal only when direct sales materially reduce end-to-end frictions. Under the welfare objective, the allocation also depends on the social return to technology diffusion and on the government's welfare priorities: manufacturer subsidies dominate only when that return is weak but heavily weighted; Otherwise, bifurcated or consumer-tilted schemes are preferred. The analysis also identifies when market-share and welfare objectives naturally align. These results yield implementable policy guidance. Governments should diagnose the binding friction in each region, classify budgets relative to the relevant threshold, and then reallocate subsidies based on channel efficiency and policy objective rather than applying a uniform national formula.

title: Conceptualizing Policy Delivery Burden: Who Absorbs the Hidden Costs of Policy Implementation?

detail.title: Conceptualizing Policy Delivery Burden: Who Absorbs the Hidden Costs of Policy Implementation?
detail.abstract: Policies do not operate automatically once adopted. As they move into practice, they generate hidden maintenance costs such as handling exceptions, resolving complaints, interpreting rules, coordinating across units, documenting decisions, and managing political exposure. Existing research explains parts of this process, but has not fully theorized who absorbs these costs and how they are distributed. This article introduces the concept of policy delivery burden to capture the hidden work required to sustain policy implementation under real-world friction. It also develops the concept of burden structure, defined as the patterned distribution of these burdens across organizational levels, institutional sites, and forms of responsibility. The article presents three linked models of burden generation, burden movement, and burden effects. It argues that policy implementation should be understood not only as a question of whether policy is carried out, but also of who bears the hidden costs required to keep it working.

title: Shenandoah Outfitters
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Shenandoah Outfitters
detail.abstract:
A small chain of retail stores selling outdoors equipment, Shenandoah Outfitters is expanding rapidly. The finance manager has to develop a financial plan for accommodating this growth and the investments it requires. Analysis reveals that the business is growing faster than can be financed from internal sources–-Shenandoah has been increasing the amount of its long-term loan and has just ended the year with a higher-than-usual balance on its bank line of credit.The operations and financing of this business are relatively simple, so students can focus on core skills. As such, this case is appropriate for all degree and nondegree programs. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, it has been used as an introduction to financial forecasting. It works best after an introduction to financial ratios, but it can also be used to build familiarity with those ratios. It has also been used successfully as a vehicle for contrasting the cash flow statement (an accounting view) with a free cash flow calculation (a valuation view). In general, the role of the case is to tie finance principals to accounting data.

Excerpt

Shenandoah Outfitters

Shenandoah Outfitters (Shenandoah) was expanding. The mid-Atlantic regional chain of outdoor equipment—focused on hiking, backpacking, and camping—had increased sales by 25% each of the last two years and was expecting about 20% growth in 2026. Founded 16 years before as a single store in a converted millhouse in the Appalachian foothills of North Carolina, the business had become a regional hub for outdoor gear and clothing during the COVID-19 pandemic. Leveraging its reputation as a place where both new and experienced hikers felt inspired and attended to, Shenandoah continued its growth with carefully planned store openings and relentless focus on hiring experienced and enthusiastic staff.

Financing Shenandoah's growth through 2025 had been relatively uncomplicated. The business had increased long-term borrowing to cover some needed investments in store infrastructure (display structures and leasehold improvements), and annual income was able to finance much of the needed investment in inventory (a major commitment of resources). However, financing the anticipated growth in 2026 was going to require careful thought. Shenandoah would need significant leasehold investments in 2026, some of which were needed to fully absorb past growth, and there was no opportunity for additional long-term borrowing. Furthermore, management was concerned by the fact that the cash balance in the business's account had not kept pace with the expansion and, in fact, was slightly below the 2023 level. Finally, as of the end of 2025, Shenandoah had $101,000 remaining on its line of credit (short-term borrowing). While this was well below the limit of $200,000, it was typically close to zero at year-end. National Bank, which provided the credit line and had handled all of Shenandoah's banking needs since its founding, typically expected Shenandoah to have fully paid down its line of credit for at least one month each year; this had not yet happened.

Shenandoah's financial manager, Blake Dietrick, who had joined Shenandoah four years before as an accountant but had taken over the top finance job two years later, was asked to put together a plan. Given the company's profitability, it was possible Shenandoah might squeak by on internally generated funds. However, it might also be the case that the company would have to seek other sources of funds and possibly renegotiate the line of credit with National Bank.

title: Bias Is No Longer a Bug: It's a Compliance Failure

detail.title: Bias Is No Longer a Bug: It's a Compliance Failure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, personal data collection, or experimental subjects. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: For many years, algorithmic bias was mainly regarded as a technical fault, something wrong with datasets, features, or modelling techniques that engineers could fix through improved data curation or by optimising fairness. That view no longer suffices. With the rise of binding regulatory frameworks such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and the ongoing enforcement of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), algorithmic bias has shifted from a technical issue to a matter of organisational responsibility and legal obligation. This paper contends that fairness has transitioned from a voluntary design aim to a core governance duty. AI systems utilised in critical sectors like credit, employment, healthcare, and public services now face legal requirements for risk management, transparency, non-discrimination, human oversight, and lifecycle oversight. In this context, biased outcomes are recognised not just as errors in modelling but as failures in governance. A significant challenge is the fairnessprivacy paradox: effective bias evaluation often requires access to sensitive demographic data, yet data protection laws impose stringent restrictions on its processing. The paper explores how new regulations, including Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, seek to address this dilemma by permitting carefully controlled processing of sensitive data for bias detection, subject to strict necessity, safeguards, and thorough documentation. Moving beyond conceptual discussions, the paper proposes an operational framework designed for audit readiness to support fairness governance. It demonstrates how fairness metrics, bias testing, mitigation measures, and monitoring procedures can be systematised into compliance evidence that withstands regulatory scrutiny, legal review, and organisational audits. Ultimately, the paper redefines bias as a governance risk: not merely a flaw in algorithms, but a failure in organisational oversight across the AI lifecycle.

title: Development Operations Management: From Frictions to Theory
affiliations: Arizona State University , University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Development Operations Management: From Frictions to Theory
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Operations management and operations research (OM/OR) insights are disproportionately drawn from assumptions grounded in high-income countries, yet a substantial share of operational systems worldwide function in emerging and developing economies under persistent feasibility, governance, and relational frictions. This creates an opportunity to develop a more disciplined framework that links these frictions to operational mechanisms, developmentally meaningful outcomes, and generalizable theory. Methodology/Results: In this lead article for the M&SOM Special Issue on Operations Management for Developing Economies, we introduce the term Development Operations Management (DOM), and propose a normative conceptual framework that defines and structures the subfield of DOM. We integrate perspectives from OM/OR and development-oriented research, articulate an agenda-setting (friction-to-theory cycle) for DOM studies, clarify what constitutes DOM, outline a research process from system definition and friction diagnosis to outcome specification, lever identification, field-informed refinement, and mechanism-based generalization, and organize contributions into complementary pathways: scouting, prototyping under frictions, bottom-up theory building, and comparative refinement. Managerial insights: The immediate audience of this paper is OM/OR scholars. However, the framework also offers managers and policymakers a structured approach to identify binding operational constraints, design implementable interventions grounded in institutional and behavioral realities, select welfare-relevant performance measures, and assess transferability across settings through explicit mechanisms and well-defined boundary conditions.

title: TOTAL QUALITY MANAGEMENT: INFALLIBLE SIGNIFICANCE IN HEALTHCARE

detail.title: TOTAL QUALITY MANAGEMENT: INFALLIBLE SIGNIFICANCE IN HEALTHCARE
detail.abstract: "Quality is never an accident; it is always the result of high intention, sincere effort intelligent direction and skilful execution; it represents the wise choice of many alternatives".-William A. Foster. Since the advent of liberalization and globalization the focus of all service providers has been to improve the quality. The word quality has been used to indicate excellence of products and service. Quality can be improved by improving customer satisfaction. Quality is considered as a basic step in meeting the requirements of customers and society as a whole. Quality management has become an important issue in every sector especially among the healthcare the increased attention of quality is because of government regulations, customers'expectations,and hospital initiatives. Total quality management is a system or philosophy applied by management of an organization in order to achieve satisfaction of customers. Healthcare sector is the most important sector of the economy. Total quality management in healthcare focuses on rendering acceptable quality service to its customers at a affordable price and within reasonable time , applying continuous improvement process with zero errors , monitoring the service , providing training , upgrading the knowledge of the staff in medical care on various aspects such as reducing delay time , error prevention , meeting the patients needs .There are many difficulties faced in managing health care organization in ability to achieve this , especially when there is very little support from official bodies in developing country like India .he paper describes importance of application of total quality management for the healthcare sector and provides a framework for them

title: Temporal Effect of Geopolitical Risks on Indian Base Metal Commodity Derivatives: A Wavelet Coherence Analysis †

detail.title: Temporal Effect of Geopolitical Risks on Indian Base Metal Commodity Derivatives: A Wavelet Coherence Analysis †

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is written by me
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding provided

detail.abstract:
Commodity derivatives have been widely researched due to their properties such as diversification, hedge, and safe haven characteristics with many studies explaining the relationship between these instruments and geopolitical risks (GPR). The present study explores the interconnectedness between GPR and base metal commodity derivatives traded in India. The uniqueness of the study lies in applying wavelet coherence analysis to explain the connectedness between GPR and base metal commodity derivatives. The daily data of GPR index and MCX-COMDEX index of five metals, i.e., aluminum, copper, lead, zinc and nickel, are considered. The period of study is from 2016 to 2023, and the study focuses on unforeseen events like Russia-Ukrainian war, Covid-19 pandemic, etc.,
which have impacted the returns from base metal trading in India. The empirical findings provide new insights for investors on making better investment decisions; for exchanges and regulators on taking timely policy decisions; and for academicians on examining this area further in future.

title: Developmental Origins of Decision Paralysis and the Structural Limits of Cognitive Intervention Working Paper • Non-Confidential Version • April 2026

detail.title: Developmental Origins of Decision Paralysis and the Structural Limits of Cognitive Intervention Working Paper • Non-Confidential Version • April 2026
detail.abstract: Decision paralysis-expressed as chronic deference, analysis loops that never close, or the phrase "I don't know what to do"-is consistently misread by organizations as a capability gap. This paper argues it is not. Drawing on convergent findings across cognitive psychology, developmental psychology, social psychology, and neuroscience, it establishes that decision paralysis is a formation-layer event: a product of three developmentally constructed disruptions that operate below the threshold of cognitive intervention. The paper then demonstrates why conventional learning and development (L&D) frameworks cannot reach this layer-not as a delivery failure, but as a structural category error. A four-stage development architecture is proposed that addresses each disruption in sequence, producing the integrated capacity this paper defines as decision sovereignty. This paper cites the Behavioral Operating System category definition (El Shazly & Adly, 2026) as the broader category architecture within which the formation layer operates. It stands as an independent contribution to that research agenda.

title: ASTOP: Anderson Shaman's Trail Observation Phenotyping A Community-Level Behavioral Surveillance Instrument for Trauma Identification and Resource Placement in Alaska Native and American Indian Communities

detail.title: ASTOP: Anderson Shaman's Trail Observation Phenotyping A Community-Level Behavioral Surveillance Instrument for Trauma Identification and Resource Placement in Alaska Native and American Indian Communities

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Background. Standard trauma screening instruments demonstrate significant limitations in Alaska Native and American Indian (AIAN) community settings, producing minimal usable clinical information and failing to identify cumulative adverse childhood experience (ACE) burden upstream of crisis presentation.

Objective. This paper proposes the Anderson Shaman’s Trail Observation Phenotyping instrument (ASTOP)—a community-level surveillance framework that uses observable behavioral, somatic, and administrative indicators to identify trauma concentrations in AIAN communities and inform upstream resource allocation.

Methods. ASTOP trains observers to capture trauma indicators across seven domains without requiring disclosure, recall, or clinical encounter. Observers apply a non-pathologizing interpretive frame, reading each indicator as adaptive intelligence rather than a pathological symptom. ASTOP produces a resource placement decision, not a clinical diagnosis.

Results. The instrument’s core innovation is the behavioral stack — co-occurring regulatory strategies pointing backward to adverse experience and forward to intervention need. ASTOP’s most empirically grounded component is Domain 7 sleep quality: American Indian peoples have the highest rates of frequent insufficient sleep of any racial group in the United States (34.2% vs. 27.4% among non-Hispanic Whites), and a graded ACE dose-response relationship with sleep disturbance is confirmed across populations exceeding 100,000 participants. Sleep quality, assessed through three non-clinical questions, is ASTOP’s most empirically validated proxy indicator of cumulative trauma burden.

Conclusions. ASTOP proposes a reorientation of trauma surveillance in AIAN communities from symptom-based clinical screening to behavioral phenotyping conducted by trained community observers in natural social contexts. A Training Within Industry observer certification architecture provides the implementation infrastructure. Validation studies are warranted.

title: Factors Influencing Individual and Team Behavior Affecting Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) in Improving Performance

detail.title: Factors Influencing Individual and Team Behavior Affecting Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) in Improving Performance
detail.abstract: This study examines the factors influencing individual and team behavior that affect Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) and, in turn, organizational performance. OCB refers to voluntary actions performed by employees beyond their formal job responsibilities that contribute to organizational effectiveness (Organ, 1988). This study uses a literature review approach, analyzing relevant theories and prior research. The findings indicate that individual factors such as personality, motivation, perception, and job satisfaction significantly influence OCB (Ilies et al., 2009). In addition, team-related factors, including leadership, communication, trust, and group dynamics, play an important role in shaping OCB (Ehrhart, 2004). Furthermore, OCB has a strong positive relationship with organizational performance, as it enhances teamwork, efficiency, and productivity (Podsakoff et al., 2009). In conclusion, organizations need to focus on both individual and team development to strengthen OCB and achieve better performance outcomes.

title: The burden and impact of COVID-19 on restaurant employment within the Mthatha District, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa
affiliations: , University of KwaZulu-Natal and University of KwaZulu-Natal

detail.title: The burden and impact of COVID-19 on restaurant employment within the Mthatha District, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors confirm no conflict of interest associated with this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical clearence was received from the university and can be made available on request.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received to conduct this study.

detail.abstract: The study examined the impact of the coronavirus disease on employment in the restaurant industry in the Mthatha District, Eastern Cape Province. The primary aim of the study was to investigate the impact of the coronavirus disease on employment contracts for restaurant workers. Additionally, the study aimed to investigate the roles of employers and the government in mitigating the pandemic's impact on restaurant workers. The study adopted a quantitative approach, and a cross-sectional survey of 75 employees from five restaurants was analysed using descriptive statistics, factor analysis, correlations, and multiple linear regression. The findings revealed that COVID-19 led to a high number of workers' contracts being terminated and perceived non-compliance with employment contracts, while government and employer measures were not sufficient to protect livelihoods. Correlation and regression analyses showed no statistically significant associations between perceived government or employer interventions and the perceived impact of COVID-19 on employees. The study recommends that employers should uphold labour and contract standards, communicate transparently with staff, and support workers in accessing available benefits. The government must strengthen labour enforcement and simplify access to relief schemes to ensure that employees receive support and understand their rights during times of crisis. Furthermore, more effective crisis-response strategies are also needed to protect vulnerable employees in future disruptions between the government and employers.

title: Artificial Intelligence Oversight: Designing Policies for Responsible Al Implementation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Vivekananda Global University, Vivekananda Global University, Jaipur and Vivekananda Global University, Jaipur

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Oversight: Designing Policies for Responsible Al Implementation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: the authors declare that there are no conflicts regarding the publication of this paper

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sectors such as healthcare, finance, education, and governance, while raising significant ethical, legal, and social challenges. Issues including algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, data privacy risks, and accountability gaps highlight the need for effective regulatory frameworks. This paper analyzes global AI governance models, including those of the European Union, the United States, and China, to identify key policy gaps and challenges. Using a qualitative and comparative approach, the study proposes a structured five-pillar policy framework focusing on risk-based classification, transparency standards, independent audit mechanisms, data protection, and adaptive regulation. The research emphasizes the importance of balancing innovation with ethical safeguards and highlights the need for collaborative, dynamic, and human-centered AI governance systems.

title: The Effect of Work Motivation Concepts on Enhancing Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB): A Literature Review

detail.title: The Effect of Work Motivation Concepts on Enhancing Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB): A Literature Review
detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of work motivation concepts on enhancing Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) through a literature review of three Scopus-indexed journals. OCB is recognized as a crucial factor in improving organizational effectiveness because it reflects employees' voluntary behaviors beyond formal job requirements. However, the emergence of OCB is highly influenced by psychological factors, particularly work motivation. This study uses a qualitative literature review approach to analyze how different types of motivation, namely intrinsic motivation, instrumental or extrinsic motivation, selfconcept internal motivation, and family motivation, influence OCB. The findings show that motivation is a multidimensional construct with different impacts on OCB. Intrinsic motivation and self-concept internal motivation have a strong and consistent positive relationship with OCB because they are driven by internal values, personal satisfaction, and individual identity. In contrast, instrumental motivation tends to have a negative relationship with OCB because it focuses on external rewards and transactional behavior. In addition, the relationship between motivation and OCB is not direct but mediated by psychological variables such as self-efficacy and job satisfaction. Family motivation influences OCB indirectly through self-efficacy, while job insecurity reduces OCB by lowering intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction. Overall, this study concludes that the relationship between work motivation and OCB is complex, indirect, and dependent on contextual and psychological factors. Therefore, organizations need to adopt a more holistic approach in managing motivation by not only relying on external incentives but also strengthening internal values, improving psychological conditions, and creating a supportive work environment to enhance OCB effectively.

title: EMOTIONS, STRESS, AND WORK PERFORMANCE: UNDERSTANDING THEIR INTERCONNECTED ROLE IN

detail.title: EMOTIONS, STRESS, AND WORK PERFORMANCE: UNDERSTANDING THEIR INTERCONNECTED ROLE IN
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the relationship between emotions, stress, and employee performance in influencing organizational effectiveness. In today's demanding work environment, employees face increasing psychological pressures that affect their behavior, decision-making, and productivity. Therefore, understanding the interaction between emotional factors and stress becomes essential for organizations aiming to achieve optimal performance. Using a literature-based approach, this paper synthesizes findings from several academic studies related to emotional intelligence, work stress, and employee performance. The results indicate that emotional intelligence has a positive impact on employee performance, as it enables individuals to regulate emotions, maintain interpersonal relationships, and respond effectively to workplace challenges. Meanwhile, stress is identified as having both positive and negative effects, depending on its intensity and how it is managed. Furthermore, emotional intelligence is found to play a moderating role in reducing the negative impact of stress on performance. Employees with higher emotional intelligence are more resilient and capable of maintaining stable performance under pressure. These findings suggest that organizations need to manage both emotional and stress-related factors simultaneously to enhance employee performance and achieve long-term organizational effectiveness.

title: Where Are the AI Governance Roles? An Early-Stage Empirical Mapping of Presence, Absence, and Structure in Organisational AI Oversight

detail.title: Where Are the AI Governance Roles? An Early-Stage Empirical Mapping of Presence, Absence, and Structure in Organisational AI Oversight
detail.abstract: Purpose: This research investigates where formal responsibility for artificial intelligence (AI) lies within organisations and how the presence, absence, or structure of that responsibility affects their ability to govern AI effectively. Method: The study surveys 351 organisations across sectors and regions to examine AI governance roles. It focuses on authority, resources, and organisational integration, using hierarchical cluster analysis to identify governance configurations. Findings: The results indicate that formal AI governance roles are unevenly distributed and often weakly integrated into organisational structures. When these roles exist, they are usually placed below the executive level, lack sufficient authority, and differ greatly in the resources available to them. A cluster analysis reveals four governance configurations-Governance Absence, Symbolic Governance, Operational Governance, and Institutionalised Governance, indicating that governance capacity is primarily influenced by how well these roles are embedded in the structure, rather than just their presence. Implications: The findings suggest that AI governance may be better understood as a structural and organisational design issue, with potential implications for accountability and oversight. However, the relationship between governance configurations and outcomes, such as ethical risk and compliance, remains an area for future research. Originality: The study takes an absence-based approach to AI ethics, establishing a baseline for future research on governance maturity, compliance, trust, and ethical risk.

title: Executive Selection Has a Criterion Problem: A Perspective on Capability-Centered Assessment Under Strategic Uncertainty

detail.title: Executive Selection Has a Criterion Problem: A Perspective on Capability-Centered Assessment Under Strategic Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Executive selection often relies on distal proxies such as personality, career history, and reputation cues, despite their limited correspondence to future role demands․ This perspective article argues that the central validity problem in executive selection is criterion specification rather than predictor optimization․ It challenges the field's reliance on distal proxies such as personality, career history, and reputation cues, and proposes a capability-centered criterion space for structuring executive assessment under changing strategic conditions․ As an initial way forward, the article outlines a provisional multi-domain capability framework for executive assessment․ Future research should establish construct distinctiveness, domain boundaries, and predictive validation to determine whether these capability domains account for executive effectiveness across strategic contexts․

title: Socially Responsible Human Resource Management and Employee Outcomes: A Moderated Mediation Model

detail.title: Socially Responsible Human Resource Management and Employee Outcomes: A Moderated Mediation Model
detail.abstract: This study examines how socially responsible human resource management (SR-HRM) influences employee behavior by specifying a moderated mediation model grounded in social exchange and psychological contract theories. Using a two-wave time-lagged design with 414 employed MBA students in Nigeria, the study tests whether affective commitment mediates the relationships between SR-HRM and two key outcomes: organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) and turnover intention. The study also examines perceived organizational support (POS) as a moderator of the relationship between SR-HRM and affective commitment. Structural equation modeling results indicate that SR-HRM is positively associated with affective commitment, which in turn increases OCB and reduces turnover intention. Bootstrapping analyses confirm that affective commitment partially mediates these relationships. Contrary to expectations, POS does not significantly moderate the relationship between SR-HRM and affective commitment, and the conditional indirect effects are not statistically different across levels of POS. These findings highlight the central role of affective commitment in linking HR practices to employee outcomes and suggest that SR-HRM exerts robust effects that are not contingent on perceived organizational support.

title: Developing Data Analytics Models for Real-Time Fraud Detection in U.S. Financial and Tax Systems

detail.title: Developing Data Analytics Models for Real-Time Fraud Detection in U.S. Financial and Tax Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest regarding the publication of this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available data and analytical models. No human participants or personal identifiable data were involved; therefore ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Fraudulent activities in financial transactions continue to pose a significant challenge for the U.S. financial sector, driving the need for advanced detection mechanisms. Traditional fraud detection methods, which are often reactive and struggle to process large volumes of data in real-time, are increasingly being supplemented or replaced by AI-driven solutions. This paper examines the use of artificial intelligence in real-time fraud detection, focusing on its potential benefits, challenges, and future directions. AI-powered techniques, such as machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, and natural language processing, offer powerful tools for identifying and mitigating fraudulent activities. Both supervised and unsupervised learning, along with anomaly detection methods, enable the detection of unusual patterns and behaviors indicative of fraud. The integration of hybrid models further enhances the accuracy and reliability of these systems. However, implementing AI-based fraud detection systems presents challenges, including ensuring data quality, addressing privacy concerns, and ensuring scalability for real-time processing. Additionally, balancing model performance with regulatory compliance and ethical considerations remains a critical issue. Despite these obstacles, advancements in AI technology offer substantial opportunities. By improving data analytics, fostering collaboration between financial institutions and AI firms, and obtaining regulatory support, the effectiveness of fraud detection can be greatly enhanced. Case studies from leading financial institutions illustrate how AI-driven solutions have successfully reduced fraud rates and improved operational efficiency. As AI technology continues to progress, its role in fraud detection holds the promise of creating a more secure financial landscape. This paper provides a thorough overview of the current state, challenges, and future potential of AI-driven fraud detection in U.S. financial transactions, offering insights for stakeholders in the financial sector.

title: Disease-Specific Oncology Units or Multidisciplinary Tumour Boards? A Critical Appraisal of an Organisational Model in the Era of Cancer Networks

detail.title: Disease-Specific Oncology Units or Multidisciplinary Tumour Boards? A Critical Appraisal of an Organisational Model in the Era of Cancer Networks
detail.abstract: Disease-specific oncology units Breast Units, Pancreas Units, Thyroid Units and analogues — were introduced across Europe over two decades ago as organisational responses to the growing complexity of cancer care and the documented absence of structured multidisciplinary mechanisms for managing complex malignancies. Their historical role in establishing multidisciplinary practice is well recognised. However, Multidisciplinary Tumour Boards (MTBs) are now mandated structures in the cancer networks of the United Kingdom, France, Australia and across Italian regional legislation, and a robust evidence base documents their independent clinical value. This paper critically examines whether disease-specific oncology units remain organisationally justified in healthcare systems that have fully established MTBs and regional cancer networks. We argue that oncology units, in their current configuration, exhibit four structural problems: a paradigmatic tension with network-based care logic; a tendency to reduce complex oncological pathways to their surgical phase; an absence of formal administrative accountability; and a systematic equity gap between tumour types with dedicated units and those served only by MTBs. International comparisons (NHS England, France, Australia) demonstrate that mature cancer systems have resolved this tension by integrating disease-specific expertise within the MTB framework rather than maintaining parallel structures. We propose four operational recommendations to reposition the MTB as the primary organisational subject for all oncological pathways. The reform is not about abolishing disease-specific structures, but about integrating them within the network rather than alongside it.

title: Toward Sustainable Industry 5.0 Manufacturing: A Systematic Review of AI-IoT-Digital Twin Integration for Real-Time Monitoring and Intelligent Decision-Making
affiliations: , LAMAR UNIVERSITY, LAMAR UNIVERSITY and Shahjalal University of Science & Technology

detail.title: Toward Sustainable Industry 5.0 Manufacturing: A Systematic Review of AI-IoT-Digital Twin Integration for Real-Time Monitoring and Intelligent Decision-Making
detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twin technologies is transforming modern manufacturing by enabling real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and intelligent decisionmaking. While existing studies often investigate these technologies individually, limited research explores their combined potential within the emerging paradigm of Industry 5.0, which emphasizes sustainability, human-centric innovation, and resilient manufacturing systems. This study addresses this gap by conducting a systematic literature review of 25 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, following the PRISMA framework. The review synthesizes findings across four key application domains: predictive maintenance, quality control, process optimization, and supply chain management. The analysis shows that machine learning and deep learning techniques dominate predictive maintenance and defect detection, while reinforcement learning and hybrid AI-IoT-digital twin architectures enable adaptive scheduling, energy optimization, and intelligent logistics coordination. Empirical evidence from the reviewed studies indicates that integrated smart manufacturing systems can reduce energy consumption by 30-40%, unplanned downtime by 15-25%, and defective outputs by 10-20%, contributing significantly to resource efficiency and carbon-emission reduction. By combining thematic synthesis with a conceptual integration framework, this study provides a strategic roadmap for the transition from Industry 4.0 to sustainable Industry 5.0 manufacturing ecosystems. The findings highlight how the convergence of AI, IoT, and digital twin technologies supports circular economy principles, cleaner production practices, and resilient industrial systems, positioning these technologies as key enablers of next-generation sustainable manufacturing.

title: Omnichannel Branding Strategies and Social Media Influence in Fashion Retail

detail.title: Omnichannel Branding Strategies and Social Media Influence in Fashion Retail
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of omnichannel branding strategies and social media influence on consumer behavior in fashion retail. It examines how integrating digital platforms with physical retail experiences shapes brand equity, customer engagement, and purchase intention. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining quantitative surveys of 400 fashion consumers with qualitative interviews of brand managers in contemporary fashion markets. The findings indicate that social media significantly enhances brand visibility and loyalty, while seamless omnichannel experiences amplify customer satisfaction and purchase likelihood. However, challenges persist in synchronizing online and offline strategies, particularly in post-COVID contexts. The study concludes that the integration of social media influence with cohesive omnichannel branding strategies is essential for maximizing customer engagement and long-term brand equity in fashion retail.

title: Hard Court Systems Ltd.: Restructuring Operations to Improve Profitability
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Hard Court Systems Ltd.: Restructuring Operations to Improve Profitability
detail.abstract:
At the start of fiscal year 2025, Hard Court Systems Ltd. (HCS), an Australian producer and installer of surfaces for tennis courts, has embarked on a major restructuring of its operations. With 2025 financial results just released, CFO Charles Walker is preparing to meet with shareholders to discuss the business's financial performance. A key transformation brought about by the restructuring is an increase in fixed costs due to investments in new equipment and other changes that added scalability to operations. The hope is that margin improvements will justify these investments. Adding dimension to the case is the observation by one analyst that HCS has placed itself at risk due to increased operating leverage. In addition to standard ratio analysis, Walker therefore needs to calculate breakeven levels and execute some form of a sensitivity analysis. This short, fictional case has been used successfully at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business in a pre-matriculation class for MBA students and in executive programs as an introduction to financial analysis. It is appropriate for undergraduate or graduate students. There is ample material for an 85-minute class, and it can likely be adapted for two undergraduate 50-minute classes: one devoted to financial statements and ratios, the other to breakeven points and sensitivity analyses emphasizing the effects of operating leverage. This case is an update that replaces UVA-F-1747.

Excerpt

Hard Court Systems Ltd.:Restructuring Operations to Improve Profitability

In contrast to all the attention paid to the grass courts at Wimbledon and the clay courts at the French Open, little notice was given to the most common surface in tennis—the humble “hard courts” of the Australian Open, the US Open, and most public tennis courts. These surfaces, typically made of acrylic layers over asphalt or concrete, were neither quite as dampening as clay nor quite as fast as grass. Hard Court Systems Ltd. (HCS) was a small company that manufactured and installed those acrylic layers in Australia. Right at the beginning of the 2025 fiscal year, HCS had taken a huge gamble and modernized its production facilities. The full-year 2025 financial results had just been made public, and an upcoming meeting of shareholders would undoubtedly focus on whether the restructuring had been successful. It fell to CFO Charles Walker to be ready for that discussion.

Despite the steady growth of tennis interest worldwide and the explosive growth of pickleball, which was played on the same surface, the manufacture of acrylic surface materials for hard courts was not a growth industry in Australia. The country had been relatively slow to emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic, and inflation had remained relatively high. Total revenue at HCS had grown only 4.3% and 4.9% over the prior two years, which was only about 1% higher than inflation. To achieve any reasonable growth, tennis-court-surface manufacturers had developed product lines that served similar surface needs, like outdoor running tracks or outdoor basketball courts. Some manufacturers had even developed materials used in swimming pools. Ultimately, the biggest hurdle for companies was finding ways to lower costs. With globalization bringing distant competitors into local markets and with new manufacturers entering on the merits of innovations related to color and durability, HCS had to contain costs in order to compete for volume through pricing, and, possibly, even to survive.

Restructuring

The overall objective of the restructuring was to lower production costs so HCS could improve margins. An expected side benefit was the reduction of inventory levels. The restructuring required capital expenditures of AUD1.2 million in 2025, which was more than double the usual level of nearly AUD500,000. As a result of all the investments and process changes, fixed costs rose dramatically: Annual fixed manufacturing costs in the cost of goods sold (COGS) doubled from AUD700,000 in 2024 to AUD2.2 million in 2025, and fixed costs in selling, general, and administrative (SGA) expenses rose from AUD1.1 million to AUD1.4 million.

title: ArboBank's Capital Game
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: ArboBank's Capital Game
detail.abstract:
This case was written to simulate the economic decisions that led to the 2008 financial crisis without explicitly referencing that crisis. It focuses on a fictional commercial bank that seeks to grow but is constrained by capital requirements. It simulates an executive committee meeting that ultimately makes the constraint less binding. The focus is on legitimate maneuvers within the scope of accounting rules that existed before the crisis.The case also includes a vignette about an investment bank increasingly funding itself using short-term repurchase agreements (repos). This is meant to capture another aspect of the 2008 financial crisis, specifically Lehman Brothers and the run on repos that led to Lehman Brothers' failure.

Excerpt

ArboBank's Capital Game

The executive committee of ArboBank, a large regional commercial bank, was meeting to discuss a familiar problem: growth. Loan demand was strong, margins were attractive, and competitors were expanding aggressively. Yet ArboBank's balance sheet was constrained. Under prevailing capital requirements, holding whole loans required substantial equity, which limited leverage and thus balance-sheet expansion. Chief Financial Officer Fiona Foster had asked the bank's structured finance team to draft a securitization deal that would optimize regulatory capital and unlock growth potential. According to Foster, ArboBank was not short of good loans—it was short of capital.

The Draft Proposal

ArboBank's loan book consisted mainly of commercial and industrial loans to middle-market firms and commercial real estate developers. The bank funded itself through a mix of insured retail deposits, uninsured wholesale funding, and unsecured term debt. Its credit performance had been strong for over a decade, with low charge-offs and conservative underwriting standards. ArboBank's Tier 1 capital ratio had declined steadily, however, as assets grew faster than retained earnings.

. . .
